questions.title: One six is enough
questions.prompt: Roll two independent fair six-sided dice. What is the probability that at least one is a six?
hints: Count the complement.
Neither die is a six with probability \(\left(\frac56\right)^2\).
questions.solution: The complement has probability \(\frac{25}{36}\). Subtract it from 1 to obtain \(\frac{11}{36}\). Adding \(\frac{1}{6}\) + \(\frac{1}{6}\) counts the double-six outcome twice.
questions.followup: Now roll n dice. How many are needed to make the probability exceed 90%?
questions.followSolution: Require \(\left(\frac56\right)^n<0.1\). Taking logs gives \(n>12.63\), so 13 dice.
rubric: Count the twenty-five no-six ordered outcomes and obtain \(\frac{11}{36}\).
Identify the double-six outcome counted twice by addition.
Use the independent n-dice complement and strict threshold to obtain thirteen.

questions.title: A sum changes the sample space
questions.prompt: Two independent fair dice have sum 8. Given this information, what is the probability that their values are equal?
hints: List ordered pairs with sum 8.
There are five possible ordered pairs.
questions.solution: The conditional sample space is (2,6), (3,5), (4,4), (5,3), (6,2). Only (4,4) is a double, so the answer is \(\frac{1}{5}\). Independence before conditioning does not imply independence after it.
questions.followup: What is the conditional mean of the first die?
questions.followSolution: By symmetry the two conditional means are equal and sum to 8, so each is 4.
rubric: List all five ordered sum-eight outcomes and justify equal conditional weights.
Obtain double probability one fifth without counting unordered records uniformly.
Use symmetry and the fixed sum to obtain conditional mean four.

questions.title: Learn which coin you picked
questions.prompt: Choose with equal probability between a fair coin and a coin that always lands heads. You flip the chosen coin once and see heads. What is the probability it is the always-heads coin?
hints: Write the likelihood under each coin.
The joint probabilities of selection and a head are \(\frac{1}{2}\) and \(\frac{1}{4}\).
questions.solution: The always-heads branch contributes \(\frac{1}{2}\) to the probability of heads. The fair branch contributes \(\frac{1}{4}\). Normalising gives \(\frac{1/2}{3/4}=\frac23\). The posterior is not the prior \(\frac{1}{2}\).
questions.followup: After k consecutive heads, derive the posterior.
questions.followSolution:
Keep the SAME chosen coin for all k flips, conditionally independent given its identity. The always-heads branch has joint mass one half; the fair branch has mass \((1/2)2^{-k}\). Normalising gives

\[P(\mathrm{always\ heads}\mid k\ \mathrm{heads})=\frac{1}{1+2^{-k}}.\]

At k=0 this recovers the equal prior; as k grows it tends to one without reaching certainty at any finite k. A tail rules out the always-heads coin under this exact model. Choosing a fresh coin before EACH flip would define a different inference problem.
rubric: Weight each coin’s head likelihood by its equal prior probability.
Normalise the joint masses one half and one quarter to obtain two thirds.
Derive the repeated-head posterior under a fixed coin and conditional independent flips.

questions.title: A promising signal with a low base rate
questions.prompt: Only 2% of candidate signals are genuinely useful. A test passes a useful signal with probability 90% and a useless one with probability 10%. Given a pass, what is the probability the signal is useful?
hints: Use base rates as well as test accuracy.
The two pass masses are \(0.02\times0.9\) and \(0.98\times0.1\).
questions.solution: \[P(\text{useful}\mid\text{pass})=\frac{0.018}{0.018+0.098}=\frac9{58}\approx0.15517.\] High sensitivity does not compensate for many false passes from the large useless population. This calculation assumes the stated base rate and test characteristics apply to the candidate pool.
questions.followup: If you independently run the test twice and both pass, what changes?
questions.followSolution: Under conditional independence given usefulness, the posterior is \[\frac{0.02\times0.9^2}{0.02\times0.9^2+0.98\times0.1^2}=\frac{81}{130}\approx0.62308.\] Independence is a substantive assumption.
rubric: Condition on the declared useful/useless population and construct both passing masses.
Normalize 0.018 by 0.116 to obtain \(\frac{9}{58}\), distinguishing sensitivity from posterior usefulness.
For repeated screens state conditional independence given usefulness; copied evidence cannot be squared.

questions.title: Without replacement
questions.prompt: An urn contains 6 red and 4 blue balls. Draw two uniformly without replacement. What is the probability that their colours differ?
hints: Count red-blue unordered pairs.
There are \(6\times4\) favourable pairs and \(\binom{10}{2}\) total pairs.
questions.solution: There are 24 mixed-colour pairs out of 45 possible pairs, giving \(\frac{8}{15}\). Alternatively sum \(\frac6{10}\frac49+\frac4{10}\frac69\). Replacement would change the second denominator.
questions.followup: Generalise to r red and b blue.
questions.followSolution:
Assume r,b are nonnegative integer counts and r+b≥2, with uniform physical sampling without replacement. Ordered mixed paths have probabilities \(r/(r+b)\) times \(b/(r+b-1)\), and the reverse product with r and b exchanged. Their sum is

\[\frac{2rb}{(r+b)(r+b-1)}.\]

It is zero if either colour is absent. Independent draws WITH replacement instead give \(2rb/(r+b)^2\). The record count and its denominator must follow the sampling procedure.
rubric: Count uniform physical pairs, with twenty-four mixed pairs out of forty-five.
Obtain \(\frac{8}{15}\) or the equivalent two ordered colour paths.
Derive the general formula with at least two balls and distinguish replacement.

questions.title: Overlapping heads
questions.prompt: Make 20 independent flips of a fair coin. Count adjacent HH pairs, allowing overlaps (HHH contains two pairs). What is the expected count?
hints: Create an indicator for each adjacent position.
Independence between the indicators is unnecessary for the mean.
questions.solution: There are 19 adjacent positions. Each indicator has expectation \(\frac{1}{4}\), so linearity gives \(\frac{19}{4}=4.75\). The indicators overlap, but linearity of expectation still holds.
questions.followup: For n flips, derive the variance of the count.
questions.followSolution: For \(n\geq2\), each indicator has variance \(\frac{3}{16}\); adjacent indicators have covariance \(\frac18-\frac1{16}=\frac1{16}\) and disjoint ones have covariance zero. The variance is \(\frac{3(n-1)+2(n-2)}{16}=\frac{5n-7}{16}\).
rubric: Use nineteen overlapping-pair indicators, each with mean one quarter.
Obtain \(\frac{19}{4}\) without assuming indicator independence.
Include adjacent covariance twice in the variance sum and handle short sequences.

questions.title: The larger die
questions.prompt: Roll two independent fair six-sided dice. What is the expected maximum?
hints: Use \(P(\max=k)\), or a tail sum.
\(P(\max\leq k)=\frac{k^2}{36}\).
questions.solution: \(P(\max=k)=\frac{k^2-(k-1)^2}{36}=\frac{2k-1}{36}\). Sum \(\frac{k(2k-1)}{36}\) from 1 to 6 to get \(\frac{161}{36}\approx4.47222\). A maximum is not the maximum of the means.
questions.followup: What is the expected minimum?
questions.followSolution: max+min equals the sum pointwise. Thus \(\mathbb E[\min]=7-\frac{161}{36}=\frac{91}{36}\).
rubric: Derive the maximum CDF from two independent die crossings.
Difference the CDF and sum to obtain \(\frac{161}{36}\).
Use the pointwise maximum-plus-minimum identity to obtain \(\frac{91}{36}\).

questions.title: The first uniform point
questions.prompt: Draw three independent \(\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\) values. What is the expected minimum?
hints: Integrate the survival function.
\(P(\min>x)=(1-x)^3\) for \(0\leq x\leq1\).
questions.solution: For a nonnegative variable, \(\mathbb E[M]=\int P(M>x)\,dx\). Here \(\int_0^1(1-x)^3\,dx=\frac14\). In general the minimum of n independent \(\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\) values has mean \(\frac{1}{n+1}\).
questions.followup: Find \(\mathbb E[\max]\) and its CDF.
questions.followSolution:
For the maximum M, all three independent draws must be at most x. Thus its CDF is zero for x<0, \(x^3\) for \(0\leq x\leq1\) and one for x>1. The nonnegative tail identity gives

\[E[M]=\int_0^1(1-x^3)\,dx=\frac34.\]

The minimum CDF is \(1-(1-x)^3\) on the same support, not x³. Reflecting each uniform draw around one also maps the maximum to one minus the minimum, checking that the two expectations sum to one.
rubric: Derive minimum survival (1−x)³ on the stated unit support.
Integrate survival to obtain one quarter.
Derive the maximum CDF, including its support boundaries, and mean three quarters.

questions.title: Collect all four
questions.prompt: Each independent draw returns one of four equally likely symbols. How many draws do you expect before seeing all four?
hints: Split the wait into stages after each new symbol.
The success probabilities are 1, \(\frac{3}{4}\), \(\frac{1}{2}\), \(\frac{1}{4}\).
questions.solution: The expected stage lengths are 1, \(\frac{4}{3}\), 2, 4. Their sum is \(\frac{25}{3}\). Geometric waiting times need not be identically distributed for their expectations to add.
questions.followup: Generalise to m equally likely symbols.
questions.followSolution: The mean is \(m\left(1+\frac12+\cdots+\frac1m\right)\). Unequal probabilities require a different argument; replacing them by their average is invalid.
rubric: Describe the four discovery stages and their success probabilities.
Count the successful draw in each geometric wait and obtain \(\frac{25}{3}\).
Derive the harmonic-sum generalisation without replacing unequal probabilities by their average.

questions.title: Wait for a head then a tail
questions.prompt: Make independent flips of a fair coin until the consecutive pattern HT appears. What is the expected number of flips?
hints: Track whether the latest flip was H.
Write one recurrence from the empty state and one from H.
questions.solution: Let \(E_0\) be the wait from no useful suffix and \(E_H\) from suffix H. \(E_0=1+\frac{E_0+E_H}{2}\) and \(E_H=1+\frac{E_H}{2}\). Thus \(E_H=2\) and \(E_0=4\). Repeated H leaves you in the H state.
questions.followup: Why does HH have a different wait?
questions.followSolution: For HH, \(E_H=1+\frac{E_0}{2}\). Solve with the same \(E_0\) equation to get \(E_0=6\). A tail destroys the partial match.
rubric: Define empty and trailing-head states and both first-step recurrences.
Explain the head self-loop and derive expectation four.
Change the reset transition for HH and obtain expectation six.

questions.title: Three heads in a row
questions.prompt: Make independent flips of a fair coin until HHH first appears. Find the expected total number of flips, including the final three.
hints: Use states with 0, 1 and 2 trailing heads.
A tail sends every nonterminal state to state 0.
questions.solution: The stated recurrences give \(E_1=E_0-2\) and \(E_2=1+\frac{E_0}{2}\). Substitution yields \(E_0-2=1+\frac{1+1.5E_0}{2}\), so \(E_0=14\). The shortcut \(\frac1{P(HHH)}=8\) treats overlapping trials as disjoint independent attempts.
questions.followup: Generalise to k heads with head probability p.
questions.followSolution:
Let k≥1 and let E_j be the expected additional flips from j trailing heads, with E_k=0. With independent flips of head probability \(0<p<1\), every nonterminal state satisfies

\[E_j=1+pE_{j+1}+(1-p)E_0.\]

Unroll from j=0 through the k states:

\[E_0=\left(\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}p^j\right)[1+(1-p)E_0].\]

Since \((1-p)\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}p^j=1-p^k\), moving the \(E_0\) term to the left yields

\[E_0=\frac{1-p^k}{(1-p)p^k}.\]

The mean is finite: every independent disjoint block of k flips has probability p^k of being all heads, so the true stopping time is bounded above by k times a geometric block count. This validates the expectation equations; overlapping windows themselves are not independent trials. At \(p=1\) the wait is exactly k, matching the continuous limit. At p=0 the target never occurs and the expected wait is infinite.
rubric: Define trailing-head states and terminal expectation zero.
Derive expectation fourteen from first-step equations, including every final flip.
Derive the k-head formula and its p=0/\(p=1\) boundaries without treating overlapping windows as trials.

questions.title: Exit a fair random walk
questions.prompt: A simple symmetric random walk starts at 5 on the integers and stops on first hitting 0 or 12. What is its expected stopping time?
hints: The mean solves \(t_i=1+\frac{t_{i-1}+t_{i+1}}2\).
Use boundary conditions \(t_0=t_{12}=0\).
Try a quadratic in i.
questions.solution:
Write t_i for expected additional steps from integer i. The boundaries are absorbing, so t₀=t₁₂=0. For an interior state, one step is taken before the remaining wait:

\[t_i=1+\tfrac12t_{i-1}+\tfrac12t_{i+1}.\]

Finite expectation is justified independently. From any interior state, twelve consecutive downward moves would hit zero within twelve steps and have probability at least 2⁻¹². Conditional on any surviving history, a new twelve-step block has at least this exit chance. Hence the block survival tail is bounded by a geometric tail, giving finite expected exit time.

Rearrange the recurrence to \(t_{i+1}-2t_i+t_{i-1}=-2\). Its general quadratic solution is \(t_i=-i^2+ai+b\); the two boundaries force b=0 and a=12. Therefore \(t_i=i(12-i)\) and t₅=35. Uniqueness follows because the difference of two solutions has zero second difference and zero boundary values, so is the zero affine function. A distance-to-nearest-boundary shortcut misses the repeated backtracking.
questions.followup: What is the probability of hitting 12 first?
questions.followSolution: Let p_i be the probability of hitting twelve before zero. First-step conditioning now gives \(p_i=(p_{i-1}+p_{i+1})/2\), with p₀=0 and p₁₂=1. There is NO added one-step time cost in this probability equation. Zero second difference makes p_i affine; the boundaries give p_i=\(\frac{i}{12}\). Starting at five gives \(\frac{5}{12}\). This is the chance of one exit side, not the expected elapsed time.
rubric: Specify absorbing boundaries and the expected-time difference equation.
Justify finite expected exit time and derive i(12−i), giving thirty-five.
Solve the distinct harmonic hitting-probability equation to obtain five twelfths.

questions.title: One reroll
questions.prompt: Roll a fair die and observe it. Either keep the value or discard it and roll once more, whose value you must accept. What is the optimal expected payoff?
hints: Compare each observed value with the mean of a fresh roll.
Keep 4, 5, 6; reroll 1, 2, 3.
questions.solution: The continuation value is 3.5. The expected optimum is \(\frac{3\times3.5+4+5+6}{6}=4.25\). The realised second roll can be worse, but the decision is based on conditional expectation.
questions.followup: If a reroll costs 1, what is the optimal value?
questions.followSolution: Continuation is 2.5. Reroll 1 and 2, keep 3 through 6. \(\text{Mean}=\frac{2\times2.5+3+4+5+6}{6}=\frac{23}{6}\).
rubric: Compare each observed value with continuation 3.5; keep 4,5,6 and reroll 1,2,3.
Average the conditional maxima to \(\frac{17}{4}\); do not move the maximum outside the expectation.
Charge a one-unit cost only on reroll branches to obtain threshold 2.5 and value \(\frac{23}{6}\).

questions.title: Three pieces, one triangle
questions.prompt: Choose two independent \(\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\) cut locations on a unit stick. Cut at both. What is the probability the three lengths form a nondegenerate triangle?
hints: A triangle exists iff no piece is at least half the stick.
Order the cuts \(U<V\); the three pieces are \(U,\ V-U,\ 1-V\).
Measure the valid region inside \(0<U<V<1\).
questions.solution:
Write U for the smaller cut location and V for the larger. Ordering two independent uniform cuts gives density TWO on the triangle \(0<U<V<1\): each ordered pair comes from two equally dense original orders, except a zero-probability diagonal. The piece lengths are U, V−U and 1−V. With total length one, the strict triangle inequalities are equivalent to every piece being less than one half. Thus

\[U<\tfrac12,\quad V>\tfrac12,\quad V<U+\tfrac12.\]

For a fixed U in (0,\(\frac{1}{2}\)), valid V runs from \(\frac{1}{2}\) to U+\(\frac{1}{2}\), an interval of length U. The valid region’s area is

\[\int_0^{1/2}U\,dU=\frac18.\]

Multiply by ordered density two, or divide by total ordered-region area one half, to obtain probability one quarter. Strict equality boundaries have probability zero under this continuous procedure. Counting three possible piece positions uniformly would not define their joint length distribution.
questions.followup: Instead, make one uniform cut on the unit stick; choose one of the resulting TWO pieces with equal probability, independently of its length; cut that chosen piece at a uniform location within it. Is the triangle probability still one quarter? Derive it for this explicitly stated procedure.
questions.followSolution:
Let the first left-piece length be u, uniform on (0,1). If u>\(\frac{1}{2}\), only choosing the left (longer) piece can succeed, because leaving it uncut violates the triangle condition. That choice has probability one half. Given it, the new cut coordinate z must satisfy u−\(\frac{1}{2}\)<z<\(\frac{1}{2}\) inside (0,u). Its success probability is (1−u)/u. If u<\(\frac{1}{2}\), choosing the right piece instead gives the symmetric condition and probability u/(1−u). Therefore

\[\begin{aligned}P(\mathrm{triangle})&=2\cdot\frac12\int_{1/2}^1\frac{1-u}{u}\,du\\&=\log 2-\frac12\\&\approx0.193147.\end{aligned}\]

The equal choice between pieces is NOT equal choice between physical locations on the whole stick: a shorter piece concentrates the conditional cut density more strongly. The new cuts therefore are not two independent uniform locations. This comparison changes the sampling measure, not the strict geometric triangle criterion.
rubric: Order the two independent uniform cut locations and retain the correct density.
Translate strict triangle inequalities into a region of area one eighth and probability one quarter.
Derive the explicitly different sequential-cut probability log(2)−\(\frac{1}{2}\) and explain its weighting.

questions.title: A memoryless wait
questions.prompt: A waiting time is Exponential with rate \(\frac{1}{2}\) per minute. Given that you have already waited 3 minutes, what is the expected total waiting time in minutes?
hints: Distinguish total time from remaining time.
The expected remaining time is \(\frac1{\text{rate}}\).
questions.solution: Memorylessness gives \(\mathbb E[T-3\mid T>3]=2\). The expected total is \(3+2=5\). Memorylessness is specific to this model; an arbitrary wait distribution does not have it.
questions.followup: What is \(P(T>7\mid T>3)\)?
rubric: Apply memorylessness to the remaining time, whose mean is two minutes.
Add the three elapsed minutes to obtain total expectation five.
Use a four-minute conditional survival interval to obtain exp(−2).

questions.title: Which clock rings first?
questions.prompt: Independent exponential clocks have rates 3 and 2. What is the probability that the rate-3 clock rings first?
hints: Integrate \(f_X(t)P(Y>t)\).
The integrand is \(3e^{-5t}\).
questions.solution: \(\int_0^\infty3e^{-3t}e^{-2t}\,dt=\frac35\). The minimum has rate 5. Ties have probability zero.
questions.followup: Are the winning clock and the time of the first ring independent?
questions.followSolution: Yes for independent exponential clocks with constant rates. The joint density of winner 1 and time t is \(3e^{-5t}\), which factors into \(\frac{3}{5}\) times \(5e^{-5t}\).
rubric: Integrate the rate-three density times the independent rate-two survival.
Obtain winning probability three fifths and first-ring rate five.
Factor the joint winner/time density and identify constant rates as an essential assumption.

questions.title: Correlation survives averaging
questions.prompt: One hundred variables each have variance 1. Every distinct pair has correlation 0.1. What is the variance of their arithmetic mean?
hints: Expand the variance of a sum, including off-diagonal terms.
There are \(n(n-1)\) ordered covariance terms.
questions.solution: \[\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)=\frac{n+n(n-1)\rho}{n^2}=\rho+\frac{1-\rho}{n}=0.109.\] The independence shortcut gives 0.01 and misses the common component.
questions.followup: What happens as n grows?
questions.followSolution:
For fixed nonnegative equicorrelation \(\rho\), the mean variance is \(\rho+(1-\rho)/n\), tending to \(\rho\). At \(\rho=0.1\) it therefore tends to 0.1, not zero. A representation \(X_i=\mu_i+\sqrt{\rho}Z+\sqrt{1-\rho}\,\varepsilon_i\), using mutually independent unit-variance centered variables, shows the common shock that averaging retains.

For a fixed dimension \(n\geq2\), the unit-variance equicorrelation matrix has eigenvalue 1+(\(n-1\))\(\rho\) on the all-ones direction and 1−\(\rho\) on directions perpendicular to it. Nonnegative variance in every direction requires

\[-\frac{1}{n-1}\leq\rho\leq1.\]

A fixed negative \(\rho\) cannot satisfy this condition for arbitrarily large n. The limit with fixed \(\rho\) is meaningful only along feasible covariance models; the positive common-factor representation above does not apply to negative \(\rho\).
rubric: Include all ordered off-diagonal covariances in the mean variance.
Obtain 0.109 and explain why independent averaging would give a different result.
Take the fixed-correlation limit and derive feasible equicorrelation bounds.

questions.title: A hundred dependent observations
questions.prompt: A stationary AR(1) series has lag-one autocorrelation \(\rho=0.8\) and marginal variance \(\sigma^2\). Define effective sample size by equating the mean-estimation variance to \(\frac{\sigma^2}{n_{\mathrm{eff}}}\). Derive the large-sample approximation, then report \(n_{\mathrm{eff}}\) for \(n=100\). Use the asymptotic result, not the finite-n tapered correction.
hints: The autocorrelation at lag k is \(\rho^k\).
The variance inflation factor is \(1+2\sum_{k=1}^\infty\rho^k=\frac{1+\rho}{1-\rho}\).
questions.solution:
For the usual stationary AR(1) covariance structure, \(\gamma_h=\gamma_0\rho^h\). Expanding all covariance pairs in the sample mean gives

\[\operatorname{Var}(\bar X_n)=\frac{\gamma_0}{n}\left[1+2\sum_{h=1}^{n-1}(1-h/n)\rho^h\right].\]

At fixed \(|\rho|<1\) and growing n, the bracket tends to the convergent geometric-sum factor \(1+2\rho/(1-\rho)=(1+\rho)/(1-\rho)\). Matching this asymptotic variance to γ₀/\(n_{\mathrm{eff}}\) gives

\[n_{eff}\approx\frac{n(1-\rho)}{1+\rho}.\]

For \(n=100\) and \(\rho=0.8\) this is \(\frac{100}{9}\)≈11.11. This is the requested fixed-correlation large-sample approximation for the MEAN, not the exact finite-window value or an independent-sample representation for every statistic. Keeping the lag taper answers the separate finite-n follow-up.
questions.followup: Write the exact finite-n variance factor.
questions.followSolution: \[\frac{\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)}{\gamma_0/n}=1+2\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\left(1-\frac{k}{n}\right)\rho^k.\] The taper matters in short samples or near unit roots.
rubric: Derive the covariance-pair count and the fixed-rho asymptotic variance factor.
Report \(\frac{100}{9}\) for the requested asymptotic mean-estimation comparison.
Give the finite-sample taper and explain its limits near a unit root.

questions.title: Measurement error shrinks a slope
questions.prompt: Let \(Y=2X+\varepsilon\). You observe \(W=X+u\). X,u,ε are mutually independent, centred, with finite second moments, with \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=1\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(u)=3\). What is the population OLS slope of Y on W with an intercept?
hints: The slope is \(\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(W,Y)}{\operatorname{Var}(W)}\).
The numerator is 2 and denominator 4.
questions.solution: \(\operatorname{Cov}(W,Y)=2\operatorname{Var}(X)=2\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(W)=1+3=4\), hence slope \(\frac{1}{2}\). Independent measurement error in the regressor attenuates the slope; error in the response alone would not.
questions.followup: What if u is correlated with ε?
questions.followSolution: The numerator gains \(\operatorname{Cov}(u,\varepsilon)\). The attenuation conclusion can fail, including sign reversal. Independence was doing real work.
rubric: Derive covariance two and observed predictor variance four under the stated independence assumptions.
Obtain the population slope \(\frac{1}{2}\) and explain which latent coefficient it differs from.
When measurement and response noise covary, include that covariance in the numerator rather than assuming attenuation.

questions.title: Three correlations must fit together
questions.prompt: Standardised variables X,Y,Z satisfy \(\operatorname{Corr}(X,Y)=\operatorname{Corr}(Y,Z)=0.8\). What is the smallest possible \(\operatorname{Corr}(X,Z)\)?
hints: The correlation matrix must be positive semidefinite.
Let \[a=\operatorname{Corr}(X,Y),\quad b=\operatorname{Corr}(Y,Z),\quad c=\operatorname{Corr}(X,Z).\]
The determinant gives \((c-ab)^2\leq(1-a^2)(1-b^2)\).
questions.solution:
Write \[a=\operatorname{Corr}(X,Y),\quad b=\operatorname{Corr}(Y,Z),\quad c=\operatorname{Corr}(X,Z).\] Standardisation gives unit variances. Remove the shared Y projection: residuals X−aY and Z−bY have variances 1−a² and 1−b² and covariance c−ab. Cauchy–Schwarz therefore requires

\[(c-ab)^2\leq(1-a^2)(1-b^2).\]

Here a=b=0.8, so the residual standard deviations are both 0.6 and c must lie in [0.64−0.36,0.64+0.36]=[0.28,1]. The smallest feasible value is 0.28. It is ATTAINED by giving the two residuals opposite signs of the same standardised random variable independent of Y, as constructed in the follow-up. Thus this is a sharp bound, not just a necessary pairwise condition. At the lower endpoint the joint covariance is singular.
questions.followup: Construct variables attaining the minimum.
questions.followSolution: Take independent standardised Y,U and set \(X=0.8Y+0.6U\), \(Z=0.8Y-0.6U\). Then \(\operatorname{Corr}(X,Z)=0.64-0.36=0.28\).
rubric: Use collective PSD or residual Cauchy–Schwarz, rather than pairwise bounds alone.
Derive the lower bound 0.28 and distinguish feasible singularity from invalidity.
Give the explicit variance-one construction attaining the bound.

questions.title: Residuals sum to zero
questions.prompt: You fit OLS with an intercept. Explain why the residuals sum to zero, and why this need not hold without an intercept.
hints: Write the derivative of squared error with respect to the intercept.
Equivalently use \(X^{\mathsf T}r=0\).
questions.solution: At a least-squares optimum, differentiating \(\sum_i(y_i-a-b^{\mathsf T}x_i)^2\) with respect to a gives \(-2\sum_i r_i=0\). In matrix terms, residuals are orthogonal to every design column, including the all-ones intercept column. Without that column there is no such normal equation.
questions.followup: Does zero residual mean imply the model is unbiased out of sample?
questions.followSolution: No. It is an in-sample algebraic property. Misspecification, leakage or a changed distribution can produce arbitrarily biased future predictions.
rubric: Differentiate with respect to the unpenalized intercept to derive the zero residual sum.
Identify the intercept column in the normal equations and explain why removing it removes that constraint.
Separate an in-sample stationarity identity from unbiased predictions on future data.

checks.prompt: Without an intercept, fit y=(1,3) on the single column x=(1,2). What is the sum of the fitted residuals?
checks.explanation: The slope is \(\frac{7}{5}\); residuals are −\(\frac{2}{5}\) and \(\frac{1}{5}\).

checks.prompt: Which statements follow from the least-squares normal equations?

options.text: Without an intercept, the residual sum can never be zero.
options.explanation: It can happen accidentally, for example with an exact fit.
options.label: Without an intercept, the residual sum can never be zero.

options.text: With a free intercept, the constant vector belongs to the design space, so \(\mathbf1^Tr=0\).
options.explanation: Residuals are orthogonal to every design column.
options.label: With a free intercept, the constant vector belongs to the design space, so the sum of residuals is zero.

options.text: The identity \(X^Tr=0\) concerns the training fit; it does not force the mean prediction error on new data to vanish.
options.explanation: There is no normal-equation constraint on unseen responses.
options.label: X transpose times residuals equals zero for the training fit; it does not force the mean prediction error on new data to vanish.

options.text: Zero residual sum establishes that the model is correctly specified.
options.explanation: This is an algebraic property, even for a misspecified regression.
options.label: Zero residual sum establishes that the model is correctly specified.

questions.title: A reversal after pooling
questions.prompt: Can a treatment have a higher success rate in each of two groups but a lower success rate overall? Construct a numerical example and explain the mechanism.
hints: Use different group weights for treatment and control.
Place most treatment observations in the harder group.
questions.solution: Example: easy group treatment \(\frac{9}{10}\) versus control \(\frac{80}{100}\); hard group treatment \(\frac{20}{100}\) versus control \(\frac{1}{10}\). Treatment wins within each (\(90\%>80\%,\quad20\%>10\%\)), but overall treatment is \(\frac{29}{110}\approx26.4\%\) and control \(\frac{81}{110}\approx73.6\%\). Group composition confounds the pooled comparison.
questions.followup: Does adjusting for every available variable fix causal inference?
questions.followSolution: No. Conditioning on colliders can introduce bias, and unmeasured confounding remains possible. Adjustment needs a causal argument.
rubric: Give valid success counts and nonzero denominators with treatment ahead in both groups.
Compute the pooled reversal and identify the different population weights.
Explain why adjustment needs a causal argument, including collider and unmeasured-confounding risks.

checks.prompt: Use this table: easy group A=\(\frac{81}{90}\) successes, B=\(\frac{19}{20}\); difficult group A=\(\frac{2}{10}\), B=\(\frac{18}{80}\). What is overall A success rate minus overall B success rate?
checks.explanation: A=\(\frac{83}{100}\); B=\(\frac{37}{100}\). B beats A within each group but has more difficult cases.

checks.prompt: Which conclusions about the pooling reversal are valid?

options.text: The displayed reversal requires either within-group rate to have been miscomputed.
options.explanation: All four rates can be correct simultaneously.
options.label: The displayed reversal requires either within-group rate to have been miscomputed.

options.text: A pooled rate uses treatment-specific group weights; different weights can reverse both within-group comparisons.
options.explanation: The two pooled quantities need not average with the same coefficients.
options.label: A pooled rate uses treatment-specific group weights; different weights can reverse both within-group comparisons.

options.text: If both treatments were averaged with the same positive group weights, strict within-group dominance would survive pooling.
options.explanation: Subtract the two weighted averages term by term.
options.label: If both treatments were averaged with the same positive group weights, strict within-group dominance would survive pooling.

options.text: This table proves A has a larger causal treatment effect.
options.explanation: Assignment and confounding have not been identified.
options.label: This table proves A has a larger causal treatment effect.

questions.title: Estimate the end of a uniform interval
questions.prompt: You observe \(n=4\) iid \(\operatorname{Uniform}(0,\theta)\) values. The sample maximum is 8. Multiply it by the appropriate factor to obtain an unbiased estimator of \(\theta\). What estimate do you get?
hints: \(\mathbb E[\max]=\frac{n\theta}{n+1}\).
Multiply by \(\frac{n+1}{n}\).
questions.solution: The maximum has CDF \(\left(\frac m\theta\right)^n\) on \([0,\theta]\) and mean \(\frac{n\theta}{n+1}\). The unbiased estimator is \(\frac{(n+1)\max}{n}\). At \(n=4,\quad\max=8\) it equals 10. The maximum itself is the MLE but is biased down.
questions.followup: Is unbiasedness alone enough to choose an estimator?
questions.followSolution: Unbiasedness describes mean error, not squared-error risk. In the declared iid uniform model, write M for the sample maximum; its second moment is \(E[M^2]=n\theta^2/(n+2)\). For estimates cM, completing the quadratic squared-error risk gives the minimum at c=(n+2)/(n+1), with risk \(\theta\)²/(n+1)². The unbiased choice c=\(\frac{n+1}{n}\) has risk \(\theta\)²/[n(n+2)], which is larger. At \(n=4\) those risks are \(\theta\)²/25 and \(\theta\)²/24; the corresponding estimates at M=8 are 9.6 and ten. This compares a specified estimator family under squared loss, not every possible loss or sampling model. The numeric question still asks the UNBIASED estimate ten.
rubric: Derive the maximum distribution and its expectation under iid uniform sampling.
Use the factor five fourths to obtain estimate ten.
Compare squared-error risks rather than assuming unbiasedness alone is decisive.

questions.title: The unbiased variance divisor
questions.prompt: For iid observations with finite variance \(\sigma^2\), explain why \(\frac1n\sum_i(X_i-\bar X)^2\) is biased down, and derive the unbiased correction.
hints: Use \(\sum_i(X_i-\bar X)^2=\sum_i(X_i-\mu)^2-n(\bar X-\mu)^2\).
Take expectations and use \(\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)=\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\).
questions.solution: Use \(\sum_i(X_i-\bar X)^2=\sum_i(X_i-\mu)^2-n(\bar X-\mu)^2\). The expectation of the first term is \(n\sigma^2\) and that of the subtracted term is \(n\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)=\sigma^2\), so the sum has expectation \((n-1)\sigma^2\). Dividing by \(n-1\) gives an unbiased estimator for n>1. Normality is not needed for this expectation identity.
questions.followup: What breaks for correlated data?
questions.followSolution: Var(X̄) is no longer \(\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\). The same identity holds, but the familiar divisor does not generally remove the bias.
rubric: Derive the centred-sum identity and use iid finite-variance sampling to get expectation \((n-1)\sigma^2\).
Require n>1 for the corrected divisor; distinguish unbiased variance from unbiased standard deviation.
Explain that dependence changes Var(sample mean), so the same \(n-1\) correction is not generally unbiased.

checks.prompt: For n=5 and \(\sigma^2=9\), what is the expectation of the variance computed with divisor n?
checks.explanation: Its expectation is (\(n-1\))\(\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\).

checks.prompt: Select the valid derivation and boundary claims.

options.text: \(\sum_i(X_i-\bar X)^2=\sum_i(X_i-\mu)^2-n(\bar X-\mu)^2\).
options.explanation: Expand both sides around the population mean.
options.label: Sum of squared deviations from the sample mean equals sum of squared deviations from mu minus n times the squared sample-mean error.

options.text: The correction depends on the observations having a normal distribution.
options.explanation: Iid observations and finite variance suffice.
options.label: The correction depends on the observations having a normal distribution.

options.text: For n=1, replacing the denominator by \(n-1\) gives a well-defined unbiased variance estimate.
options.explanation: The centred sum is zero and the proposed denominator is zero.
options.label: For n=1, replacing the denominator by n−1 gives a well-defined unbiased variance estimate.

options.text: For n>1, dividing the centred sum by \(n-1\) gives an unbiased variance estimator.
options.explanation: The sample-mean term has expectation \(\sigma^2\).
options.label: For n>1, dividing the centred sum by n−1 gives an unbiased variance estimator.

questions.title: At least one false discovery
questions.prompt: You run 20 independent tests of true null hypotheses. Each has an EXACT true-null rejection probability of 5%. What is the probability that at least one rejects?
hints: Work with the complement.
Independence is explicitly assumed.
questions.solution: The probability of no rejection is \(0.95^{20}\). The complement is about 0.641514. A single-test error rate is not a familywise error rate. Dependence changes the exact calculation.
questions.followup: Give a threshold that controls familywise error at 5% without independence.
questions.followSolution: Bonferroni uses \(\frac{0.05}{20}=0.0025\) per test. The union bound gives control for arbitrary dependence, assuming valid individual p-values.
rubric: Use independence of rejection decisions and complement the event of no rejections.
Obtain 1−0.95^20; a nominal level alone supplies an upper bound, not necessarily equality.
Justify Bonferroni by the union bound without requiring independence.

questions.title: A p-value is not a posterior
questions.prompt: A paper reports \(p=0.03\). Is there a 97% probability its hypothesis is true? Define the p-value precisely and identify the missing ingredients for a posterior probability.
hints: The conditioning is on the null model, not the observed data.
A posterior needs a prior and an alternative likelihood.
questions.solution: A p-value is the probability, under the specified null and test procedure, of a statistic at least as extreme as observed. It is not \(P(\text{null}\mid\text{data})\). A posterior needs prior model probabilities and likelihoods under null and alternatives. Selection and multiple tests also affect interpretation.
questions.followup: Does a large p-value establish the null?
questions.followSolution: No. The test may have low power. Equivalence or noninferiority questions need their own margins and tests.
rubric: Define the p-value under a specified null, statistic and extremeness rule.
Distinguish the probability of extreme data under the null from a posterior hypothesis probability.
Identify prior model probabilities and alternative likelihoods, and explain why a large p-value need not establish equivalence.

checks.prompt: Which interpretations of \(p=0.03\) are valid?

options.text: A posterior comparison needs prior model weights and likelihoods under the models being compared.
options.explanation: Bayes normalization uses both likelihoods and prior masses.
options.label: A posterior comparison needs prior model weights and likelihoods under the models being compared.

options.text: The null is false with posterior probability 0.97.
options.explanation: A p-value is not a posterior model probability.
options.label: The null is false with posterior probability 0.97.

options.text: Under the specified null law, the pre-specified statistic is at least as extreme as the observed statistic with probability 0.03.
options.explanation: Extremeness and the null sampling model must be declared.
options.label: Under the specified null law, the pre-specified statistic is at least as extreme as the observed statistic with probability 0.03.

options.text: Repeating this experiment has a 3% chance of reproducing its result.
options.explanation: The p-value does not specify replication probability.
options.label: Repeating this experiment has a 3% chance of reproducing its result.

checks.prompt: For a separate model comparison, take P(H1)=0.1, P(D|H1)=0.8 and P(D|H0)=0.2. Compute P(H1|D). These are event likelihoods, not the reported p-value.

questions.title: Random folds on overlapping labels
questions.prompt: Every sample at time t predicts the return from t to t+5. A researcher randomly splits rows into train and test and gets excellent results. Diagnose at least three problems and design a replacement validation scheme.
hints: Think label intervals, temporal dependence and preprocessing.
A training label may include outcomes inside a test interval.
Separate model selection from the final performance estimate.
questions.solution: Random splitting can put overlapping label outcomes in both sets; it can train on regimes after the tested date; and full-sample preprocessing or tuning can leak test information. Use chronological walk-forward splits, purge training labels whose intervals overlap test-label information, fit transforms only within each training fold, and keep a final untouched holdout. An embargo can add a gap for further dependence, chosen from the information horizon.
questions.followup: Why is merely shuffling less aggressively insufficient?
questions.followSolution: It does not explicitly remove label overlap or enforce a deployment-time information set. Validation must correspond to what was knowable at prediction time.
rubric: Diagnose shared target outcomes, future-to-past training and fitted-transform/selection leakage separately.
Specify decision-time availability, target-interval endpoint conventions, chronological refits and fold-local transformations.
Separate inner selection from outer evaluation and final reserved evidence; justify any extra embargo rather than asserting independence.

checks.prompt: Which flaws can make the original random-row validation unsuitable for deployment?

options.text: Keeping exactly five rows between splits guarantees safety for any timestamp spacing and receipt delay.
options.explanation: Time intervals and availability matter, not a fixed row count.
options.label: Keeping exactly five rows between splits guarantees safety for any timestamp spacing and receipt delay.

options.text: Preprocessing or feature selection fitted before splitting creates an additional leakage channel.
options.explanation: Learned transforms are part of the fitted procedure.
options.label: Preprocessing or feature selection fitted before splitting creates an additional leakage channel.

options.text: Training and validation targets can share the same underlying returns.
options.explanation: Their five-period label intervals overlap.
options.label: Training and validation targets can share the same underlying returns.

options.text: A training row later in time can use information unavailable at an earlier test decision.
options.explanation: Random row placement is not a historical fit cutoff.
options.label: A training row later in time can use information unavailable at an earlier test decision.

checks.prompt: Select the valid replacement requirements.

options.text: Fit transforms inside training folds and reserve final evaluation from model-selection decisions.
options.explanation: Both preprocessing and adaptive selection must respect the split.
options.label: Fit transforms inside training folds and reserve final evaluation from model-selection decisions.

options.text: Evaluate past-to-future fits using only labels mature and available by each fit cutoff.
options.explanation: A label end timestamp alone need not be its receipt time.
options.label: Evaluate past-to-future fits using only labels mature and available by each fit cutoff.

options.text: An embargo repairs every source of information leakage automatically.
options.explanation: Embargo is one boundary control, not a proof of pipeline validity.
options.label: An embargo repairs every source of information leakage automatically.

options.text: Purging overlap alone makes future training rows permissible.
options.explanation: Disjoint future rows still violate historical availability.
options.label: Purging overlap alone makes future training rows permissible.

questions.title: A fitted scaler leaks quietly
questions.prompt: You split chronologically but fit a normalisation transform on the entire series before training. Explain the leakage and give a correct pipeline.
hints: Preprocessing learns parameters too.
The test distribution has influenced the training representation.
questions.solution: The full-series mean and scale incorporate future test observations. Fit each transform on training data, apply it unchanged to validation/test, and repeat inside every model-selection fold. After selection, refit on permitted pre-holdout data only.
questions.followup: Is using a rolling normaliser always safe?
questions.followSolution: Only if each value uses data available then, with an appropriate shift. A centred window or same-time data unavailable at execution leaks.
rubric: Identify the full-series fitted parameters as future information, without asserting every model benefits from every affine leak.
Fit preprocessing inside each eligible training fold and freeze it for the corresponding evaluation decisions.
Check receipt times, shifts and fitted state when claiming a rolling transformation is causal.

checks.prompt: Training values are 0 and 2; the later test value is 100. Use population mean/variance scaling. What is the correctly scaled test value?
checks.explanation: Training mean=1 and standard deviation=1.

checks.prompt: Which pipeline statements are correct?

options.text: Refitting the scaler separately on the test set is the normal deployment evaluation of the same trained model.
options.explanation: It changes the coordinate system relative to training.
options.label: Refitting the scaler separately on the test set is the normal deployment evaluation of the same trained model.

options.text: A transform that ignores target labels cannot leak information.
options.explanation: Future feature distribution information can leak too.
options.label: A transform that ignores target labels cannot leak information.

options.text: Past-only online updating can be evaluated if that updating rule is part of the declared deployed procedure.
options.explanation: Availability and the pre-specified algorithm determine validity.
options.label: Past-only online updating can be evaluated if that updating rule is part of the declared deployed procedure.

options.text: Fit the scaler on the training fold, then apply its frozen parameters to that fold’s validation observations.
options.explanation: Validation values must not affect learned parameters.
options.label: Fit the scaler on the training fold, then apply its frozen parameters to that fold’s validation observations.

questions.title: Minimum-variance combination
questions.prompt: Two unbiased independent estimates of the same mean have variances 1 and 4. Combine them as \(wX+(1-w)Y\). What weight w minimises variance?
hints: Minimise \(w^2+4(1-w)^2\).
Differentiate and solve.
questions.solution: The derivative is \(2w-8(1-w)=0\), yielding \(w=\frac45\). The resulting variance is 0.8. Greater weight goes to the more precise estimator. Independence and common target are required.
questions.followup: With covariance c, derive the weight.
questions.followSolution: \(w=\frac{v_Y-c}{v_X+v_Y-2c}\), provided the denominator is positive. The optimum can lie outside [0,1] if unrestricted weights are allowed.
rubric: Use common-target unbiasedness and independence in the variance expression.
Derive weight \(\frac{4}{5}\) and the resulting variance \(\frac{4}{5}\).
For dependent estimates, include covariance and check the difference-variance denominator and permitted weights.

questions.title: Ridge changes the geometry
questions.prompt: For objective \(\lVert y-X\beta\rVert^2+\lambda\lVert\beta\rVert^2\) with \(\lambda>0\), derive \(\hat\beta\). Explain what happens along a nearly singular direction of X.
hints: Differentiate the quadratic objective.
Diagonalise \(X^{\mathsf T}X\).
questions.solution: The normal equation is \((X^{\mathsf T}X+\lambda I)\hat\beta=X^{\mathsf T}y\), so \[\hat\beta=(X^{\mathsf T}X+\lambda I)^{-1}X^{\mathsf T}y.\] Along an eigenvector with eigenvalue d, the OLS coefficient is multiplied by \(\frac d{d+\lambda}\) when OLS is defined. Small-eigenvalue directions shrink most. Usually an intercept is excluded from the penalty.
questions.followup: Why standardise features before ridge?
questions.followSolution: The penalty is scale-dependent. A change of units changes relative shrinkage unless the feature scale or penalty is adjusted.
rubric: Derive (\(X^{\mathsf T}X\)+\(\lambda I\))β=Xᵀy from the stated penalty on every coefficient.
Use eigen-directions to explain shrinkage when the ordinary least-squares coefficients are identified.
Explain why changing feature units changes the stated coefficient penalty and motivates consistent scaling.

checks.prompt: Take X=diag(1,0.01), y=(1,1), λ=0.01. What is the second ridge coefficient?
checks.explanation: β₂=0.01/(0.0001+0.01); unregularized coefficient would be 100.

checks.prompt: Which ridge identities are valid for the stated objective?

options.text: Ridge training residuals always satisfy \(X^Tr=0\).
options.explanation: They satisfy Xᵀr=λβ under this penalty.
options.label: Ridge training residuals always satisfy X transpose r equals zero.

options.text: \(\hat\beta=(X^TX+\lambda I)^{-1}X^Ty\), even when X lacks full column rank.
options.explanation: Adding \(\lambda I\) makes the Gram matrix positive definite.
options.label: Beta hat equals inverse of X transpose X plus lambda I, times X transpose y, even when X lacks full column rank.

options.text: The displayed objective leaves an intercept unpenalized automatically.
options.explanation: Every component of β is penalized unless the objective excludes it.
options.label: The displayed objective leaves an intercept unpenalized automatically.

options.text: Along singular value s, the response-to-coefficient factor is \(s/(s^2+\lambda)\).
options.explanation: The penalty suppresses small-singular-value amplification.
options.label: Along singular value s, the response-to-coefficient factor is s divided by s squared plus lambda.

questions.title: A Sharpe ratio needs dependence assumptions
questions.prompt: Someone annualises a daily Sharpe by multiplying by \(\sqrt{252}\). Derive the rule for iid daily returns and explain why it may fail with autocorrelation.
hints: Compute the mean and variance of a 252-day sum.
Include all cross-covariances in the dependent case.
questions.solution: For iid excess returns with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\), a k-day sum has mean \(k\mu\) and variance \(k\sigma^2\), giving \(\sqrt k\,\frac\mu\sigma\). With autocovariance \(\gamma_h\), variance is \(k\gamma_0+2\sum_{h=1}^{k-1}(k-h)\gamma_h\). Positive autocorrelation increases this denominator relative to the iid rule. The derivation uses summed returns; compounding and costs introduce additional distinctions.
questions.followup: Can a smooth equity curve be evidence against a strategy?
questions.followSolution: It can signal stale pricing or smoothing that hides dependence and risk. Investigate the construction before trusting a high annualised Sharpe.
rubric: Define the summed excess-return object, its mean and all covariance terms.
Derive square-root scaling under vanishing nonzero-lag covariances and explain the dependent denominator.
Distinguish summing from compounding and investigate smoothing, marks and costs before interpreting Sharpe.

checks.prompt: For stationary daily returns with marginal variance 1, lag-one covariance 0.25 and all larger-lag covariances zero, what is the variance of the sum over 252 days?
Which annualization statements are valid?

options.text: Zero lag-one covariance alone guarantees the square-root rule at every horizon.
options.explanation: Higher-lag covariance can remain.
options.label: Zero lag-one covariance alone guarantees the square-root rule at every horizon.

options.text: The same additive derivation is exact for compounded returns.
options.explanation: Compounding has a different nonlinear payoff.
options.label: The same additive derivation is exact for compounded returns.

options.text: Under stationarity, sum variance is \(k\gamma_0+2\sum_{h=1}^{k-1}(k-h)\gamma_h\).
options.explanation: Each lag contributes its actual number of covariance pairs.
options.label: Under stationarity, sum variance is k gamma zero plus twice the sum, for h from one through k minus one, of k minus h times gamma h.

options.text: For iid additive returns, k-period mean is kµ and variance is \(k\sigma^2\).
options.explanation: This yields \(\sqrt{k}\) times the one-period mean/SD ratio.
options.label: For iid additive returns, k-period mean is k mu and variance is k sigma squared.

questions.title: Fit the best of a thousand
questions.prompt: You choose the best of 1,000 models using one validation set, then report that model’s validation score as expected future performance. What is wrong, and how would you fix it?
hints: The validation set has become part of the fitting procedure.
Distinguish selection from estimation.
questions.solution: Selection favours models with positive validation noise. The winning score is optimistically biased even if every candidate was fitted only on training data. Use nested time-aware validation for selection and an untouched final test for estimation; record all trials and uncertainty. Retesting repeatedly on the final test turns it into another validation set.
questions.followup: What if the 1,000 models are strongly correlated?
questions.followSolution: The effective search is smaller than 1,000 independent trials, but selection bias remains. The independence formula cannot be imported without checking dependence. Perfectly identical copies of one unbiased score add no selection gain: their maximum is that same score. Partial correlation can reduce optimism, but the joint distribution and selection rule, not a universal scalar effective count, determine it.
rubric: Identify selecting and reporting the best noisy in-sample score as a changed evaluation procedure.
Specify a frozen independent confirmation or outer evaluation that repeats the complete inner search.
Record the actual search and handle correlated candidates without inventing a universal effective test count.

checks.prompt: Which statements about selecting among 1,000 models are valid?

options.text: The selected validation score is generally optimistic because the same scores chose the winner.
options.explanation: Selection favors favorable evaluation noise.
options.label: The selected validation score is generally optimistic because the same scores chose the winner.

options.text: Nested selection evaluates the entire tuning procedure on an outer evaluation split.
options.explanation: The inner stage selects; the outer stage evaluates.
options.label: Nested selection evaluates the entire tuning procedure on an outer evaluation split.

options.text: A new filename for the chosen validation set makes it an untouched test set.
options.explanation: Its role is determined by actual use.
options.label: A new filename for the chosen validation set makes it an untouched test set.

options.text: Only the number of free parameters in the winning model matters for the search bias.
options.explanation: The selection procedure and dependence among candidates also matter.
options.label: Only the number of free parameters in the winning model matters for the search bias.

checks.prompt: Which proposed fixes preserve a credible final evaluation?

options.text: Freeze the selection procedure before evaluating on genuinely unused deployment-like data.
options.explanation: The final data must not become a tuning signal.
options.label: Freeze the selection procedure before evaluating on genuinely unused deployment-like data.

options.text: Try more variants on the final test and report the best one.
options.explanation: This repeats the original problem on the final test.
options.label: Try more variants on the final test and report the best one.

options.text: Report what was searched and compare candidates using uncertainty that respects score dependence.
options.explanation: Nominal model count alone does not describe effective search.
options.label: Report what was searched and compare candidates using uncertainty that respects score dependence.

options.text: Subtract one universal penalty determined only by the number 1,000.
options.explanation: A valid penalty requires assumptions about noise and dependence.
options.label: Subtract one universal penalty determined only by the number 1,000.

questions.title: Predictable is not executable
questions.prompt: Your model predicts the next recorded trade price with high accuracy. Design the checks needed before claiming a tradable edge.
hints: A recorded price is not necessarily an executable price.
Define the timestamp and action your strategy could take.
Include spreads, fees, latency, inventory and capacity.
questions.solution: Specify the prediction timestamp, publication delays and available features. Rebuild labels from executable bid/ask prices after realistic latency. Compare to a persistence baseline. Audit time ordering, stale prices, leakage and survivorship. Include fees, spread crossing, impact, turnover, shorting constraints and capacity. Evaluate chronological holdouts and P&L under an explicit decision rule. Forecast accuracy alone does not establish profit.
questions.followup: Why might a highly accurate model lose money?
questions.followSolution: Small wins and rare large losses, adverse selection, or transaction costs can dominate. Accuracy ignores payoff sizes and action constraints.
rubric: Define the decision-time information, forecast target and actually permitted action before claiming profit.
Reconstruct receipts, revisions, label maturity, latency and baseline information on identical records.
Specify fills, spread, fees, turnover, inventory liquidation and capacity; distinguish assumed execution from measured execution.
Audit chronological selection/evaluation and uncertainty, naming a diagnostic that can contradict the proposed mechanism.

checks.prompt: Concrete audit: 40 filled trades each earn 2 ticks gross and pay 1.5 ticks in total costs; 60 opportunities do not fill and earn zero. A remaining inventory position costs 30 ticks to liquidate. What is the total net episode profit?
checks.explanation: 40×(2−1.5)−30=−10; no-fill opportunities are not profitable executions.

checks.prompt: Which evidence is needed before converting price prediction into a trading claim?

options.text: Exclude no-fill opportunities from all policy evaluation.
options.explanation: Fill conditioning can select outcomes and changes the evaluated quantity.
options.label: Exclude no-fill opportunities from all policy evaluation.

options.text: High directional accuracy establishes positive expected net profit.
options.explanation: Payoff sizes, fills, costs and inventory can dominate accuracy.
options.label: High directional accuracy establishes positive expected net profit.

options.text: Verify that every feature was available before the decision and that the target is not leaking execution information.
options.explanation: Historical availability must match the decision.
options.label: Verify that every feature was available before the decision and that the target is not leaking execution information.

options.text: Evaluate executable prices, latency, fills and terminal inventory liquidation against an executable baseline.
options.explanation: A complete trading episode differs from predicting a recorded print.
options.label: Evaluate executable prices, latency, fills and terminal inventory liquidation against an executable baseline.

questions.title: Explain a research failure
questions.prompt: A strategy works in one period and fails in the next. Give a structured diagnosis that distinguishes implementation error, overfitting, regime change and costs.
hints: Start with invariants and a minimal baseline.
Compare signal quality with execution economics separately.
questions.solution: First reconcile data, timestamps, universe, labels and positions, and reproduce the earlier period. Then audit trials, tuning and overlap for overfit. Evaluate feature/return distributions and subperiod stability for a regime change. Finally decompose gross versus net returns, turnover, spread, fees and impact. Multiple causes can coexist; a story alone does not identify one.
questions.followup: What evidence would falsify your preferred explanation?
questions.followSolution: State a predicted diagnostic before running it: for example, a cost explanation predicts persistent gross edge but net erosion that tracks spreads or turnover.
rubric: Reproduce the earlier implementation and reconcile timestamps, universe, transformations, labels and positions first.
Separate search/overfitting evidence, conditional regime changes and gross-to-net cost accounting without insisting on one cause.
Give a pre-specified diagnostic with an observable prediction that could falsify the preferred explanation.

checks.prompt: Classify the evidence without claiming more than it establishes.

options.text: A distribution shift proves the model has lost skill conditional on each market state.
options.explanation: Changed mixture weights can change aggregate scores without conditional deterioration.
options.label: A distribution shift proves the model has lost skill conditional on each market state.

options.text: Stable gross performance but larger measured fees can explain a decline in net performance.
options.explanation: Compare the same episodes before and after actual costs.
options.label: Stable gross performance but larger measured fees can explain a decline in net performance.

options.text: If a timestamp-safe replay removes performance, investigate availability or implementation before asserting regime change.
options.explanation: The replay directly tests an information/implementation mechanism.
options.label: If a timestamp-safe replay removes performance, investigate availability or implementation before asserting regime change.

options.text: A bad second period by itself proves the model was overfit.
options.explanation: Many distinct mechanisms can produce the same observation.
options.label: A bad second period by itself proves the model was overfit.

checks.prompt: Which diagnostic comparisons are appropriately controlled?

options.text: Compare the model and baseline on matched opportunities and inspect state-specific performance and net costs.
options.explanation: Matched evaluation separates mixture, prediction and execution effects.
options.label: Compare the model and baseline on matched opportunities and inspect state-specific performance and net costs.

options.text: Choose the best explanation after repeatedly tuning on the failed period and treat that period as confirmation.
options.explanation: The failed period is now part of selection.
options.label: Choose the best explanation after repeatedly tuning on the failed period and treat that period as confirmation.

options.text: Reproduce the old run with frozen data, code and settings; then vary one suspected mechanism.
options.explanation: Reproducibility distinguishes changed inputs from changed inference.
options.label: Reproduce the old run with frozen data, code and settings; then vary one suspected mechanism.

options.text: Compare different sets of filled trades and attribute every difference to the model.
options.explanation: Selection of opportunities can confound the comparison.
options.label: Compare different sets of filled trades and attribute every difference to the model.

questions.title: Three rolls and a quoted market
questions.prompt: A contract pays the sum of three independent fair dice. A dealer quotes bid 10 and ask 11. Ignoring costs and risk aversion, what is your fair value?
hints: Use linearity of expectation.
Each die has mean 3.5.
questions.solution: The fair value is \(3\times3.5=10.5\). Buying at 11 or selling at 10 each has expected loss 0.5 per unit, so there is no positive expected-value trade for an uninformed risk-neutral taker.
questions.followup: One die is revealed as 6. What is fair value now?
questions.followSolution: \(6+2\times3.5=13\). Buying at an unchanged ask of 11 has expected edge 2 per unit, before costs and constraints.
rubric: Use the sum of three die means to obtain 10.5, separately from the quoted midpoint.
Compare buying at 11 and selling at 10 with expected payoff 10.5.
After a six, retain its payment and use independence for the other two means to obtain 13.

questions.title: The counterparty knows more
questions.prompt: A contract pays either 0 or 100 with equal prior probabilities. Your ask is 55. Independently of the payoff, a buyer is equally likely to be informed (buys only when \(\text{payoff}=100\)) or uninformed (always buys). Conditional on a buy, what is the expected payoff?
hints: Condition on who buys and the outcome.
A buy occurs with probability \(\frac{1}{4}\) from informed and \(\frac{1}{2}\) from uninformed.
questions.solution: The event buy has mass \(\frac{3}{4}\). The joint mass buy and high payoff is \(\frac14+\frac14=\frac12\). Thus \(P(\text{high}\mid\text{buy})=\frac23\) and \(\text{conditional fair value}=\frac{200}{3}\). Selling at 55 loses expected value despite being above the prior mean 50.
questions.followup: At what ask do you break even on buys under this fixed behavioural model?
questions.followSolution: At \(\frac{200}{3}\). This assumes uninformed buyers buy regardless of the ask and informed buyers still buy in the high state; in realistic models behaviour depends on price.
rubric: Compute buy mass \(\frac{3}{4}\) and buy-plus-high mass \(\frac{1}{2}\) under the stated independent types.
Normalise to posterior high probability \(\frac{2}{3}\) and conditional value \(\frac{200}{3}\).
Separate prior value 50 from value among fills; keep the fixed-behaviour qualification on the break-even ask.

questions.title: A risk budget for a repeated bet
questions.prompt: A repeated independent bet wins even money with probability 0.6. Before each round you stake a fixed fraction 0≤f<1 of current positive wealth. A win multiplies wealth by 1+f and a loss by 1−f; there are no fees or other outcomes. What f maximises expected natural-log wealth growth? Derive and justify the global optimum under this stated toy objective.
hints: Maximise \(0.6\log(1+f)+0.4\log(1-f)\).
Set the derivative to zero.
questions.solution:
For fixed initial positive wealth W, its log contributes a constant. The one-round expected log multiplier is

\[g(f)=0.6\log(1+f)+0.4\log(1-f).\]

The derivative is \(0.6/(1+f)-0.4/(1-f)\), which vanishes at \(f=0.2\). Its second derivative is

\[g''(f)=-\frac{0.6}{(1+f)^2}-\frac{0.4}{(1-f)^2}<0.\]

Strict concavity proves the unique global maximum on 0≤f<1; g(0)=0 and g(f) tends to minus infinity as f approaches one. Expected total log growth over a fixed number of independent rounds is that round count times g(f), so the same fraction optimises the declared repeated objective. The optimum is conditional on this specified probability, payoff and loss model.
questions.followup: How does uncertainty in p change the decision?
questions.followSolution: First specify what uncertainty means and which objective judges the decision. For ONE round, if p itself has a prior distribution and the objective averages expected log utility over that prior, linearity gives \(E[p]\log(1+f)+(1-E[p])\log(1-f)\). When E[p]<1, the nonnegative optimum is max(0,2E[p]−1); uncertainty alone does not force a smaller fraction than the same mean would give. If E[p]=1, growth increases up to the excluded boundary f=1, so there is only a supremum on the stated domain. For an ambiguity SET p∈[p_low,p_high] and a worst-case objective, every fixed positive f has growth increasing in p, so the least-favourable probability is p_low and the optimum is max(0,2p_low−1), assuming the interval lies strictly below one. Those two interpretations can produce different answers. Estimation error, dynamic learning, constraints and additional loss outcomes need their own model; merely saying “uncertainty” does not establish a universal fractional rule. The linked Hard practice develops these distinctions.
rubric: Specify even-money multipliers 1+f and 1−f with admissible 0≤f<1.
Differentiate expected log growth and use concavity to obtain \(f=0.2\) under known p=0.6.
Separate the log objective from one-round arithmetic gain and identify probability, dependence, costs and tail assumptions.

questions.title: Do not double-count diversification
questions.prompt: Two returns each have variance 4 and correlation 0.5. What is the variance of an equal-weight portfolio?
hints: Covariance equals correlation times both standard deviations.
Use both off-diagonal terms.
questions.solution: \(\operatorname{Cov}=0.5\times2\times2=2\). \[\text{Portfolio variance}=0.25\times4+0.25\times4+2\times0.25\times2=3.\] An average of marginal variances alone would miss diversification; assuming zero covariance would overstate it.
questions.followup: What if the correlation is −1?
questions.followSolution: The equal-weight portfolio has zero variance under the exact equal-volatility model. That perfect cancellation is fragile to estimated correlations and differing exposures.
rubric: Compute covariance two in the same units/horizon and include both cross terms.
Obtain equal-weight variance three and distinguish variance from standard deviation.
Explain why the exact negative-correlation cancellation needs matching volatilities/exposures.

questions.title: Gamma is not delta
questions.prompt: A portfolio has delta 0 and gamma 0.08. Under a small underlying move \(\Delta S=5\), ignoring time decay and higher-order terms, what is its approximate value change?
hints: Use the second-order Taylor term.
The gamma contribution has a factor of \(\frac{1}{2}\).
questions.solution: \[\Delta V\approx\delta\,\Delta S+\frac12\gamma(\Delta S)^2=0+0.5\times0.08\times25=1.\] Delta neutrality removes the first-order term locally, not all risk.
questions.followup: What happens for \(\Delta S=-5\)?
questions.followSolution: The same gamma contribution +1, within the approximation. Theta, volatility changes and rehedging costs are not included.
rubric: Include the one-half coefficient and obtain retained change one.
Explain that initial delta neutrality removes a local first-order response, not all risk.
Handle the negative move and name the omitted time, volatility, rehedging and higher-order terms.

questions.title: A synthetic forward
questions.prompt: For European options on a non-dividend asset, same strike \(K=100\) and maturity \(T=1\), \(S=100\) and continuously compounded rate \(r=0\). What is \(C-P\)?
hints: Use put-call parity.
questions.solution: Put-call parity gives \(C-P=100-100=0\). A call minus a put has terminal payoff \(S_T-K\), equal to a forward payoff. European exercise and identical strike/maturity matter.
questions.followup: What changes with known dividend present value D?
questions.followSolution: \(C-P=S-D-Ke^{-rT}\). American exercise can prevent equality.
rubric: Match long-call/short-put terminal payments state by state for identical European contracts.
Replicate with underlying and strike financing under the stated no-dividend/frictionless assumptions.
Obtain price difference zero without claiming each option is worthless; correct for known dividend present value.

questions.title: A fair-looking auction
questions.prompt: You bid for an asset with unknown common value. Your estimate is unbiased before bidding. Why can winning make your estimate too high, and how should that enter your bid?
hints: Winning is a selection event.
The highest noisy estimate tends to have positive error.
questions.solution: In a common-value auction, winning usually means your estimate exceeded others. Conditional on winning, your estimation error can be positive even when the unconditional error has mean zero. Bid using \(\mathbb E[\text{value}\mid\text{your signal},\text{winning}]\) and the auction/payment rules, not the raw estimate. The adjustment depends on competitors and information structure.
questions.followup: Does this apply identically to private-value auctions?
questions.followSolution: No. If your own consumption value is private and known, rivals’ lower bids need not be bad news about that value. Strategic bid shading can still arise for other reasons.
rubric: Explain how winning can select an optimistic noise realization despite an unbiased estimate before selection.
Condition value on both the observed signal and the winning event, with an explicit information model.
Separate value inference from an optimal bid, which also depends on payment rules and rival strategies.
Distinguish common-value inference from a known private consumption value.

checks.prompt: Transfer case: V is 100 or 200 with equal priors. Conditional winning probabilities for a fixed bid are 0.8 and 0.2 respectively. What is E[V|win]?
checks.explanation: Normalize joint masses 0.4 and 0.1; winning selects the low-value state.

checks.prompt: Which bidding claims are justified?

options.text: Unbiasedness before selection does not guarantee unbiasedness after winning.
options.explanation: Winning is another observation about common value.
options.label: Unbiasedness before selection does not guarantee unbiasedness after winning.

options.text: A winner’s curse necessarily occurs in every auction with an uncertain value.
options.explanation: Its direction and existence depend on the joint information/selection law.
options.label: A winner’s curse necessarily occurs in every auction with an uncertain value.

options.text: Expected profit must account jointly for the bid-dependent winning event and payment.
options.explanation: Optimize E[(V−b)1{win at b}], with the stated rules and costs.
options.label: Expected profit must account jointly for the bid-dependent winning event and payment.

options.text: The optimal first-price bid always equals E[V|win] for the current bid.
options.explanation: Changing a bid changes both win probability and conditional margin.
options.label: The optimal first-price bid always equals E[V|win] for the current bid.

questions.title: Two constraints, one quote
questions.prompt: Your inventory is already long. You can lower both your bid and ask by the same amount or widen your spread symmetrically. Explain how these actions differ, and what information you need to choose.
hints: A skew changes the quote centre.
A wider spread changes execution probabilities on both sides.
questions.solution: Lowering the centre encourages selling and discourages further buying, helping reduce long inventory. Symmetric widening reduces fills on both sides and may protect against information risk but need not resolve the position. Choose using fair value, inventory risk, flow sensitivity, adverse selection, horizon and limits. Exact optimal prices require a model.
questions.followup: Why can a profitable expected edge still violate a sensible policy?
questions.followSolution: Position limits, correlated exposures, capital, tail risk or liquidity can make the trade infeasible even with positive standalone expectation.
rubric: Explain how lowering both prices changes the quote centre and, under price-responsive demand, inventory-reducing versus inventory-increasing flow.
Contrast symmetric widening, which changes width and can suppress both sides including inventory-reducing sales.
Identify information, flow response, horizon, correlated exposure and constraints needed to choose; do not claim an unspecified optimum.
Explain why standalone positive expectation does not make a trade feasible under capital or risk limits.

checks.prompt: Starting bid/ask is \(\frac{99}{101}\). Lower both by 0.5. What is the new spread?
checks.explanation: The midpoint shifts but ask−bid is unchanged.

checks.prompt: Which distinctions matter for a long dealer’s choice?

options.text: The choice needs fill responses, adverse-selection estimates, inventory limits and the risk/horizon objective.
options.explanation: Quote changes affect both selection and inventory dynamics.
options.label: The choice needs fill responses, adverse-selection estimates, inventory limits and the risk/horizon objective.

options.text: Symmetric widening mechanically guarantees inventory reduction.
options.explanation: It may also discourage the selling fills that reduce a long position.
options.label: Symmetric widening mechanically guarantees inventory reduction.

options.text: One may calculate a new quote’s payoff using an unchanged fill-conditioned fair value without checking the flow model.
options.explanation: Changing quotes can change who trades.
options.label: One may calculate a new quote’s payoff using an unchanged fill-conditioned fair value without checking the flow model.

options.text: Lowering both prices reduces the bid and ask; widening symmetrically reduces the bid but raises the ask.
options.explanation: A shift and a width change create different customer incentives.
options.label: Lowering both prices reduces the bid and ask; widening symmetrically reduces the bid but raises the ask.

questions.title: An antithetic pair
questions.prompt: For \(U\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\), estimate \(\mathbb E[U^2]\) using the average of \(U^2\) and \((1-U)^2\). Derive whether its variance is smaller than the average of two independent squared uniforms.
hints: Compute \(\operatorname{Cov}(U^2,(1-U)^2)\).
\(\mathbb E[U^2(1-U)^2]=\frac1{30}\) and \(\mathbb E[U^2]=\frac13\).
questions.solution: \(\operatorname{Var}(U^2)=\frac15-\frac19=\frac4{45}\). The covariance is \(\frac1{30}-\frac19=-\frac7{90}\). Pair-average variance is \(\frac12\left(\frac4{45}-\frac7{90}\right)=\frac1{180}\). The average of two independent \(U^2\) values has variance \(\frac{2}{45}\). The antithetic pair is unbiased and reduces variance eightfold.
questions.followup: Does antithetic sampling always reduce variance?
questions.followSolution: No. It needs a favourable covariance structure. For a function symmetric about \(\frac{1}{2}\), the paired observations are identical: their average has the variance of one draw, twice the variance of two independent draws.
rubric: Preserve uniform marginals and target mean, and compute both fourth and product moments.
Derive covariance −\(\frac{7}{90}\), pair variance \(\frac{1}{180}\) and equal-two-evaluation independent variance \(\frac{2}{45}\).
Use independent pairs for uncertainty and give a symmetric-function counterexample to automatic improvement.

checks.prompt: Compute the variance of the antithetic pair average.
checks.explanation: The centered polynomial \(U^2\)−U+\(\frac{1}{2}\) has variance \(\frac{1}{180}\).

checks.prompt: Compute the variance of the average of two independent squared uniforms.
checks.explanation: \(\operatorname{Var}(U^2)=\frac15-\frac19=\frac4{45}\); average two independent terms halves it.

checks.prompt: Select the valid comparison claims.

options.text: \(\operatorname{Cov}(U^2,(1-U)^2)=-7/90\).
options.explanation: \(\mathbb E[U^2(1-U)^2]=\frac1{30}\); subtract \(\frac{1}{9}\).
options.label: Covariance of U squared and the square of the quantity one minus U is minus seven divided by ninety.

options.text: The two antithetic outputs constitute two independent simulation units.
options.explanation: The pair shares U.
options.label: The two antithetic outputs constitute two independent simulation units.

options.text: Both averages are unbiased for \(\frac{1}{3}\).
options.explanation: Each squared uniform has expectation \(\frac{1}{3}\).
options.label: Both averages are unbiased for 1/3.

options.text: Antithetic coupling reduces variance for every possible integrand.
options.explanation: The covariance can be positive, for example for a symmetric integrand.
options.label: Antithetic coupling reduces variance for every possible integrand.

options.text: The antithetic pair variance is \(\frac{1}{90}\), since averaging two equal-variance terms divides covariance by two.
