options.explanation: Variance of (A+B)/2 is [Var(A)+Var(B)+2Cov(A,B)]/4, giving \(\frac{1}{180}\).
options.label: The antithetic pair variance is 1/90, since averaging two equal-variance terms divides covariance by two.

questions.title: When a sample was available
questions.prompt: A feature is labelled with event time 10:00:00 but arrives at 10:00:02. A simulated trade acts at 10:00:01. Is joining the feature by event time valid? Design the join.
hints: Event time and availability time are different.
Your information set must respect receipt/publication delay.
questions.solution: It is invalid if the feature was unavailable until 10:00:02. Join on the most recent feature whose availability time is at or before the decision time, respecting any execution delay. Keep both event and availability timestamps and define tie rules. An as-of join on event time alone can manufacture a predictive edge.
questions.followup: When is an event-time join sufficient?
questions.followSolution: Only when event time also represents actual availability at the decision point, or a correctly modelled delay is applied. Document that assumption.
rubric: Reject the time-10:00:01 use of a feature that first arrives at 10:00:02.
Specify an availability-based as-of join, explicit missing value, key and tie convention.
Retain event/availability timestamps and distinguish a genuinely available event-time join from assumed availability.

checks.prompt: Choose the valid historical join rules.

options.text: The feature can be used at 10:00:01 because its event label is 10:00:00.
options.explanation: It had not arrived.
options.label: The feature can be used at 10:00:01 because its event label is 10:00:00.

options.text: A fixed one-second lag is sufficient for arbitrarily delayed receipts.
options.explanation: Receipt delays are not necessarily bounded by one second.
options.label: A fixed one-second lag is sufficient for arbitrarily delayed receipts.

options.text: Join the appropriate latest eligible vintage rather than the final revised value.
options.explanation: Revisions can change both values and historical signals.
options.label: Join the appropriate latest eligible vintage rather than the final revised value.

options.text: Eligibility requires receipt time no later than the decision, with the declared timestamp tie rule.
options.explanation: Information must actually be available.
options.label: Eligibility requires receipt time no later than the decision, with the declared timestamp tie rule.

checks.prompt: Two rows have (event,receipt,value)=(0,2,4) and (1,4,9). At decision time 3, select the latest-event row whose receipt is ≤3. What value is available?
checks.explanation: The later-event row has not arrived.

questions.title: Scaling squares; translation disappears
questions.prompt: A variable has variance 9. What is the variance after multiplying it by 2 and adding 7?
hints: Translations do not affect variance.
Scaling multiplies variance by the square of the scale.
questions.solution: \(\operatorname{Var}(2X+7)=4\operatorname{Var}(X)=36\). The standard deviation doubles; the variance quadruples.
questions.followup: What is \(\operatorname{Corr}(X,-2X+7)\) when \(\operatorname{Var}(X)>0\)?
questions.followSolution: It is −1. Linear translation preserves covariance and negative scaling reverses its sign.
rubric: Square the scale factor and remove the translation from variance.
Obtain variance thirty-six and distinguish the standard-deviation change.
Use positive variance to derive correlation minus one after negative scaling.

questions.title: A biased coin, twice
questions.prompt: A Bernoulli success probability p has a \(\operatorname{Beta}(2,2)\) prior. Conditional on a common fixed p, observe four independent trials with 3 successes and 1 failure. What is the posterior mean of p?
hints: Add successes and failures to the Beta parameters.
The posterior is \(\operatorname{Beta}(5,3)\).
questions.solution: Conjugacy gives \(\operatorname{Beta}(2+3,2+1)=\operatorname{Beta}(5,3)\), with mean \(\frac{5}{8}\). The empirical rate \(\frac{3}{4}\) and posterior mean differ because the prior contributes information.
questions.followup: What is the predictive probability of success on the next trial?
questions.followSolution: It equals the posterior mean \(\frac{5}{8}\). This uses exchangeable Bernoulli observations with a common fixed p.
rubric: Use a common Bernoulli parameter and its stated Beta prior.
Derive posterior \(\operatorname{Beta}(5,3)\) and mean five eighths.
Integrate the next success probability over the posterior rather than replacing it by the empirical rate.

questions.title: Stop when you look good
questions.prompt: You repeatedly compute an ordinary fixed-sample 5% significance test and stop the first time it rejects. Why is the claimed 5% error rate invalid? Give two principled alternatives.
hints: The sampling and stopping plan is part of the test.
Repeated opportunities to reject inflate the chance of crossing.
questions.solution: A fixed-sample p-value is calibrated for its specified sample size and procedure. Repeated looks with a data-dependent stop change that procedure and can inflate type-I error. Precommit to the sample size and test, or use a valid sequential procedure such as alpha spending or an appropriate always-valid test. Do not claim every stopping rule is invalid; the test must match it.
questions.followup: Does a martingale automatically justify optional stopping?
questions.followSolution: No. Optional-stopping equalities require conditions such as bounded stopping times or suitable integrability. Ignoring those conditions causes classic paradoxes.
rubric: Identify the union of rejection events induced by repeated inspection and data-dependent stopping.
Give a precommitted fixed-sample procedure and a justified sequential alternative without assuming independent looks.
Explain why optional-stopping identities need conditions and why appropriately calibrated stopping can be valid.

checks.prompt: Which claims about repeated testing are correct?

options.text: A pre-specified single fixed-horizon test is a principled alternative.
options.explanation: Its advertised sampling guarantee then applies.
options.label: A pre-specified single fixed-horizon test is a principled alternative.

options.text: Pointwise 5% validity at each fixed sample size does not bound the probability of ever rejecting at 5%.
options.explanation: The rejection event is now a union over inspections.
options.label: Pointwise 5% validity at each fixed sample size does not bound the probability of ever rejecting at 5%.

options.text: Stopping immediately after a rejection preserves the original fixed-sample level.
options.explanation: That is the selected stopping rule being audited.
options.label: Stopping immediately after a rejection preserves the original fixed-sample level.

options.text: The inspections must be independent for optional stopping to be a problem.
options.explanation: Dependence does not supply a general 5% guarantee.
options.label: The inspections must be independent for optional stopping to be a problem.

checks.prompt: Which sequential controls have a valid stated justification?

options.text: Calling the ordinary p-value an e-value makes the same threshold rule valid.
options.explanation: The required expectation property must be proved.
options.label: Calling the ordinary p-value an e-value makes the same threshold rule valid.

options.text: Use a nonnegative null supermartingale starting at one and reject at threshold 20, with an appropriate maximal bound.
options.explanation: This controls crossing at any time.
options.label: Use a nonnegative null supermartingale starting at one and reject at threshold 20, with an appropriate maximal bound.

options.text: Pre-specify levels \(\alpha_t\) with \(\sum_t\alpha_t\leq0.05\); if each inspection is null-valid, the union bound controls any rejection.
options.explanation: No cross-inspection independence is needed.
options.label: Pre-specify levels alpha t whose sum is at most 0.05; if each inspection is null-valid, the union bound controls any rejection.

options.text: Use 5% at every look and average the reported p-values after stopping.
options.explanation: This is not a demonstrated anytime-valid test.
options.label: Use 5% at every look and average the reported p-values after stopping.

questions.title: Choose a control variate
questions.prompt: To estimate \(\mathbb E[Y]\), you use \(Z=Y-c(X-\mathbb E[X])\) where \(\mathbb E[X]\) is known. Derive the variance-minimising c and the residual variance, assuming finite second moments and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)>0\).
hints: Expand \(\operatorname{Var}(Y-cX)\).
Differentiate the quadratic in c.
questions.solution: \[\operatorname{Var}(Z)=\operatorname{Var}(Y)+c^2\operatorname{Var}(X)-2c\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y).\] The optimum is \(c^*=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)}{\operatorname{Var}(X)}\). Substitution gives Var(Y)−Cov(X,Y)²/Var(X). If Var(Y)>0 this equals \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)\left(1-\operatorname{Corr}(X,Y)^2\right)\); if Var(Y)=0 the minimum is zero and correlation is undefined. The estimator remains unbiased for fixed c; estimating c on the same sample can require care in a finite-sample unbiasedness claim.
questions.followup: How would you estimate c without that complication?
questions.followSolution: Estimate c on an independent pilot sample, then hold it fixed on the main Monte Carlo sample.
rubric: Expand the fixed-coefficient variance under finite second moments and known control mean.
Derive \(c^*=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)}{\operatorname{Var}(X)}\) and the general residual variance, treating constant Y without undefined correlation.
Prove fixed/independent-pilot unbiasedness and separate it from fitting on the same main sample.

checks.prompt: For \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=4\), Var(Y)=9 and Cov(X,Y)=3, give the optimal control coefficient c.
checks.explanation: Differentiate 9+4c²−6c.

checks.prompt: For that coefficient, give the residual variance.
Which general control-variate statements are valid?

options.text: Any fixed coefficient preserves unbiasedness when the declared control mean is correct.
options.explanation: The adjustment has mean zero.
options.label: Any fixed coefficient preserves unbiasedness when the declared control mean is correct.

options.text: The optimal coefficient is Var(X) divided by Cov(X,Y) when the covariance is nonzero.
options.explanation: The derivative sets c Var(X)=Cov(X,Y), not its reciprocal.
options.label: The optimal coefficient is Var(X) divided by Cov(X,Y) when the covariance is nonzero.

options.text: The optimal coefficient must be positive.
options.explanation: Its sign follows the covariance.
options.label: The optimal coefficient must be positive.

options.text: \(c_*=\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)/\operatorname{Var}(X)\).
options.explanation: Complete the square in the variance.
options.label: The optimal c is covariance of X and Y divided by variance of X.

options.text: Fitting c on the same observations automatically preserves finite-sample unbiasedness.
options.explanation: The fitted coefficient can correlate with the control sample mean.
options.label: Fitting c on the same observations automatically preserves finite-sample unbiasedness.

questions.title: Count events, keep the exposure
questions.prompt: Four independent exponential waiting times, with a common unknown rate λ > 0, are fully observed: 1, 2, 3 and 4 seconds. Derive the likelihood, verify its maximum, and report the maximum likelihood rate in events per second.
hints: An exponential density is λ exp(−λx) for x ≥ 0.
Sum the exposure times before differentiating the log-likelihood.
questions.solution: The joint density is λ^4 exp(−10λ), and the log-likelihood is 4 log λ − 10λ. Its derivative is 4/λ − 10, zero at λ = 0.4. The second derivative −4/λ² is negative, and the likelihood approaches zero at both limits. Thus this is the unique global maximum, in inverse seconds. The mean wait is 2.5 seconds; the rate is its reciprocal.
questions.followup: Now suppose only two events were observed over 10 seconds of total exposure, with the other waits independently right-censored. Derive the rate estimate. What changes if no events occur?
questions.followSolution: Each event supplies a density λ exp(−λx); each censored observation supplies survival exp(−λc). The likelihood is proportional to λ² exp(−10λ), so the MLE is 0.2 per second. With no events it is exp(−10λ), decreasing on λ > 0: the supremum is at the excluded boundary λ → 0, so no positive-rate MLE exists. Informative censoring requires a different observation model.
rubric: Multiply independent event densities to obtain λ⁴ exp(−10λ).
Verify a unique global maximum at 0.4 and give inverse-second units.
Include censored exposure in the follow-up and distinguish an excluded zero-rate limit from a positive-rate MLE.

questions.title: The derivative missed the support
questions.prompt: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be iid uniform on \([0,\theta]\), \(\theta\) > 0, n ≥ 1. Use the density f(x;\(\theta\))=1/\(\theta\) for 0 ≤ x ≤ \(\theta\) and zero otherwise. Your observed maximum M is positive. A colleague differentiates −n log \(\theta\), finds no stationary point, and concludes that no MLE exists. Diagnose the error, derive the MLE, and decide whether it is unbiased.
hints: Could a proposed endpoint below an observed value have generated the record?
Optimize on the feasible support, then use the distribution of the sample maximum to check bias.
questions.solution: The full likelihood is \(\theta\)^(−n) times the indicator that \(\theta\) ≥ M. It is zero below M and decreases on [M,∞), so the MLE is M using the specified closed-support density. There is no need for an interior stationary point. Under the model P(M ≤ m)=\(\left(\frac m\theta\right)^n\) on \([0,\theta]\), so E[M]=\(\frac{n\theta}{n+1}\). M is downward biased; (n+1)M/n is unbiased but is not the likelihood maximizer. Likelihood fit and unbiasedness are different criteria.
questions.followup: What if the density convention instead excludes x=\(\theta\)? Does this change the probability law or the literal existence of a likelihood maximizer?
questions.followSolution: The probability law is unchanged because endpoints have probability zero. With the strict-support density \(\theta\) > M, the same supremum is approached as \(\theta\) decreases to M but is not attained. This subtlety is why the density version and parameter domain were specified. Regular asymptotic MLE arguments should not be applied automatically to a parameter-dependent support.
rubric: Include the support indicator \(\theta\)≥M before optimising; use the specified closed-support density.
Show decreasing likelihood on the feasible interval and derive E[M]=\(\frac{n\theta}{n+1}\).
Distinguish the strict-support unattained supremum from an unchanged continuous probability law.

checks.prompt: For \(n=4\) and observed maximum M=6, what is the MLE?
checks.explanation: The likelihood vanishes below M and decreases above it.

checks.prompt: Select the valid general likelihood claims.

options.text: \(E[M]=n\theta/(n+1)\), so the MLE is biased down.
options.explanation: The maximum’s CDF is \(\left(\frac m\theta\right)^n\).
options.label: Expected M is n theta divided by n plus one, so the MLE is biased down.

options.text: A likelihood maximum must occur at a zero derivative in the interior.
options.explanation: Boundary maxima exist.
options.label: A likelihood maximum must occur at a zero derivative in the interior.

options.text: Multiplying M by \(\frac{n+1}{n}\) gives another MLE under the same model.
options.explanation: It is an unbiased correction, not the maximizing parameter.
options.label: Multiplying M by (n+1)/n gives another MLE under the same model.

options.text: \(L(\theta)=\theta^{-n}\mathbf1\{\theta\geq M\}\) for the stated observed record.
options.explanation: Parameter-dependent support cannot be dropped.
options.label: Likelihood is theta to power minus n, times the indicator that theta is at least M, for the stated observed record.

questions.title: One observation copied a hundred times
questions.prompt: One Bernoulli draw Y with unknown success probability p is observed to be 1. A pipeline copies it into 100 identical rows and fits an iid Bernoulli model. Compare the correct and naive likelihoods. Do their MLEs differ on [0,1]? Does agreement of the MLE mean the inferred precision is valid?
hints: There was one random draw. The copies are deterministic given it.
Compare likelihood ratios at p=0.5 and \(p=1\), not only the location of the maximum.
questions.solution: The correct likelihood is p, because the whole copied record occurs exactly when Y=1. The naive iid likelihood is p^100. Both maximize at \(p=1\) on [0,1], but the likelihood ratio of 0.5 to 1 is 0.5 in the real model and 2^(−100) in the naive one. Copying created apparent concentration without information. The endpoint also means an interior normal approximation is unjustified. Identical fitted estimates can hide a radically wrong uncertainty model.
questions.followup: In market data, distinct rows may still be dependent. How would you improve the model without claiming that every repeated value is a duplicate?
questions.followSolution: Identify the observation unit and sampling mechanism first. Distinguish true duplicate records from distinct events with identical values. A joint model may factor into conditional probabilities given history rather than marginal iid probabilities. Fit and validate an appropriate dependence model; use resampling or robust uncertainty methods only with assumptions matching that dependence. Row count alone is not effective sample size.
rubric: Identify one random observation and deterministic copies, giving likelihood p rather than p¹⁰⁰.
Compare the same endpoint MLE with likelihood ratios \(\frac{1}{2}\) versus 2⁻¹⁰⁰.
Explain why agreement of estimates does not validate precision and why distinct equal-valued events need a sampling argument.

checks.prompt: When the observed Y=1, compute naive likelihood divided by correct likelihood at p=\(\frac{1}{2}\).
checks.explanation: The ratio p^100/p=p^99.

checks.prompt: Which conclusions survive the duplicated-row comparison?

options.text: The copies give 100 independent Bernoulli observations because they occupy different rows.
options.explanation: Their values are perfectly dependent.
options.label: The copies give 100 independent Bernoulli observations because they occupy different rows.

options.text: The correct likelihood is p; the falsely iid likelihood is p to power 100.
options.explanation: There is only one random draw.
options.label: The correct likelihood is p; the falsely iid likelihood is p to power 100.

options.text: One can infer valid iid uncertainty merely from agreement of the two MLEs.
options.explanation: The curvature and sampling law differ.
options.label: One can infer valid iid uncertainty merely from agreement of the two MLEs.

options.text: Both likelihoods attain their maximum at \(p=1\) on the closed interval.
options.explanation: Agreement of point maxima does not imply equal information.
options.label: Both likelihoods attain their maximum at p=1 on the closed interval.

questions.title: The mean belongs inside the leaf
questions.prompt: A regression tree is restricted to the split x≤2. Its equally weighted training records (x,y) are (0,0),(1,2),(3,4),(4,8). Each leaf minimizes the SUM of squared training errors with a constant prediction. What is the total residual sum of squares after fitting both leaves?
hints: Differentiate the squared loss within each leaf.
Compute errors around two different leaf means, not the overall mean.
questions.solution: The left mean is one and the right mean is six. Left errors contribute 1+1=2; right errors contribute 4+4=8, totaling 10. The parent mean is \(\frac{7}{2}\) and parent RSS is 35, so this split gains 25. This calculation chooses leaf values for a supplied split; it does not establish future performance.
questions.followup: What prediction does this fitted tree give at x=100, and what does that tell you about extrapolation?
questions.followSolution: It gives six: the query is in the right leaf. The ordinary constant-leaf tree extends its region value, not a learned slope. If the real response keeps increasing outside training support, this is a consequential inductive assumption.
rubric: Derive the two constants from the loss.
Keep total RSS distinct from MSE.
Explain constant-leaf extrapolation.

questions.title: Nonlinear features still have a linear solve
questions.prompt: Use the feature map \(\phi(x)=(x,x^2)\), with NO intercept. Training points are x=−1 and x=1 with responses both one. Minimize \(\frac1{2n}\sum_i(y_i-\phi(x_i)^Tb)^2+\frac\lambda2\|b\|^2\), n=2 and lambda=1. What is the fitted prediction at x=2?
hints: The two feature columns are orthogonal on the training points.
The averaged Gram is the identity; the cross-product vector is (0,1).
questions.solution: The slope vector is (0,\(\frac{1}{2}\)), since (I+I)b=(0,1). The prediction at two is 0*2+(\(\frac{1}{2}\))*4=2. The map is nonlinear in x but the fitting problem is a convex quadratic in b. Shrinkage changes the coefficient, not the fact that x² extrapolates quadratically.
questions.followup: Compute the same result using the kernel k(x,z)=xz+x²z².
questions.followSolution: K=diag(2,2). The average-loss convention gives alpha=(K+n*lambda*I) inverse y=(\(\frac{1}{4}\),\(\frac{1}{4}\)). The query kernel row is (2,6), giving prediction two. Using K+lambda*I would incorrectly give \(\frac{8}{3}\).
rubric: Introduce the fixed map and intercept convention.
Use the average-loss normal equation.
Distinguish nonlinear input behavior from coefficient optimization.

questions.title: A forest has a variance floor
questions.prompt: At one fixed input, consider B=20 RANDOM fitted tree predictions, each with variance 9 and each distinct pair with covariance \(\frac{9}{4}\). Their mean prediction across fitting randomness has bias one relative to the true conditional response mean. Fresh response noise, independent of all fitting randomness at this input, has variance two. What is the expected squared prediction error of the unweighted forest average on this fresh response?
hints: Expand the variance of a sum into B diagonal and B(B−1) off-diagonal terms.
Bias is not divided by B. Include fresh noise separately.
questions.solution: The average variance is [20*9+20*19*(\(\frac{9}{4}\))]/20²=\(\frac{207}{80}\). Add squared bias one and fresh noise two to get \(\frac{447}{80}\)=5.5875. Pairwise correlation is \(\frac{1}{4}\). In general the variance is sigma²[rho+(1−rho)/B], so increasing B leaves a limit \(\frac{9}{4}\) rather than zero under this covariance model.
questions.followup: Can this positive correlation always be interpreted as correlation conditional on the observed training data?
questions.followSolution: No. Independently randomized trees can be conditionally independent given the dataset but share variability when datasets are also random. The expectation/covariance law must be stated. Random-feature selection can change both strength and correlation; it is not a guarantee of improved risk.
rubric: Specify the source of randomness.
Count covariance contributions.
Preserve bias and fresh noise.

questions.title: A Newton leaf corrects logits
questions.prompt: Four binary training labels (1,1,1,0) currently have logits all zero. Add ONE constant logit correction v to their shared leaf. Use the second-order Taylor surrogate of SUMMED logistic loss plus lambda*v²/2, with lambda=1. Return the minimizing FULL Newton correction v, before any shrinkage. This is not a leaf probability or an exact logistic optimizer.
hints: At zero each probability is \(\frac{1}{2}\) and each curvature is \(\frac{1}{4}\).
Sum gradients p−y and curvatures before adding lambda.
questions.solution: G=sum(p−y)=−1, H=sum(p(1−p))=1. The surrogate variable part is Gv+(H+lambda)v²/2, minimized at v=−G/(H+lambda)=\(\frac{1}{2}\). With learning rate eta=\(\frac{1}{5}\), the actual logit addition is \(\frac{1}{10}\) and the resulting probability is sigmoid(\(\frac{1}{10}\)), about 0.52498. Neither v nor eta*v is itself a probability.
questions.followup: Find the exact unpenalized constant-logit optimum for these labels. Does an all-one leaf have a finite such optimum?
questions.followSolution: For the mixed leaf, sigmoid(v)=\(\frac{3}{4}\) so v=log(3). For an all-one leaf the unpenalized infimum occurs at v→infinity; there is no finite optimum. The Newton surrogate and the exact loss must not be confused, especially at near-zero curvature.
rubric: Differentiate the loss with respect to logits.
Use summed normalization and the supplied penalty.
Separate surrogate optimum, shrinkage and exact loss.

questions.title: A kernel coefficient is not a feature coefficient
questions.prompt: Let training feature vectors be phi1=phi2=(1,0), with responses y=(1,−1). Minimize \(\frac12\sum_i(y_i-\phi_i^Tw)^2+\frac12\|w\|^2\) with no intercept. Let K be their Gram matrix and write w=sum(alpha_i*phi_i). A canonical kernel solve uses alpha=(K+I) inverse y. Derive alpha, the fitted feature vector, the RKHS penalty alphaᵀK alpha, training RSS, and prediction at a query with feature vector (2,0). Characterize all alpha giving the same optimal feature vector. Then suppose someone instead minimizes ||y−K alpha||²/2+||alpha||²/2. Explain why this is a DIFFERENT penalty in general; compute its two training predictions when the response is changed to y=(1,1).
hints: Resolve response vectors into the sum direction (1,1) and contrast direction (1,−1).
The Gram is all ones: its nullspace destroys coefficient identifiability but not the fitted feature vector.
Ridge on feature weights penalizes alphaᵀK alpha, not alphaᵀalpha.
questions.solution: K has eigenvalues two and zero. Canonical alpha=(1,−1); w=(0,0), penalty zero, RSS two and query prediction zero. Every alpha=(t,−t) represents the same optimum. The positive-lambda canonical solve selects a coefficient representation; it does not make that representation uniquely required by the RKHS objective when K is singular. For y=(1,1), correct feature ridge yields w=(\(\frac{2}{3}\),0), training predictions both \(\frac{2}{3}\). Coefficient ridge instead solves (K²+I)alpha=Ky, yielding alpha=(\(\frac{2}{5}\),\(\frac{2}{5}\)), predictions both \(\frac{4}{5}\). Along an eigenvalue d>0, correct fitted shrinkage is d/(d+lambda), while coefficient ridge gives d²/(d²+lambda). These are different geometries. The nullspace responses cannot be fitted by either representation.
questions.followup: If the feature-weight loss is AVERAGED over n observations, what canonical matrix changes, and what is unique when lambda>0?
questions.followSolution: Use K+n*lambda*I. The penalized feature weight is unique because the feature objective is strictly convex; fitted predictions are unique. Alpha representations can still differ by ker(K). A finite-data Gram being PSD is necessary, but a proposed kernel must be PSD on every finite input collection to define a valid feature inner product.
rubric: Derive the span reduction and eigen-directions.
Distinguish representation nonuniqueness from prediction uniqueness.
Compare feature-norm and coefficient-norm penalties.
Preserve the average/sum convention.

checks.prompt: What is the training RSS with responses (1,−1)?
checks.explanation: Both fitted values are zero.

checks.prompt: What is alphaᵀK alpha for canonical alpha and responses (1,−1)?
checks.explanation: The response contrast is in ker(K).

checks.prompt: With y=(1,1), what is either training prediction under the INCORRECT coefficient L2 penalty?
checks.explanation: K² has eigenvalue four along the sum direction.

checks.prompt: Select all valid conclusions.

options.text: A positive feature-weight L2 penalty gives a unique feature weight, even though singular K allows different alpha representations.
options.explanation: The feature objective is strictly convex; the representation map can have a nullspace.
options.label: A positive feature-weight L2 penalty gives a unique feature weight, even though singular K allows different alpha representations.

options.text: Every alpha=(t,−t) represents the optimal feature vector for responses (1,−1).
options.explanation: Their feature sum is zero.
options.label: Every alpha=(t,−t) represents the optimal feature vector for responses (1,−1).

options.text: Averaging the feature data loss gives the canonical matrix K+n*lambda*I.
options.explanation: Multiplying the average objective by n scales its penalty.
options.label: Averaging the feature data loss gives the canonical matrix K+n*lambda*I.

options.text: Penalizing alphaᵀalpha is the same RKHS norm penalty for every Gram matrix.
options.explanation: Feature norm is alphaᵀK alpha.
options.label: Penalizing alphaᵀalpha is the same RKHS norm penalty for every Gram matrix.

options.explanation: It makes K+lambda*I invertible, not K or the feature map.
options.label: Positive lambda implies the singular feature map itself becomes injective.

questions.title: When greedy learning cannot see the interaction
questions.prompt: Let X1,X2 be independent uniform signs in {−1,1}, and Y=X1*X2 with NO response noise. First use the four corner points with equal training weights. Derive the best affine squared-loss predictor and its MSE. Show the gain of either root axis split, and construct an exact depth-two axis tree. Prove that any finite additive ensemble of one-feature stumps has mixed corner difference zero and cannot reproduce Y. Then change ONLY the TRAINING distribution to independent signs with P(X1=1)=\(\frac{3}{4}\) and P(X2=1)=\(\frac{1}{2}\), keeping Y=X1*X2. Derive the training RSS-per-unit-weight gain from splitting on X2. Fit its population optimal stump, then compute its MSE on the ORIGINAL uniform deployment distribution. Explain why this apparent training gain does not remove the representational limitation.
hints: Under uniform signs, Y is orthogonal to 1, X1 and X2.
Under changed training weights E[X1]=\(\frac{1}{2}\); condition on X2, then evaluate under the ORIGINAL law.
questions.solution: The affine optimum is zero, MSE one. Either root split leaves conditional response mean zero; its gain is zero. Split on X1 then on X2 in each child and assign their products for a perfect depth-two fit. Additive one-variable functions have mixed difference zero, but Y has mixed difference four; no finite sum of stumps fits it. Under shifted training weights E[Y|X2]=(\(\frac{1}{2}\))X2. Parent mean is zero; conditional-mean variance is \(\frac{1}{4}\), so the split gains \(\frac{1}{4}\) and training MSE is \(\frac{3}{4}\). Deployment MSE of (\(\frac{1}{2}\))X2 is E[(X1−\(\frac{1}{2}\))²]=\(\frac{5}{4}\). On uniform corners, Y is orthogonal to the entire additive subspace, so the minimum additive MSE remains one: more stumps cannot solve the structural gap. A positive-gain-only greedy tree stops on the balanced case despite a depth-two solution; allowing a zero-gain first split is an optimization policy, not proof that all future splits help.
questions.followup: Does an additive logistic MODEL have no interactions in its probabilities?
questions.followSolution: Additive logits imply zero mixed difference on the logit scale, not generally on the probability scale: the sigmoid is nonlinear. State the scale when saying additive or interaction. In this regression problem the prediction scale is the squared-loss response itself.
rubric: Prove orthogonality and the mixed-difference obstruction.
Separate representability from greedy discovery.
Compute the shifted-law gain and the original-law risk.
State the scale on which additivity holds.

checks.prompt: What is the root-split squared-error gain on uniformly weighted corners?
checks.explanation: Each child still has mean zero.

checks.prompt: What is the X2 split gain under the changed training distribution?
checks.explanation: The conditional mean is X2/2.

checks.prompt: What is its stump MSE on ORIGINAL uniform deployment?
checks.explanation: Average (X1−\(\frac{1}{2}\))² under uniform signs.

checks.prompt: Select all valid claims.

options.explanation: Its deployment MSE is \(\frac{5}{4}\), exceeding the constant-zero risk one.
options.label: The changed training law guarantees that its positive-gain stump improves uniform deployment risk.

options.text: A greedy tree refusing zero-gain splits can stop before a useful interaction is exposed.
options.explanation: Both initial gains vanish.
options.label: A greedy tree refusing zero-gain splits can stop before a useful interaction is exposed.

options.text: Additivity must identify a scale, such as response or logit.
options.explanation: An additive logit can become nonadditive after sigmoid.
options.label: Additivity must identify a scale, such as response or logit.

options.text: A depth-two axis-aligned tree can fit the balanced four-corner target exactly.
options.explanation: The second split exposes the conditional relationship.
options.label: A depth-two axis-aligned tree can fit the balanced four-corner target exactly.

options.text: Enough one-feature regression stumps can exactly fit these four corner responses.
options.explanation: Every additive ensemble has mixed difference zero; the target has four.
options.label: Enough one-feature regression stumps can exactly fit these four corner responses.

questions.title: Averaging changes the penalty convention
questions.prompt: Two observations have features x=\([-1,1]\) and responses y=[−2,2]. Fit intercept a and slope b by minimizing \(\frac1{2n}\sum_i(y_i-a-bx_i)^2+\frac\lambda2 b^2\), with n=2 and lambda=1. The intercept is NOT penalized. What is the minimizing slope?
hints: Both sample means are zero. Differentiate with respect to the unpenalized intercept.
The average feature square is one and average feature-response product is two.
questions.solution: The intercept equation gives a=0. The objective becomes (2−b)²/2+b²/2. Its derivative is b−2+b=2b−2 and its curvature is two, so the unique slope is one. The averaging factor is part of the objective. Using summed half-loss with the same lambda instead gives slope \(\frac{4}{3}\), a different fit.
questions.followup: What lambda would the summed-half-loss version need to reproduce slope one?
questions.followSolution: Multiply lambda by n: use two. Multiplying the entire original objective by two changes neither its minimizer nor its unpenalized intercept rule.
rubric: Treat the intercept separately.
Keep the average-loss normalization.
Verify the minimum from positive curvature.

questions.title: A new response adds noise you cannot fit away
questions.prompt: At a fixed feature value x, a fresh response has conditional mean 2 and conditional variance 3. A predictor fitted on a RANDOM training dataset is independent of this fresh response conditional on x; over training datasets its predicted value has mean 1 and variance \(\frac{1}{2}\). What is its expected squared prediction error on the fresh response?
hints: Insert the conditional mean between the new response and the random fitted value.
Training-dataset variability and fresh-response noise are separate.
questions.solution: Conditional independence makes the cross covariance vanish. The error is noise variance 3 plus squared prediction bias (1−2)²=1 plus prediction variance \(\frac{1}{2}\), for \(\frac{9}{2}\). The fresh response was not used to fit or select this predictor. Without that independence, the simple decomposition is not justified.
questions.followup: A second predictor always returns one. Is it better here despite having the same bias?
questions.followSolution: Its error is 3+1=4, lower than \(\frac{9}{2}\) because its training variation is zero. A predictor that always returned the true conditional mean two would attain noise risk three. Fixed predictions can reduce variance without making bias disappear.
rubric: Define the expectation over both training and fresh response.
Use conditional independence at the fixed feature value.
Include irreducible noise rather than reporting only excess risk.

questions.title: Changing feature units changes shrinkage
questions.prompt: For a centered single feature x and centered responses y, let \(x^Tx/n=1\) and \(x^Ty/n=2\). Ridge minimizes average half-squared loss plus lambda times b²/2, with lambda=1. Replace x by x′=2x. What numerical penalty lambda′ on the NEW coefficient b′ makes fitted predictions x′b′ equal the original ridge predictions xb? The original intercept convention is unchanged.
hints: The same prediction requires b′=b/2.
Express the old coefficient penalty using b=2b′.
questions.solution: The old penalty is b²/2=4b′²/2, so lambda′=4. The new Gram and cross-product are four and four, giving b′=4/(4+4)=\(\frac{1}{2}\); multiplying by x′ recovers xb with b=1. Keeping lambda′=1 instead gives b′=\(\frac{4}{5}\) and an original-x effective slope \(\frac{8}{5}\). Reparameterizing a penalized model without changing its penalty changes the learning procedure.
questions.followup: How does an L1 penalty parameter change for a positive rescaling x′=c x?
questions.followSolution: Since b=c b′, lambda|b|=c lambda|b′|, so use lambda′=c lambda. With a negative nonzero scaling, use |c| for L1 and c² for L2. Train-only standardization supplies a documented convention, not invariance to every feature transformation.
rubric: Separate coefficient size from predicted contribution.
Transform the penalty as well as the feature.
Check the resulting normal equation explicitly.

questions.title: One Newton step for a probability model
questions.prompt: Binary observations (x,y) are (−1,0) and (1,1). Let z=a+bx. Minimize average logistic loss \(\frac1n\sum_i[\log(1+e^{z_i})-y_i z_i]+\frac\lambda2 b^2\), with n=2, lambda=\(\frac{1}{2}\) and unpenalized intercept a. Starting at a=b=0, take one undamped JOINT Newton step using its exact gradient and Hessian. What is the new slope b? This is one iteration, not the optimum.
hints: At zero, both predicted probabilities are \(\frac{1}{2}\).
Differentiate loss with respect to the logit first; then multiply by x for the slope.
Symmetry makes the cross Hessian and intercept gradient vanish.
questions.solution: At zero the residual probabilities are \(\frac{1}{2}\) and −\(\frac{1}{2}\). The intercept gradient averages to zero; the slope gradient is −\(\frac{1}{2}\). Logistic curvature p(1−p)=\(\frac{1}{4}\) gives Hessian diag(\(\frac{1}{4}\),\(\frac{1}{4}\)+\(\frac{1}{2}\))=diag(\(\frac{1}{4}\),\(\frac{3}{4}\)); the off-diagonal is zero because mean x=0. Newton subtracts H inverse times the gradient, giving a=0 and b=\(\frac{1/2}{3/4}=\frac23\). This step is not a claim of exact convergence or universal full-step descent.
questions.followup: Why can an unpenalized intercept still diverge if every training label is one?
questions.followSolution: Set every slope to zero and let the intercept tend to positive infinity. Each logistic loss tends to zero with no intercept penalty, but no finite intercept achieves that infimum. Penalizing slopes alone is not a universal existence guarantee. The mixed-label symmetric example avoids that particular failure.
rubric: Use average loss and an unpenalized intercept.
Derive probability residuals and curvature.
Distinguish a Newton update from a stationary solution.

questions.title: Future feature geometry belongs in the risk
questions.prompt: Use the UNNORMALIZED objective \(\frac12\|y-Xb\|^2+\frac\lambda2\|b\|^2\), with a fixed full-rank design satisfying \(X^{\mathsf T}X\)=diag(4,\(\frac{1}{4}\)). Data obey y=Xβ+ε with β=(1,0), E[ε]=0 and Cov(ε)=I. A new feature vector is independent of training noise, has mean zero and covariance H=diag(1,4); the same linear coefficient β governs its response. At lambda=1 derive coefficient bias/covariance and the expected squared prediction error AGAINST THE NOISE-FREE CONDITIONAL MEAN (excess risk). Also compute the trace of the ridge fitted-value smoother and compare excess risk with OLS. State why test feature geometry and loss normalization matter.
hints: Diagonalize the fixed design: each coefficient has its own shrinkage and noise amplification.
Prediction error weights coefficient mistakes by H, not automatically by the identity.
Effective degrees of freedom is trace of the smoother, not the number of nonzero coefficients.
questions.solution: For A=\(X^{\mathsf T}X\), coefficient bias is −lambda(A+lambda I) inverse β and covariance is (A+lambda I) inverse A(A+lambda I) inverse. At lambda=1, bias is (−\(\frac{1}{5}\),0), covariance diag(\(\frac{4}{25}\),\(\frac{4}{25}\)). Excess risk is biasᵀH bias+tr(H Cov)=\(\frac{1}{25}\)+\(\frac{4}{25}\)+\(\frac{16}{25}\)=\(\frac{21}{25}\). OLS is unbiased with covariance diag(\(\frac{1}{4}\),4), giving risk \(\frac{1}{4}\)+16=\(\frac{65}{4}\). The smoother S=X(A+lambda I) inverse Xᵀ has trace \(\frac{4}{5}\)+\(\frac{1}{5}\)=1. There are two coefficients but only one effective fitted degree of freedom. This example favors ridge for this specified β/noise/H; it is not a universal dominance result. Fresh response noise would add its variance to both risks.
questions.followup: Derive the risk for a general positive-semidefinite future second-moment matrix H and explain why rotating the training design is not enough to remove every test cross term.
questions.followSolution: For error mean \(\mu\) and covariance V, E[(x_newᵀ error)²]=\(\mu\)ᵀH\(\mu\)+tr(HV). In a training eigenbasis V is diagonal under the stated isotropic noise, but \(\mu\) may have several nonzero entries and rotated H need not be diagonal. Off-diagonal entries of H can contribute to the squared-bias quadratic. General train-to-test distribution changes can also invalidate the fixed-coefficient model itself.
rubric: Derive the linear estimator and its training-noise moments.
Compute prediction risk using the specified future second moment.
Distinguish trace degrees of freedom from support size.
Separate this conditional fixed-design calculation from tuning or a future-noise guarantee.

checks.explanation: Weight coefficient variance and squared bias by the future matrix H.

checks.prompt: What is the trace of the fitted-value smoother at lambda=1?
checks.explanation: Add four fifths and one fifth.

options.text: Increasing lambda must decrease prediction risk for every possible true coefficient.
options.explanation: A growing shrinkage bias can outweigh variance reduction.
options.label: Increasing lambda must decrease prediction risk for every possible true coefficient.

options.explanation: Trace measures sensitivity of fitted responses, not coefficient support.
options.label: The smoother trace equals the count of nonzero estimated coefficients.

questions.title: A sparse fit needs a joint certificate
questions.prompt: Consider the lasso quadratic \(\frac12 b^T G b-z^Tb+\lambda\|b\|_1\), where G=[[1,\(\frac{4}{5}\)],[\(\frac{4}{5}\),1]], z=(1,\(\frac{9}{10}\)), lambda≥0. Derive and verify the optimizer at lambda=\(\frac{3}{10}\), and find the smallest lambda at which its second coefficient is zero. Then change the design to EXACTLY DUPLICATED columns, G=[[1,1],[1,1]], z=(1,1), lambda=\(\frac{3}{10}\). Characterize all lasso coefficient minimizers and whether fitted predictions are unique. Finally add rho times ||b||²/2 with rho=\(\frac{1}{5}\) and compute either coefficient. Independent coordinate thresholding is not a valid joint solve for correlated columns.
hints: For an active positive coefficient, (Gb−z)j+lambda=0. For a zero coefficient use |(Gb−z)j|≤lambda.
When only the first coordinate is active, b1=1−lambda; verify the zero-coordinate inequality.
With duplicates the squared loss depends on the coefficient sum. Among nonnegative splits the L1 norm is the same.
questions.solution: G is positive definite with eigenvalues \(\frac{9}{5}\) and \(\frac{1}{5}\). At lambda=\(\frac{3}{10}\) solve Gb=z−lambda(1,1): b=(\(\frac{11}{18}\),\(\frac{1}{9}\)), both positive, certifying the unique optimizer. The second coefficient can be zero with b1=1−lambda when |\(\frac{9}{10}\)−(\(\frac{4}{5}\))(1−lambda)|≤lambda. On 0≤lambda≤1 this becomes \(\frac{1}{10}\)+(\(\frac{4}{5}\))lambda≤lambda, so its first zero occurs at lambda=\(\frac{1}{2}\); both vanish by lambda=1. For duplicates, let s=b1+b2. Triangle inequality gives |b1|+|b2|≥|s|; minimizing s²/2−s+(\(\frac{3}{10}\))|s| gives s=\(\frac{7}{10}\). Every nonnegative split of that sum is optimal. Individual coefficients are nonunique, but duplicated-column predictions depend only on s and are unique. Adding rho=\(\frac{1}{5}\) makes the objective strictly convex; symmetry gives b1=b2=(\(\frac{7}{10}\))/(2+\(\frac{1}{5}\))=\(\frac{7}{22}\). Small L2 regularization selects a definite split rather than identifying two separate causal effects.
questions.followup: Can the number or identity of active lasso coefficients be assumed to change monotonically along every correlated-design penalty path?
questions.followSolution: No. The simple monotone soft-threshold path is an orthogonal special case. Correlated active sets can enter, leave or change sign as the coupled optimum moves. Verify the joint subgradient certificate rather than extrapolating the two-coordinate example into a universal rule.
rubric: Verify active signs and inactive subgradient inequalities.
Derive the entry/exit boundary instead of independently thresholding z.
Characterize nonuniqueness and distinguish coefficients from fitted predictions.
Explain how a positive L2 term changes uniqueness without supplying causal identification.

questions.title: Which variance does the bootstrap estimate?
questions.prompt: An iid dataset is [1,2,4]. Conditional on this observed dataset, draw THREE independent indices uniformly with replacement from {1,2,3} and take their observed values. Let \(\bar X^*\) be their mean. Compute its exact CONDITIONAL bootstrap variance, not the variance of one resampled observation or the Monte Carlo error of a simulation average.
hints: First compute the variance of the three-point empirical distribution, using denominator three.
Three independent bootstrap draws make the variance of their mean one third of that variance.
questions.solution: The observed mean is \(\frac{7}{3}\). Centered squared deviations are \(\frac{16}{9}\),\(\frac{1}{9}\),\(\frac{25}{9}\), so the empirical variance is \(\frac{14}{9}\). The draws are conditionally independent from this empirical law, giving \(\operatorname{Var}_*(\bar X^*)=(14/9)/3=14/27\). The unbiased sample variance is instead \(\frac{7}{3}\), whose iid mean-variance estimate is \(\frac{7}{9}\). The bootstrap conditional value is smaller by (\(n-1\))/n here; no extra resamples alter this exact law.
questions.followup: If B independent replicate means are averaged, what is the conditional variance of that simulation average?
questions.followSolution: It is 14/(27B). This measures simulation error when estimating the conditional mean, not the original experiment’s uncertainty. The standard deviation of the replicate means stays √(\(\frac{14}{27}\)); dividing it by √B answers a different question.
rubric: Use the empirical rather than unbiased variance.
Apply conditional independence of bootstrap draws.
Separate estimator variation from simulation-average variation.

questions.title: Replacement leaves some records out
questions.prompt: A dataset contains four physical records, labelled 1 through 4; their numerical values may coincide. A bootstrap sample draws four record indices independently and uniformly with replacement. What is the expected number of DISTINCT original record indices appearing at least once?
hints: Use an indicator for whether each particular record appears.
A particular record is absent only if every draw chooses one of the other three.
questions.solution: A record is absent with probability (\(\frac{3}{4}\))^4=\(\frac{81}{256}\) and present with probability \(\frac{175}{256}\). Summing four presence indicators gives \(4[1-(3/4)^4]=175/64\). Presence indicators need not be independent for this expectation. Distinct physical indices are the object counted; deduplicating equal observed values changes the empirical sampling weights.
questions.followup: Generalize to n records and interpret the large-n proportion without claiming the out-of-bag records form a new independent dataset.
questions.followSolution: The expectation is \(n[1-(1-1/n)^n]\), with proportion tending to 1−e^(−1), about 0.632. A given record is out of the bootstrap sample with probability approaching e^(−1). Different replicates reuse and overlap the same original records; increasing their count does not create new independent held-out observations.
rubric: Count distinct indices, not distinct numerical values.
Derive one record’s inclusion probability.
Use linearity without assuming independent inclusion events.

questions.title: Reflect the error, not the estimate
questions.prompt: The original estimate is \(\hat\theta=10\). Under a specified bootstrap approximation, the 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles of the CENTERED error \(\hat\theta^*-\hat\theta\) are −3 and 5. Construct the 95% BASIC bootstrap interval by approximating the law of \(\hat\theta-\theta\) with those error quantiles. Report the lower endpoint. This is a construction rule, not a claim of exact coverage.
hints: Write −3 ≤ original estimation error ≤ 5.
Solve both inequalities for the unknown parameter, reversing the order of the error quantiles.
questions.solution: Approximate the error event by −3≤10−\(\theta\)≤5. Rearranging gives 5≤\(\theta\)≤13. The lower endpoint is 10−5=5. Replicate estimate quantiles would instead be 7 and 15, giving percentile interval [7,15]. Both widths are eight, but their centers differ. A basic interval reflects the error law; copying its two quantiles directly as a parameter interval gets the sign and centering wrong.
questions.followup: The exact conditional mean of the bootstrap estimates is 11. What is the estimated bootstrap bias and corresponding bias-corrected point estimate?
questions.followSolution: The estimated bias is 11−10=1, and the corrected point estimate is 10−1=9. This does not prove smaller mean-squared error or repair an invalid resampling model. The interval construction, a point-bias correction and Monte Carlo precision are separate decisions.
rubric: Center on the original estimate.
Invert the signed error bounds correctly.
Keep interval construction separate from a coverage guarantee.

questions.title: Do not tear apart a paired comparison
questions.prompt: Three independent matched records contain losses for models A and B: (1,2), (2,3), (4,5). Compare their mean losses with A minus B. In a paired bootstrap, draw three record indices with replacement and reuse each index for BOTH columns. A colleague instead bootstraps the two columns independently, with three draws in each. Compute independent-column bootstrap variance MINUS paired bootstrap variance of the mean difference, conditional on these data.
hints: Look at the three within-record differences.
Independent column resampling deletes the empirical covariance.
questions.solution: Every paired difference is −1, so every paired bootstrap mean difference is −1 and its conditional variance is zero. Each column has empirical variance \(\frac{14}{9}\); shifting a column by one does not change its variance. Independent resampled means each have variance \(\frac{14}{27}\) and have zero covariance, giving difference variance \(\frac{28}{27}\). Thus the requested gap is \(\frac{28}{27}\). The independent scheme changed the joint experiment instead of merely using more randomness.
questions.followup: Does paired resampling always produce less variance than independent resampling? Does zero variance here prove certainty about all future model comparisons?
questions.followSolution: Neither. Pairing adds the covariance term: variance of A−B is Var(A)+Var(B)−2Cov(A,B). Negative covariance can make the paired variance larger. Zero conditional variance here describes the degenerate empirical distribution of observed differences; it does not establish that a population difference is always constant or that model performance is known without uncertainty.
rubric: Preserve matched records when defining the paired law.
Compute both conditional variances and their gap.
Avoid universal covariance or future-certainty claims.

questions.title: An endpoint that cannot be resampled
questions.prompt: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be iid \(\operatorname{Uniform}(0,\theta)\), \(\theta\)>0, and M=max Xᵢ. Values are distinct with probability one. Conditional on the observed sample, form an ordinary n-out-of-n empirical bootstrap maximum M*. Define \(Z^*=n(M-M^*)/M\). Derive its mass at zero and its limit as n grows. Compare it with the true sampling gap \(Z=n(\theta-M)/\theta\), and decide whether the bootstrap approximates that gap law consistently. Give the zero mass for \(n=4\) and its large-n limit; select the valid statements. Increasing simulation count B must be distinguished from increasing n.
hints: The unique observed maximum must be absent from every draw for M* to be strictly smaller.
The true continuous sampling maximum has no atom at the endpoint.
For fixed t≥0, derive P(Z>t) from the CDF of the uniform sample maximum.
questions.solution: At least one draw selects the unique maximum with probability \(1-(1-1/n)^n\), which is exactly P*(Z*=0). For \(n=4\) it is \(\frac{175}{256}\); its limit is 1−e^(−1). In contrast, for 0≤t≤n the true gap has \(P(Z>t)=(1-t/n)^n\), tending to e^(−t). Thus Z tends to a continuous Exponential(1) law, with no atom at zero. The nonvanishing bootstrap atom already rules out consistency: a sufficiently small positive t still has at least that much bootstrap CDF mass, whereas the exponential CDF can be arbitrarily small. More B estimates the wrong conditional law more precisely. Every empirical maximum satisfies M*≤M<\(\theta\) almost surely; consequently any percentile interval using only these maximum quantiles has zero coverage for \(\theta\), regardless of its nominal positive confidence level.
questions.followup: Use the specified Uniform model to derive an exact one-sided 1−α confidence interval for \(\theta\), with 0<α<1. Explain how this differs from ordinary empirical percentile bootstrapping.
questions.followSolution: Since P(M/\(\theta\)≤u)=u^n on [0,1], the event M≥α^(1/n)\(\theta\) has probability 1−α. Also M≤\(\theta\) almost surely. Hence \([M,M/\alpha^{1/n}]\) has exactly 1−α coverage under this model. This uses a known pivot and a justified parametric family, not an empirical sample that cannot generate unseen endpoint values. An m-out-of-n bootstrap needs a defensible statistic-specific rescaling and limit argument; simply choosing fewer draws is not a universal remedy.
rubric: Derive the bootstrap atom exactly and its nonzero limit.
Derive the continuous limiting sampling law with the correct scaling.
Diagnose inconsistency rather than Monte Carlo noise.
Give a model-specific interval without an unsupported universal repair.

questions.title: The cluster is the draw, the row mean is the target
questions.prompt: Two observed independent clusters contain A=[0,0] and B=[10,10,10,10]. The statistic is the POOLED ROW mean, total sum divided by total retained row count. A cluster bootstrap independently draws TWO whole cluster labels with replacement, each label A or B having probability \(\frac{1}{2}\), and retains every member of each selected cluster (including all members again on repeated selection). Compute the exact conditional bootstrap mean and variance of this statistic. Explain its bias relative to the observed statistic and why neither independently drawing rows nor averaging two cluster means reproduces the specified procedure. This finite two-cluster example illustrates the law; it is not a claim that two clusters suffice for reliable inference.
hints: Enumerate AA, AB, BA and BB before taking moments.
The denominator changes when clusters have unequal sizes.
Combine the two mixed outcomes, then compute variance around the bootstrap expectation.
questions.solution: The four equally likely draws give pooled means 0,\(\frac{20}{3}\),\(\frac{20}{3}\),10. Their expectation is \(\frac{35}{6}\). Their second moment is \(\frac{425}{9}\); subtracting (\(\frac{35}{6}\))² gives variance \(\frac{475}{36}\). The observed pooled mean is \(\frac{20}{3}\), so conditional bootstrap bias is −\(\frac{5}{6}\). A ratio statistic need not be conditionally unbiased. Averaging selected cluster means gives outcomes 0,5,5,10 and targets an equally weighted cluster mean instead, with expectation five. Independently drawing six individual rows from the empirical row distribution instead gives conditional mean \(\frac{20}{3}\) and variance \(\frac{100}{27}\); it breaks the within-cluster shared values and defines another experiment. Repeating an entire selected cluster preserves its internal configuration, but cannot manufacture more independent clusters.
questions.followup: Suppose the population consists of equally likely A-type and B-type clusters. Compare the population average-cluster-mean target with the limiting pooled-row-mean target over many iid sampled clusters.
questions.followSolution: The equally weighted cluster-mean target is (0+10)/2=5. For pooled rows, the law of large numbers gives E[cluster sum]/E[cluster size]=(0+40)/(2+4)=\(\frac{20}{3}\). Larger clusters contribute more rows. Both can be legitimate targets, but they answer different questions. Cluster bootstrap consistency also needs appropriate conditions and an increasing number of independent clusters; a large row count inside only two clusters does not supply that limit.
rubric: Enumerate resampled cluster counts and changing row denominators.
Compute expectation, second moment, variance and bias.
Distinguish cluster-mean and row-weighted targets.
Respect the independent-cluster rather than row sample size.

questions.title: A derivative has an inner factor
questions.prompt: Let \(\ell(\theta)=\tfrac12(2\theta-3)^2\), for real \(\theta\). Compute \(\ell^{\prime}(1)\). Give the signed derivative, not a proposed update.
hints: Differentiate both the outer square and the inner affine function.
Evaluate the residual at \(\theta\)=1 after applying the chain rule.
questions.solution: Write r=2\(\theta\)−3. The outer derivative is r and the inner derivative is 2, so \(\ell^{\prime}(\theta)=2(2\theta-3)\). At \(\theta\)=1 this is −2. Increasing \(\theta\) slightly lowers the loss. The factor one half cancels the outer factor two, but not the inner derivative.
questions.followup: What is the exact loss change from \(\theta\)=1 to \(\theta\)=1+h?
questions.followSolution: Expanding gives \(\Delta\ell=-2h+2h^2\). The linear prediction is reliable locally; h=1 gives zero change, despite a negative derivative at the starting point.
rubric: Retain the inner factor two.
Distinguish a signed slope from a finite update.

questions.title: Choose a direction, then take the dot product
questions.prompt: Let \(f(x,y)=\tfrac12(x+2y-5)^2\). At (1,1), find the directional derivative along the UNIT vector \(u=(3/5,4/5)\), defined as the derivative at t=0 of f((1,1)+tu).
hints: Compute the residual before the two partial derivatives.
A unit-direction derivative is the dot product with the gradient.
questions.solution: The residual is −2, giving gradient (−2,−4). The directional derivative is \(\nabla f^Tu=(-2)(3/5)+(-4)(4/5)=-22/5\). Normalizing a direction matters: the parameter t measures distance because u has unit Euclidean norm.
questions.followup: Which unit direction gives the most negative derivative?
questions.followSolution: The direction is \(-\nabla f/\|\nabla f\|=(1,2)/\sqrt5\), with derivative \(-\sqrt{20}\). Cauchy–Schwarz bounds every unit-direction dot product below by minus the gradient norm.
rubric: Compute the full gradient.
Use the stated unit vector and signed dot product.

questions.title: The same loss in different coordinates
questions.prompt: For \(\theta\)>0 define \(\ell(\theta)=\tfrac12(\theta-4)^2\). Set \(\theta\)=e^β and F(β)=ℓ(e^β). Compute F′ at β=log 2.
hints: Differentiate the map \(\theta\)=e^β as well as the loss.
At β=log 2, the coordinate-map derivative equals two.
questions.solution: At \(\theta\)=2 the original derivative is −2. The chain rule adds \(d\theta/d\beta=\theta=2\), so F′=−4. A derivative is a sensitivity per unit of its coordinate; these are two coordinate descriptions of one loss, not inconsistent calculations.
questions.followup: Compare small gradient steps of size α in \(\theta\) and in β, starting at \(\theta\)=2.
questions.followSolution: The direct step is \(\theta\)new=2+2α. The β step is βnew=log2+4α, hence \(\theta\)new=2e^(4α)=2+8α+O(α²). Equal numerical learning rates in different coordinates are not the same movement. The transformed Hessian is \(\theta\)²ℓ″+\(\theta\)ℓ′; here it is zero, although ℓ″=1.
rubric: Apply composition at the specified coordinate.
Interpret coordinate-dependent gradient updates.

questions.title: The axes conceal a saddle
questions.prompt: For \(f(x,y)=x^2+4xy+y^2\), find the smallest directional second derivative at the origin over all UNIT Euclidean vectors u. Report its signed value.
hints: Write the mixed derivative twice in the symmetric Hessian.
Bound the product of the two unit-vector coordinates.
questions.solution: The Hessian is \(H=\begin{pmatrix}2&4\\4&2\end{pmatrix}\). For a unit vector, \(u^THu=2+8u_xu_y\). Since \(u_xu_y\ge-1/2\), the minimum is −2, attained at (1,−1)/√2. Along either coordinate axis the curvature is +2, yet along x=−y the function is negative. The origin is a saddle.
questions.followup: What changes if the mixed term is 2xy instead of 4xy?
questions.followSolution: Then H has eigenvalues 0 and 4 and f=(x+y)². Every point on x=−y is a global minimum. Semidefinite curvature permits flat directions; positive definiteness would rule those out for this quadratic.
rubric: Find the least directional curvature.
Give its attaining direction and explain the missed saddle.

questions.title: Both partials exist, but the local plane fails
questions.prompt: Define \(f(x,y)=xy/\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\) away from (0,0), and f(0,0)=0. Determine continuity, both coordinate partials, and total differentiability at the origin. Test the proposed linear approximation on x=y=t>0. Use the numerical and exact-choice checkpoints below; your scratchpad is ungraded.
hints: Compute the axes, then the diagonal.
Divide the remainder by distance, not by distance squared.
questions.solution: For r=√(x²+y²), |xy|≤r²/2, so |f|≤r/2→0: f is continuous. On either axis f is zero, hence both coordinate partials are zero. If a total derivative existed, its linear map would therefore be zero. But at (t,t), t>0, f=t/√2 while the distance is √2t, so the normalized remainder is \(\frac{1}{2}\) for every t>0, not a quantity tending to zero. Total differentiability fails. On the unit diagonal, f(hu)=|h|/2, so even the two-sided directional derivative fails there. Existing partials alone do not justify the gradient approximation.
questions.followup: Would squaring the numerator, f=x²y²/√(x²+y²), restore differentiability?
questions.followSolution: Yes. Its absolute value is at most r³/4. Dividing by r gives a remainder bound r²/4→0, proving total differentiability with zero derivative. A proof must control all approaches, not only a handful of paths.
rubric: Prove continuity with a uniform bound.
Evaluate the normalized diagonal remainder.
Distinguish partials and total differentiability.

questions.title: One parameter is used three times
questions.prompt: A recurrence has x₀=2, \(x_t=a x_{t-1}+u_t\), t=1,2,3, with a=\(\frac{1}{2}\) and inputs [1,0,−1]. All targets are zero. Let \(\ell=(x_1^2+x_2^2+x_3^2)/6\). Derive its derivative with respect to the SHARED a and with respect to x₀, holding inputs fixed. Select the valid reverse-derivative claims. These derivatives concern this finite computation, not a stationary distribution.
hints: Carry the future loss contribution backwards through a.
Sum the parameter contribution from every time index.
questions.solution: The states are 2,1,−\(\frac{1}{2}\) and loss \(\frac{7}{8}\). Set λ₄=0 and \(\lambda_t=x_t/3+a\lambda_{t+1}\). Working backwards gives λ₃=−\(\frac{1}{6}\), λ₂=\(\frac{1}{4}\), λ₁=\(\frac{19}{24}\). Each occurrence of a contributes λt times its input state, so \(d\ell/da=(19/24)2+(1/4)2+(-1/6)1=23/12\). Also \(d\ell/dx_0=a\lambda_1=19/48\), and derivatives with respect to the three inputs are λ₁,λ₂,λ₃. A forward check differentiates the recurrence: s₀=0, st=x(t−1)+a s(t−1), giving s=[2,3,\(\frac{5}{2}\)]; then \(\Sigma\)xt st/3=\(\frac{23}{12}\). Detaching states drops real paths through the computation.
questions.followup: What happens if each time uses its own independent parameter aₜ?
questions.followSolution: The three separate derivatives are [\(\frac{19}{12}\),\(\frac{1}{2}\),−\(\frac{1}{6}\)]. The derivative for a shared a is their sum, because changing a changes every aₜ simultaneously. A negative final contribution can coexist with a positive total derivative. Reverse mode computes all input sensitivities in linear time.
rubric: Normalize the direct residual by three.
