questions.title: A significance filter changes interval coverage
questions.prompt:
One observation X has distribution N(µ,1), where µ is a fixed unknown real number. Write Φ for the standard-normal CDF, α=0.05, and c=Φ⁻¹(1−α/2). The ordinary interval I(X)=[X−c,X+c] has unconditional coverage 1−α. You REPORT it only when the pre-specified positive-significance filter S={X>c} passes.

Derive \(P_\mu(\mu\in I(X)\mid S)\) as an explicit piecewise function of µ, including µ≤0, 0<µ<2c and µ≥2c. Explain the zero-mean case and why the original unconditional guarantee is not a conditional guarantee for reported intervals. Do not turn selection into a prior probability for µ.
hints: Coverage requires µ−c≤X≤µ+c; intersect this event with X>c.
Under fixed µ, standardize the intersection endpoints and divide by the probability of selection.
Check whether the upper coverage endpoint reaches the selection threshold before applying a CDF difference.
questions.solution:
Selection has probability 1−Φ(c−µ)>0 for every finite µ. The intersection is empty if µ≤0, because every reported interval has strictly positive lower endpoint. For µ>0 its lower observation endpoint is max(c,µ−c) and its upper endpoint is µ+c. Standardizing gives upper endpoint c and lower endpoint max(c−µ,−c). Consequently

\[C(\mu)=\begin{cases}0,&\mu\leq0,\\\displaystyle\frac{\Phi(c)-\Phi(c-\mu)}{1-\Phi(c-\mu)},&0<\mu<2c,\\\displaystyle\frac{1-\alpha}{1-\Phi(c-\mu)},&\mu\geq2c.\end{cases}\]

At µ=0, NONE of the reported intervals contains zero, although 95% of intervals over all samples do. At µ=c the conditional coverage is 1−α; at µ=2c it is \((1-\alpha)/(1-\alpha/2)=38/39\), about 97.44%, and it approaches 95% as µ tends to positive infinity. Conditioning changes the sample distribution and can decrease or increase coverage. The reported subset is not a repeated unselected sample from the original normal law.
questions.followup: Give two ways to restore 95% coverage CONDITIONAL on reporting: first using an independent replication Y∼N(µ,1), and second by inverting a conditional pivot from the selected X itself. Derive the pivot and its coverage argument, rather than merely saying “adjust for selection.”
questions.followSolution:
If Y is independent of X at every fixed µ, report [Y−c,Y+c] when X>c. Its coverage event is independent of the selection event, so its conditional coverage remains 95%; the same X cannot play the independent-replication role.

Alternatively, for x>c define the truncated-normal CDF

\[F_\mu^S(x)=\frac{\Phi(x-\mu)-\Phi(c-\mu)}{1-\Phi(c-\mu)}.\]

Conditional on S, the continuous probability-integral transform makes Fµˢ(X) uniform on (0,1) for each fixed µ. The confidence SET \(\{m:\alpha/2\leq F_m^S(x)\leq1-\alpha/2\}\) therefore covers the true µ with conditional probability 1−α. This inversion uses the actual selection rule and its truncated sampling law, not a posterior distribution. Its endpoints generally differ from x±c and can be very wide near the selection threshold. A more complex data-dependent reporting rule would require conditioning on that actual rule, not importing this particular formula.
rubric: Intersect the coverage and reporting events before standardizing.
Derive all three coverage branches and the zero-mean failure, including boundary consistency.
Separate unconditional coverage, conditional selected-sample coverage and a posterior interpretation.
Justify independent replication and the truncated-CDF confidence-set inversion with its conditional uniform pivot.

questions.title: Three observations, counted covariance pairs
questions.prompt: A stationary AR(1) process has constant mean µ, marginal variance 4 and autoregressive coefficient \(\rho\)=\(\frac{1}{2}\). Innovations are iid, centered, independent of the past and have variance 3, so these marginal assumptions are consistent. You observe THREE consecutive values and estimate µ by their arithmetic mean. What is the EXACT variance of this estimate? Count pairs at each separation; do not use a large-sample effective-size formula.
hints: Lag-one covariance is 2; lag-two covariance is 1.
There are two unordered lag-one pairs and one lag-two pair. Each appears twice in the variance of the sum.
questions.solution: The sum variance is 3·4+2(2·2+1·1)=22. Dividing by \(3^2\) gives \(\frac{22}{9}\). The iid shortcut gives \(\frac{4}{3}\) and misses the covariance pairs. The exact variance factor is (\(\frac{22}{9}\))/(\(\frac{4}{3}\))=\(\frac{11}{6}\); its standard-error factor is √(\(\frac{11}{6}\)), not \(\frac{11}{6}\). Equating mean-estimation variance to 4/\(n_{\mathrm{eff}}\) gives \(n_{\mathrm{eff}}\)=\(\frac{18}{11}\). The asymptotic AR factor three would instead give \(n_{\mathrm{eff}}\)=1; that is not the requested finite calculation.
questions.followup: Change ONLY \(\rho\) to −\(\frac{1}{2}\), retaining stationary marginal variance 4 and innovation variance 3. What changes? Can this target-specific effective count exceed three?
questions.followSolution: Lag-one covariance becomes −2 while lag-two remains +1. Sum variance is 12+2(−4+1)=6, hence mean variance \(\frac{2}{3}\). The effective count is 4/(\(\frac{2}{3}\))=6, exceeding three because adjacent noise partly cancels. This is a variance comparison for the mean, not six observed independent rows. Negative lag-one correlation does not make every later covariance negative.
rubric: Count both separations and both covariance orientations.
Obtain exact mean variance \(\frac{22}{9}\) and distinguish variance from standard-error inflation.
Keep the positive lag-two term under negative rho and interpret effective count six.

questions.title: Forecast error accumulates future innovations
questions.prompt: A stationary process satisfies Xₜ−2=(\(\frac{1}{2}\))(Xₜ₋₁−2)+εₜ. Its iid innovations have mean zero and variance 3 and are independent of the past. All parameters are known, and Xₜ=10 is observed exactly. Forecast Xₜ₊₂ using the information through t. What is the conditional mean-squared error of the optimal conditional-mean forecast? Do not confuse it with variance of a sample mean or impose Gaussian innovations.
hints: Iterate the recurrence twice before separating known and unknown terms.
Future innovations are independent, so add their weighted variances.
questions.solution: Two steps give Xₜ₊₂=2+(\(\frac{1}{4}\))(Xₜ−2)+(\(\frac{1}{2}\))εₜ₊₁+εₜ₊₂. The conditional mean is 4 and the forecast error is (\(\frac{1}{2}\))εₜ₊₁+εₜ₊₂. Its conditional variance and mean-squared error are 3(\(\frac{1}{4}\)+1)=\(\frac{15}{4}\). A zero-mean independent innovation assumption justifies this conditional mean without normality. The stationary marginal variance is 3/(1−\(\frac{1}{4}\))=4, slightly larger than this finite-horizon uncertainty.
questions.followup: Derive the h-step forecast and error variance for h≥1. Are the one-step and two-step forecast errors independent? Can this variance alone justify an exact Gaussian prediction interval?
questions.followSolution: The forecast is 2+(\(\frac{1}{2}\))^h(Xₜ−2), and its error variance is \(3\sum_{j=0}^{h-1}(1/4)^j=4(1-4^{-h})\), approaching four. The one-step error εₜ₊₁ and two-step error share that innovation; their covariance is \(\frac{3}{2}\), so they are not independent. Finite variance alone does not specify their distribution or justify exact normal quantiles. A Gaussian innovation assumption would make these weighted errors jointly Gaussian.
rubric: Iterate the model and identify forecast four and the future-innovation error.
Add independent weighted innovation variances to obtain \(\frac{15}{4}\).
Derive horizon dependence, shared-error covariance and the distributional limit of a variance-only statement.

questions.title: White returns can hide dependent risk
questions.prompt: Let εₜ be iid standard Gaussian over all integer times and Xₜ=εₜεₜ₋₁. You may use E[ε²]=1 and E[ε⁴]=3. Show that X has mean zero, variance one and ZERO autocovariance at every nonzero lag, yet adjacent X values are dependent. Define \(Y_t=X_t^2\), then derive the EXACT variance of \(\bar Y_n=n^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^nY_t\) for n≥1. Is the iid shortcut for that risk estimator valid?
hints: The lag-one product contains two independent factors with mean zero.
For dependence, compare E[Xₜ²Xₜ₊₁²] with E[Xₜ²]E[Xₜ₊₁²].
Squared values have variance eight; only adjacent squared values share an innovation.
questions.solution:
E[Xₜ]=0 and E[Xₜ²]=1. At lag one, E[εₜ₋₁εₜ²εₜ₊₁]=0; at larger lags the innovation sets are disjoint, so covariance is again zero. But E[Xₜ²Xₜ₊₁²]=1·3·1=3, whereas the product of the second moments is one. This proves dependence. For Yₜ=Xₜ², \(\mathbb E[Y]\)=1, E[Y²]=\(3^2\)=9 and Var(Y)=8. Its lag-one covariance is 3−1=2; further lags vanish by independence. Therefore

\[\operatorname{Var}(\bar Y_n)=\frac{8n+4(n-1)}{n^2}=\frac{12n-4}{n^2}.\]

The iid risk shortcut 8/n understates uncertainty for n>1 even though ordinary X autocorrelations vanish. Second-order whiteness of returns does not imply independence or second-order whiteness of a nonlinear target.
questions.followup: Compare exact mean-estimation effective counts for X and Y using EACH target’s own marginal variance. Does an iid-looking variance for the X mean imply iid data?
questions.followSolution: The X mean has variance 1/n, so its variance-comparison effective count is exactly n. For Y, it is 8n²/(12n−4)=2n²/(3\(n-1\)), approaching 2n/3. The reference marginal variance changed from one to eight with the target. The X mean variance identity is exact, but it does not establish an iid sampling distribution, independence, or a Gaussian interval. Effective size belongs to the estimator and assumptions.
rubric: Compute vanishing return autocovariances without claiming independence.
Prove dependence through the shared fourth moment.
Derive squared-return marginal variance eight, lag-one covariance two and finite tapered mean variance.
Compare target-specific effective counts and avoid an iid-distribution claim.

questions.title: Overlapping labels manufacture autocorrelation
questions.prompt: One-period returns rₜ are iid with mean µ and positive variance \(\sigma^2\). Define k-period SUM labels \(Y_t=\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}r_{t+j}\) for a fixed positive integer k. Observe Y₁,…,Yₙ, with n≥k, and estimate the one-period mean by \(\hat\mu=(nk)^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^nY_t\). Derive the label autocovariances and EXACT variance of \(\hat\mu\). Explain why treating the n labels as independent fails even when the underlying returns are iid. These are sums, not compounded returns.
hints: Covariance comes only from underlying returns shared by two labels.
At lag h<k, exactly k−h returns overlap.
Use the finite pair count n−h, then divide by (nk)².
questions.solution:
\(\mathbb E[Y]\)=kµ and \(\gamma_0\)=\(k\sigma^2\). For 1≤h<k, the shared returns give \(\gamma_h\)=(k−h)\(\sigma^2\); at h≥k the blocks are disjoint and independent. Thus

\[\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\sum_{t=1}^nY_t\right)=\sigma^2\left[nk+2\sum_{h=1}^{k-1}(n-h)(k-h)\right]=\sigma^2\left[nk^2-\frac{k(k^2-1)}3\right].\]

Dividing by n²k² gives Var(\(\hat\mu\))=\(\sigma^2\)[1/n−(k²−1)/(3n²k)]. The independent-label shortcut \(\sigma\)²/(nk) omits the reused observations. For fixed k and large n the actual variance is approximately \(\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\), about k times the shortcut. This persistence arises from label construction, not necessarily an economically predictable daily-return process. The n≥k condition matters for the displayed polynomial; shorter samples require truncating at min(\(n-1\),k−1).
questions.followup: Use only labels starting at 1,1+k,1+2k,… within 1…n. What variance results? If all n+k−1 underlying returns are available, can their direct mean improve on the overlapping-label estimator?
questions.followSolution: There are m=1+floor((\(n-1\))/k) disjoint labels. Their mean divided by k has variance \(\sigma\)²/(mk). The direct mean of all n+k−1 iid underlying returns has variance \(\sigma\)²/(n+k−1). The overlapping estimator instead gives each underlying return a weight proportional to its multiplicity: smaller near the endpoints, larger inside. All weights sum to one, so Cauchy–Schwarz gives \(\sum_i w_i^2\geq1/(n+k-1)\). Thus the direct equal-weight mean has no larger variance, with equality precisely when these multiplicities are uniform (including k=1). For n≥k>1 they are unequal. Overlapping labels create repeated use, not extra independent information.
rubric: Count shared underlying returns and derive the finite label autocovariances.
Retain the lag taper, the n≥k condition and the exact one-period-mean variance.
Distinguish construction-induced dependence from predictable daily returns.
Derive disjoint-label variance and justify the direct-mean comparison with weights.

questions.title: The arithmetic mean need not be the best mean estimate
questions.prompt: Observe \(n\geq2\) consecutive values of a weakly stationary process with unknown constant mean µ and KNOWN covariance \(\Sigma_{ij}=\gamma_0\rho^{|i-j|}\), where \(\gamma_0\)>0 and −1<\(\rho\)<1. Among estimators \(\hat\mu=\sum_iw_iX_i\) with deterministic weights summing to one, derive the unique minimum-variance weights and variance. Give explicit endpoint and interior weights, rather than only citing a generalized least-squares formula. Justify the covariance inverse or verify the vector it needs. Gaussianity is NOT assumed.
hints: Minimize \(w^{\mathsf T}\Sigma w\) with the sum constraint, or separate any weights from a proposed optimum.
The inverse AR correlation matrix is tridiagonal: endpoint diagonals one, interior diagonals 1+\(\rho\)², off-diagonals −\(\rho\), all divided by 1−\(\rho\)².
Apply this matrix to the all-ones vector and normalize its sum.
questions.solution:
Let \(R_{ij}=\rho^{|i-j|}\) and let B be the stated tridiagonal matrix before division by 1−\(\rho\)². Multiplying a row of B by column j of R cancels the geometric terms off the diagonal; its diagonal is 1−\(\rho\)². Hence R⁻¹=B/(1−\(\rho\)²). It is positive definite: \(x^\top Bx=(1-\rho^2)x_1^2+\sum_{i=2}^n(x_i-\rho x_{i-1})^2>0\) for x≠0. Its row sums divided by 1−\(\rho\)² are 1/(1+\(\rho\)) at both endpoints and (1−\(\rho\))/(1+\(\rho\)) inside. Write D=n−(n−2)\(\rho\)=2+(n−2)(1−\(\rho\)). Then

\[w_1=w_n=\frac1D,\qquad w_i=\frac{1-\rho}D\ (2\leq i\leq n-1),\qquad\operatorname{Var}(\hat\mu)=\frac{\gamma_0(1+\rho)}D.\]

The weights sum to one and are positive. For \(w^*=\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf1/(\mathbf1^\top\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf1)\), \(\Sigma w^*\) is a constant times 1. Any other unbiased weights w*+v have \(\mathbf1^\top v=0\); the cross term vanishes and their variance is \(\operatorname{Var}(\hat\mu_{w^*})+v^\top\Sigma v\), strictly larger unless v=0. This proves uniqueness among deterministic linear unbiased estimates without normality. For n=2 both weights are one half; for n>2 positive correlation gives endpoints more weight than interior observations.
questions.followup: Compare n=3, \(\rho\)=\(\frac{1}{2}\), \(\gamma_0\)=4 with the arithmetic mean. Then someone estimates weights from the same sample and claims that weights summing to one still guarantee unbiasedness. Give an explicit counterexample under iid N(µ,1) data.
questions.followSolution: Here D=\(\frac{5}{2}\); weights are (\(\frac{2}{5}\),\(\frac{1}{5}\),\(\frac{2}{5}\)) and variance is \(\frac{12}{5}\), below arithmetic variance \(\frac{22}{9}\). The gain concerns mean estimation with known covariance; it is not a universal sampling policy. For random same-sample weights, \(\sum_i w_i=1\) only gives \(\hat\mu=\mu+\sum_iw_i(X_i-\mu)\); the last term need not have mean zero. With three iid Gaussian observations, choose weights (1,0,0) if X₁≥X₃ and (0,0,1) otherwise. The estimate is max(X₁,X₃)= (X₁+X₃+|X₁−X₃|)/2 and has mean µ+1/√π, because X₁−X₃∼N(0,2). The sum constraint alone therefore does not preserve unbiasedness after data-dependent selection.
rubric: Establish positive definiteness and verify the needed inverse or precision-vector identity.
Derive explicit normalized endpoint/interior weights and their variance.
Prove optimality and uniqueness in the deterministic linear unbiased class.
Compare the finite example and demonstrate same-sample random-weight bias.

questions.title: A limit that holds rho fixed can fail
questions.prompt: For EACH n, take a stationary Gaussian AR(1) sample of n observations with common mean µ, marginal variance \(\gamma_0\)>0 FIXED across n, and \(\rho_n=e^{-c/n}\) for fixed c>0. Its innovation variance is \(\gamma_0(1-\rho_n^2)\), and its initial distribution is stationary. Derive the limit of \(\operatorname{Var}(\bar X_n)/\gamma_0\) and of the exact mean-estimation effective count \(\gamma_0/\operatorname{Var}(\bar X_n)\). Compare with substituting \(\rho_n\) into the usual fixed-\(\rho\) asymptotic count \(\frac{n(1-\rho)}{1+\rho}\). Is \(\bar X_n\) a consistent estimator here? State which assumptions differ from a single fixed-\(\rho\) model.
hints: Start with \(n^{-2}\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n e^{-c|i-j|/n}\), not an infinite-lag shortcut.
Treat the double sum as a Riemann integral on the unit square.
The integral equals 2∫₀¹(1−u)exp(−cu)du.
questions.solution:
The sample changes its persistence with n while retaining its marginal noise scale. The continuous kernel gives the Riemann-sum limit

\[\begin{aligned}g(c)&=\int_0^1\!\int_0^1 e^{-c|s-t|}\,ds\,dt\\&=2\int_0^1(1-u)e^{-cu}\,du\\&=\frac{2(c-1+e^{-c})}{c^2}>0.\end{aligned}\]

Thus \(\operatorname{Var}(\bar X_n)\)→γ₀g(c) and \(n_{\mathrm{eff}}\)→1/g(c), a finite number. In contrast, the substituted fixed-\(\rho\) formula tends to c/2 and is not valid uniformly in this changing model. At c=1 the exact limit is e/2≈1.359, whereas that shortcut is \(\frac{1}{2}\). As c→0, g(c)→1 and the true count tends to one; it does not tend to zero. Each centered sample mean is Gaussian, so its positive limiting variance implies nonvanishing probabilities of fixed estimation errors, not consistency. Variance alone would not establish this probability conclusion for arbitrary non-Gaussian triangular arrays; Gaussianity supplies it here. Absolute lag summability for each n does not supply a uniform fixed-model limit.
questions.followup: Keep \(\rho_n\) and innovation variance \(\gamma_0(1-\rho_n^2)\), but initialize X₀=µ deterministically instead of stationarily. Derive the changed covariance kernel and mean-variance limit. Separately, what if stationary initialization is retained but innovation variance τ²>0 is fixed across n?
questions.followSolution:
For deterministic initialization, \(X_i-\mu=\sum_{j=1}^i\rho_n^{i-j}\epsilon_j\). Summing shared innovation covariances gives \(\gamma_0(\rho_n^{|i-j|}-\rho_n^{i+j})\); it is no longer weakly stationary. The mean-variance ratio tends to

\[g(c)-\left(\frac{1-e^{-c}}c\right)^2.\]

This subtracts the random stationary initial component that the deterministic experiment removed. Its c→0 limit is zero, contrasting with g(c)→1; using the stationary formula for a zero-start simulation changes the experiment. This ratio is to the original stationary scale \(\gamma_0\), not a common marginal variance in the nonstationary sample. If instead τ² is fixed with stationary initialization, the marginal variance \(\gamma_{0,n}=\tau^2/(1-\rho_n^2)\) grows like τ²n/(2c). Consequently \(\operatorname{Var}(\bar X_n)\) grows like \(\tau^2 n(c-1+e^{-c})/c^3\). Specify the initialization and which variance scale is fixed before interpreting persistence.
rubric: Derive the finite covariance Riemann sum and positive limiting function g(c).
Compare exact and incorrectly substituted effective counts, including c=1 and small-c behavior.
Use the Gaussian sampling law to justify nonconsistency, rather than a variance-only assertion.
Derive both changed initialization and fixed-innovation limits with their variance scales.

checks.prompt: For c=2, compute the limiting variance ratio Var(mean)/γ0.
checks.explanation: The integral is 2(c−1+e^(−c))/c².

checks.prompt: Which changing-model limits are valid?

options.text: The limiting ratio is \(2(c-1+e^{-c})/c^2>0\).
options.explanation: The covariance sum becomes the integral of e^(−c|u−v|) on the unit square.
options.label: The limiting ratio is two times c minus one plus exp of minus c, divided by c squared, and is positive.

options.text: The sample mean is consistent because every row n has |\(\rho\)_n|<1.
options.explanation: The Gaussian estimation error retains positive limiting variance.
options.label: The sample mean is consistent because every row n has |ρ_n|<1.

options.text: The limiting variance ratio is (1−exp(−c))/c.
options.explanation: That integrates a single covariance row without the full two-dimensional lag multiplicity.
options.label: The limiting variance ratio is (1−exp(−c))/c.

options.text: Substituting \(\rho\)_n into the fixed-\(\rho\) asymptotic count always gives the exact limiting effective count.
options.explanation: That substitution gives c/2 and omits the finite-horizon taper that remains material.
options.label: Substituting ρ_n into the fixed-ρ asymptotic count always gives the exact limiting effective count.

options.text: The exact effective count tends to the reciprocal of this ratio.
options.explanation: Its definition uses γ0 divided by actual mean variance.
options.label: The exact effective count tends to the reciprocal of this ratio.

questions.title: A historical row can still be unavailable
questions.prompt: Each row below is [original decision time, feature receipt time, label receipt time]: [[0,0,3],[2,3,5],[4,4,9],[7,7,10],[8,8,12],[9,11,10]]. At fit time T=10 all receipts stamped at most 10 have arrived. A training row must have a decision strictly before T, a feature received no later than its ORIGINAL decision, and a label received no later than T. Each label uses future outcomes after its decision; its receipt includes any publication delay. How many rows qualify? Having a feature now does not mean it was usable at the original decision.
hints: Apply the feature boundary at the original decision, not the later fit time.
A label received exactly at ten is allowed under this explicit inclusive rule.
questions.solution: Original rows 0,2,3 qualify: their decisions are 0,4,7, their features were received on time, and their labels arrived at 3,9,10. Thus the count is three. Row 1 uses a feature received at three for a decision at two; row 4 has an unfinished label; row 5 has a late feature even though its label is available. Sorting decision timestamps or checking only the fit-time receipt boundary misses different violations.
questions.followup: If fitting happens immediately BEFORE receipts stamped 10, how does the count change? If the late features were replaced by explicit missing values through a pre-specified causal pipeline, would discarding those rows still be compulsory?
questions.followSolution: The label criterion becomes strictly less than ten, excluding row 3 and leaving two. The declared original feature was unavailable, so it cannot be retroactively substituted. A different pre-specified model that can act on genuine missing inputs may keep such decisions with those missing values; its performance evaluates that different pipeline. This problem counts rows usable with the declared received feature, not every conceivable missing-value policy.
rubric: Check feature receipt against original decision and label receipt against fit cutoff.
Identify rows 0,2,3 and obtain count three.
Apply the strict-cutoff change and distinguish exclusion from a different missing-input procedure.

questions.title: Averaging folds changes the population
questions.prompt: Two nonoverlapping evaluation blocks contain two and eight decisions. Their average squared prediction losses are respectively 1 and 4. Predictions were recorded before outcomes, and the deployment estimand is average loss per decision over these TEN decisions, each weighted equally. What is the pooled average loss? Distinguish this from an unweighted average of the two block scores. No iid assumption is supplied.
hints: Recover the total loss in each block before pooling.
The denominator is ten decisions, not two blocks.
questions.solution: Total loss is 2·1+8·4=34, giving \(\frac{34}{10}\)=\(\frac{17}{5}\)=3.4. The unweighted block average is (1+4)/2=2.5. It assigns each decision in the short block four times the weight of each decision in the long block. This is an estimand choice, not an arithmetic approximation. Serial dependence does not alter this identity, but does affect the uncertainty assigned to the estimate.
questions.followup: Could 2.5 be the intended estimate under a different deployment target? Do two block scores justify estimating uncertainty as though there were ten independent losses?
questions.followSolution: Yes: choose a block with equal probability, then a decision uniformly inside that block. That population weights the blocks equally and has average loss 2.5. It differs from selecting one of the ten decisions uniformly. Two block means and counts do not identify within-block variance or cross-block dependence, so they cannot justify an iid ten-loss standard error. State both the target weighting and the dependence assumptions.
rubric: Recover block totals 2 and 32 and pool over ten decisions.
Explain the different decision weights behind the value 2.5.
Separate a loss identity from unsupported independence and uncertainty claims.

questions.title: Disjoint labels can still be future training
questions.prompt: At fit cutoff 10, all receipts with timestamp ≤10 are available. Five candidate rows have [label start,label end,label receipt] [[2,6,6],[6,10,10],[9,12,12],[14,17,17],[8,10,13]]. Labels use half-open intervals [start,end), and all features were available at their original starts. Protect the validation information interval [10,14). First identify original indices retained by OVERLAP PURGING ALONE. Then identify indices usable for a strict past-to-future fit at ten, requiring start<10 and label receipt≤10 as well as non-overlap. Explain why an arbitrary row-count gap is insufficient.
hints: Touching half-open endpoints do not intersect.
Purging alone knows neither the fit cutoff nor publication delay.
Compare row 3, which is disjoint but future, with row 4, which ends on time but is released late.
questions.solution: Purging alone retains indices [0,1,3,4]. Row 2 intersects [10,14); row 1 ends exactly at ten and row 3 starts exactly at fourteen, so neither touches the protected interior. The deployment fit retains only [0,1]. Row 3 is future training; row 4 has an unavailable label despite an end timestamp of ten. The correct maturity criterion is receipt, not end alone. An index gap counts rows rather than elapsed information time and cannot generally represent variable horizons, irregular timestamps or delayed publication.
questions.followup: For a strictly historical fit at T, suppose every selected label ends no later than its receipt, and every receipt is ≤T. If protected evaluation begins at T, can any selected half-open label overlap it? Does this imply independence or make embargo irrelevant in all resampling designs?
questions.followSolution: No selected label can overlap a protected interval beginning at T: its end is ≤T, so it lies on the non-overlap side of that boundary. Here the actual maturity rule already removes target spillover; a redundant purge is not an additional source of independence. Shared features, common factors and temporal dependence can remain. In resampling that reuses later rows or protects an earlier block, overlap and additional exclusion mechanisms may still matter. An embargo needs a stated information/dependence reason and does not universally turn data iid.
rubric: Apply half-open overlap exactly and retain [0,1,3,4] under purging alone.
Apply history and receipt constraints separately to obtain [0,1].
Prove the forward-boundary implication without claiming independence.
Explain why irregular timing and publication delays defeat a fixed row gap.

checks.prompt: How many rows are eligible for the strict past-to-future fit?
checks.explanation: Original rows 0 and 1 meet both receipt and interval constraints.

checks.prompt: Which row-selection statements are valid?

options.text: Replacing receipt checks with a fixed row-count gap establishes the same information boundary.
options.explanation: Row order does not supply availability timestamps.
options.label: Replacing receipt checks with a fixed row-count gap establishes the same information boundary.

options.text: Row 3 is valid training at time 10 because its label is disjoint from validation.
options.explanation: Its start and receipt are future.
options.label: Row 3 is valid training at time 10 because its label is disjoint from validation.

options.text: Row 4 is invalid training at time 10 despite a label ending at 10.
options.explanation: Its receipt is at 13.
options.label: Row 4 is invalid training at time 10 despite a label ending at 10.

options.text: Using zero-based indices, overlap purging alone retains [0,1,3,4].
options.explanation: Half-open endpoints allow [6,10) and [14,17) outside [10,14).
options.label: Using zero-based indices, overlap purging alone retains [0,1,3,4].

questions.title: An adaptive evaluation can be honest
questions.prompt: At each of n≥1 pre-specified decisions, a binary prediction \(a_t\) is fixed before binary outcome \(Y_t\) arrives. Let \(\mathcal F_{t-1}\) denote EVERYTHING legitimately known when \(a_t\) is fixed, including earlier mature outcomes, past model choices and any already drawn prediction randomization. Define loss \(L_t=\mathbf1\{a_t\ne Y_t\}\) and conditional risk \(r_t=E[L_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]\). All prior losses and risks are measurable at later decision information sets. Outcomes need NOT be iid. Prove that the mean realized loss minus the mean of these possibly RANDOM conditional risks has expectation zero, derive its second moment, and give a distribution-free 95-percent error band using only Chebyshev. What procedure does that band evaluate? Contrast refitting from mature past evaluation outcomes with retrospectively choosing a model using all the evaluation scores.
hints: The centered increment \(D_t=L_t-r_t\) has conditional mean zero.
For s<t, \(D_s\) is known in \(\mathcal F_{t-1}\), so compute the cross expectation by conditioning.
A binary loss has conditional variance \(r_t(1-r_t)\leq1/4\). The target here is the average conditional risk along the recorded procedure.
questions.solution:
Write \(\bar L_n=n^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^n L_t\), \(\bar r_n=n^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^n r_t\), and \(D_t=L_t-r_t\). By definition \(E[D_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]=0\). For s<t, tower conditioning gives \(E[D_sD_t]=E[D_s E[D_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]]=0\). This does not assert independent losses or constant risks. Since the binary loss has conditional probability \(r_t\) of being one, \(E[D_t^2\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]=r_t(1-r_t)\). Consequently

\[\begin{aligned}E[\bar L_n-\bar r_n]&=0,\\E[(\bar L_n-\bar r_n)^2]&=\frac1{n^2}\sum_{t=1}^n E[r_t(1-r_t)]\\&\leq\frac1{4n}.\end{aligned}\]

Chebyshev gives probability at least 0.95 that the recorded average conditional risk lies within \(\sqrt{5/n}\) of the average realized loss; intersect this band with [0,1]. It can be very wide. The radius uses a PRE-SPECIFIED n: selecting when to report after inspecting errors is a different stopping problem. It evaluates the recorded adaptive forecasting procedure and the risk along its realized information history. It is not automatically a confidence interval for one frozen final model, a future regime, or an iid population parameter. Refitting on earlier mature outcomes may imitate deployment, provided the originally recorded predictions are not rewritten. A retrospectively selected candidate was not generally predictable at the times whose losses are reported; that selection changes the evaluation question.
questions.followup: For two iid fair outcomes, evaluate the two constant classifiers zero and one on BOTH outcomes, then report the smaller average loss, breaking ties arbitrarily. Calculate its expected reported loss and its expected loss on an independent future fair outcome. If instead the classifier may adapt only to earlier outcomes before each prediction, what is its expected reported loss?
questions.followSolution: Of the four equally likely pairs 00,01,10,11, the smaller average loss is zero on 00 and 11 and one half on the mixed pairs. Its expectation is one quarter. Whichever constant is selected has error probability one half on an independent future fair bit. Under any genuinely predictable adaptive rule, each next fair bit is independent of its already fixed prediction, so \(E[L_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]=1/2\) and average expected loss is one half. Updating from past scores and using future scores to choose which past prediction to report are different procedures. The cheap selected score is not unbiased evidence for the chosen model.
rubric: Define predictable predictions, nested information and the random conditional-risk target.
Prove zero conditional increments and zero cross moments without claiming iid losses.
Derive the finite second-moment bound and \(\sqrt{5/n}\) 95-percent band for fixed n.
Distinguish adaptive procedure risk from final-model/future-regime claims and calculate selected loss \(\frac{1}{4}\) versus future risk \(\frac{1}{2}\).

checks.prompt: For n=500, what is the Chebyshev 95% error-band half-width using only the stated bound?
checks.explanation: The squared-error bound is 1/(4n), so half-width is √(5/n).

checks.prompt: Which adaptive-evaluation proof claims are valid?

options.text: D_t=L_t−r_t has conditional mean zero; earlier D values are measurable at later information sets.
options.explanation: These conditions make distinct D values orthogonal in expectation.
options.label: D_t=L_t−r_t has conditional mean zero; earlier D values are measurable at later information sets.

options.text: The second moment of mean realized loss minus mean conditional risk always equals the variance of mean realized loss.
options.explanation: The conditional risk average is itself random and correlated with realized losses; the martingale difference is the object being bounded.
options.label: The second moment of mean realized loss minus mean conditional risk always equals the variance of mean realized loss.

options.text: The risk sequence must be deterministic for the expectation-zero result.
options.explanation: It can adapt predictably to earlier mature outcomes.
options.label: The risk sequence must be deterministic for the expectation-zero result.

options.explanation: Bernoulli conditional variance and martingale-difference orthogonality give the bound.
options.label: Expected square of the average D t equals one over n squared times the sum of expected r t times one minus r t, at most one over four n.

options.text: The resulting band automatically evaluates a retrospectively chosen winner among all models.
options.explanation: It evaluates the actual pre-outcome decisions, not a hindsight selection.
options.label: The resulting band automatically evaluates a retrospectively chosen winner among all models.

questions.title: A discovery fraction has a random denominator
questions.prompt: A repeated procedure has exactly two equally likely outcomes: (V,R)=(1,1) or (0,9), where V counts false rejections and R counts all rejections. Define false discovery rate as \(E[V/\max(R,1)]\), assigning zero when R=0. What is its value? These are stipulated count outcomes, not a claim about calibrated individual p-values.
hints: Calculate the false fraction inside each repetition before averaging.
A ratio of average counts is a different quantity.
questions.solution: The within-run fractions are one and zero, so FDR is one half. In contrast, \(E[V]=1/2\) and \(E[R]=5\); their ratio is one tenth. Pooling discoveries weights a run with nine discoveries nine times as much as a run with one. FDR weights repetitions according to their probabilities. Here family-wise error \(P(V>0)\) happens also to equal one half; that equality is not a general identity.
questions.followup: Change the two outcomes to (0,0) and (1,2), still equally likely. Calculate FDR, family-wise error and the ratio of expected counts. Why must the zero-rejection convention be explicit?
questions.followSolution: The fractions are zero and one half, giving FDR one quarter. Family-wise error is one half, and the pooled population ratio is (\(\frac{1}{2}\))/1=one half. A run without any rejection contributes zero to the false-discovery proportion; it must neither cause division by zero nor be silently removed from the repetition average. Dropping it changes the target to a conditional average given at least one rejection.
rubric: Average the two within-run fractions to obtain \(\frac{1}{2}\).
Distinguish FDR from a ratio of expected counts and from family-wise error.
Apply the zero-rejection convention and obtain follow-up values \(\frac{1}{4}\),\(\frac{1}{2}\),\(\frac{1}{2}\).

questions.title: Copies repeat a rejection event
questions.prompt: Twelve true-null tests are arranged in three blocks of four. Inside a block the four rejection decisions are IDENTICAL copies of one decision. Each block decision has exact false-rejection probability 0.1, and the three block decisions are independent. What is the probability of at least one false rejection among the twelve reported tests?
hints: There are three distinct random decisions, not twelve independent ones.
Complement the event that all three blocks accept.
questions.solution: No rejection occurs precisely when all three block decisions accept. Thus \(P(V>0)=1-0.9^3=271/1000\). The independent twelve-test formula counts copied evidence as new randomness. Nevertheless \(E[V]=12(0.1)=1.2\): linearity of expectation does not require independence, and four false reports are counted whenever a block falsely rejects. Expected counts and the chance of any error answer different questions.
questions.followup: If the blocks contain two, four and seven identical copies, does the family-wise error change? What are the expected false count and FDR when all hypotheses are true?
questions.followSolution: The three underlying decisions still determine the same event, so family-wise error remains \(\frac{271}{1000}\). Expected false count is (2+4+7)·0.1=1.3. Under the global null V=R, so V/max(R,1) equals the indicator of any rejection; FDR equals family-wise error. This last identity depends on ALL hypotheses being true, not on independence.
rubric: Identify three independent block decisions and calculate \(\frac{271}{1000}\).
Use linearity for expected false reports without asserting independent copies.
Explain the global-null identity between FDR and family-wise error.

questions.title: Correlated winners and shared confirmation noise
questions.prompt: Two candidates have the SAME true value \(\theta\), and observed scores \(X_i=\theta+\varepsilon_i\). The errors are jointly Gaussian, mean zero, with variance \(\sigma^2>0\) each and correlation \(\rho\in[-1,1]\). Select \(J=\arg\max_i X_i\), breaking ties toward candidate one. Derive the mean and variance of the selected score, including both singular endpoints of rho. Then let confirmation errors be \(\eta_i=a\varepsilon_i+\sqrt{1-a^2}\,\zeta_i\), where \(a\in[-1,1]\), the zeta errors are iid \(N(0,\sigma^2)\), and are independent of the original pair. Derive the mean of the selected candidate’s confirmation score \(\theta+\eta_J\). Does calling a file a holdout make that mean unbiased?
hints: Use \(S=(\varepsilon_1+\varepsilon_2)/2\) and \(D=(\varepsilon_1-\varepsilon_2)/2\). Their Gaussian covariance is zero.
The winning error is S+|D|. A centered Gaussian with standard deviation t has mean absolute value \(t\sqrt{2/\pi}\).
Condition on the original errors before averaging the independently indexed confirmation noise.
questions.solution:
The Gaussian variables S and D are independent, including the degenerate cases. Their variances are \(\sigma^2(1+\rho)/2\) and \(\sigma^2(1-\rho)/2\). Let \(b=\sigma\sqrt{(1-\rho)/\pi}\). The winning error is S+|D|, so

\[\begin{aligned}E[X_J]&=\theta+b,\\\operatorname{Var}(X_J)&=\sigma^2\left(1-\frac{1-\rho}{\pi}\right).\end{aligned}\]

The variance uses \(\operatorname{Var}|D|=E[D^2]-(E|D|)^2\), plus the independent S variance. At rho=1 both scores are identical: b=0 and variance sigma squared. At rho=−1 they are opposite errors: the winner is theta plus a folded normal, with bias \(\sigma\sqrt{2/\pi}\) and variance \(\sigma^2(1-2/\pi)\). At rho=0 the bias is sigma divided by square root pi.

Conditional on the original pair, J is fixed and the chosen zeta has mean zero. Therefore \(E[\theta+\eta_J]=\theta+ab\). Separate storage says nothing about a. Independent confirmation has a=0; reused noise has a=1 and keeps the full optimism; negative a can make confirmation pessimistic. The expected original-minus-confirmation gap is (1−a)b. This model makes the dependence mechanism explicit rather than equating a held-out filename with independent evidence.
questions.followup: Now let true candidate values differ, with delta=theta1−theta2. For \(s=\sigma\sqrt{2(1-\rho)}>0\), express the expected TRUE value of the selected candidate and its expected score optimism in terms of the standard normal density phi and distribution function Phi. Give the confirmation mean and handle s=0. Is score optimism measured relative to the better candidate’s true value?
questions.followSolution:
Write W=epsilon1−epsilon2, so W is N(0,s squared), and J=1 when W≥−delta. Hence \(E[\theta_J]=\theta_2+\delta\Phi(\delta/s)\). The selected error equals \(\varepsilon_2+W\mathbf1\{W\geq-\delta\}\), whose mean is

\[E[\varepsilon_J]=\int_{-\delta}^{\infty} w\frac{\phi(w/s)}s\,dw=s\phi(\delta/s).\]

The selected observed mean is the selected TRUE mean plus this optimism, and confirmation mean is \(E[\theta_J]+a s\phi(\delta/s)\). No independence between epsilon2 and W was used: only its unconditional zero mean. When s=0 the error is common to both candidates; select the higher true value deterministically (tie to one), with zero added bias. For delta=0 the formula recovers b; large absolute delta/s makes selection optimism vanish. Relative to the BEST true value, the difference also includes the loss from sometimes choosing the worse candidate. Confusing that benchmark with the selected candidate’s own truth hides a different source of error.
rubric: Derive independent Gaussian sum/difference variables and the folded-normal mean and variance.
Check rho=1,0,−1 rather than applying a nonsingular density at the endpoints.
Condition correctly on selection to derive theta+ab; identify the needed confirmation independence.
For unequal means derive selected truth and s phi(delta/s), distinguish its benchmark and handle s=0.

checks.prompt: With \(\sigma\)=2, \(\rho\)=\(\frac{1}{2}\) and a=−\(\frac{1}{2}\), what is the selected confirmation score’s mean minus \(\theta\)?
checks.explanation: Selection bias is \(\sigma\)√((1−\(\rho\))/π); confirmation retains a times that bias.

checks.prompt: Which correlated-selection identities are valid?

options.text: \(E[X_J]=\theta+\sigma\sqrt{(1-\rho)/\pi}\).
options.explanation: Use max=(sum+absolute difference)/2.
options.label: Expected selected score is theta plus sigma times square root of one minus rho divided by pi.

options.text: \(\operatorname{Var}(X_J)=\sigma^2[1-(1-\rho)/\pi]\), including both endpoints.
options.explanation: The Gaussian sum and difference are independent; handle degeneracies by their exact laws.
options.label: Variance of selected score is sigma squared times one minus one minus rho divided by pi, including both endpoints.

options.text: A confirmation filename makes shared selection noise vanish.
options.explanation: Its bias is a times the selection bias; a must be zero for this guarantee.
options.label: A confirmation filename makes shared selection noise vanish.

options.text: At \(\rho\)=−1 the selected score has variance \(\sigma^2\).
options.explanation: It is \(\theta\)+|ε1|, with variance \(\sigma^2\)(1−2/π).
options.label: At ρ=−1 the selected score has variance σ².

options.text: The selected score variance is sigma squared times (1−rho)/pi.
options.explanation: That term is the squared selection bias, which is subtracted from the uncentered second moment sigma squared.
options.label: The selected score variance is sigma squared times (1−rho)/pi.

questions.title: Ninety percent correct can lose money
questions.prompt: A fixed toy action rule took exactly 1000 trades. In this stipulated payoff model, each correct prediction earns 1 tick gross and each incorrect prediction loses 12 ticks gross. There were 900 correct and 100 incorrect predictions. Every trade costs 0.2 ticks in total, regardless of outcome, with no other costs or remaining inventory. What is the REALIZED mean NET payoff per trade, in ticks? These explicit payoffs connect labels to money in this toy; accuracy alone would not supply that connection.
hints: Count the magnitudes of gains and losses, not only their frequencies.
The total fee is charged on all one thousand trades.
questions.solution: Gross payoff is 900·1−100·12=−300 ticks. Total cost is 1000·0.2=200 ticks. The mean net payoff is (−300−200)/1000=−\(\frac{1}{2}\) tick per trade. A 90-percent hit rate does not offset the asymmetric loss sizes. Flat has zero under the declared toy accounting; it is a relevant economic baseline even when it makes no market prediction. This finite arithmetic does not require independent trades, nor does it determine a standard error or future expected payoff.
questions.followup: If a future trade follows the SAME fixed payoff/cost model and has correct-prediction probability p, what p gives strictly positive expected net payoff? How many correct predictions among 1000 would give strictly positive realized net payoff under this model?
questions.followSolution: Expected net payoff is p−12(1−p)−0.2=13p−12.2. It is strictly positive when p>\(\frac{61}{65}\), approximately 0.93846. With integer correct count k out of 1000, total net payoff is 13k−12200, so the smallest profitable count is 939. Equality gives zero rather than profit. Neither threshold is universal: changing costs, loss magnitudes, fill selection or action frequency changes the calculation.
rubric: Derive total gross −300, total costs 200 and mean net −\(\frac{1}{2}\) tick.
Explain why label accuracy and arithmetic profit are different evidence.
Derive p>\(\frac{61}{65}\) and the strict integer threshold of 939 successes.

questions.title: The paths that fill are a selected sample
questions.prompt: At one hypothetical passive entry price, 100 equally likely complete market paths are declared. On 60 paths the one-unit order fills and is later sold at an executable bid 2 ticks BELOW its entry price. On the other 40 paths it does not fill; their eventual bid is 6 ticks ABOVE the proposed entry price. Unfilled orders earn zero, filled orders are completely liquidated, and this toy charges no fees or other costs. What is expected strategy payoff PER POSTED OPPORTUNITY, in ticks? A future bid relative to a price at which no purchase occurred is not a realized gain.
hints: Attach zero trading payoff to unfilled paths.
Averaging all future bid changes answers a different question.
questions.solution: The opportunity payoff is −2 on the 60 filled paths and zero on the 40 unfilled paths. Hence its expectation is −1.2=−\(\frac{6}{5}\) ticks. Mean bid change relative to the proposed entry price is 0.6(−2)+0.4(6)=+1.2 ticks, but those favourable paths contain no entry. Conditional payoff given a fill is −2, while payoff per posted opportunity is 0.6 times that amount. Using unconditional future-price changes to evaluate only filled orders substitutes a different sampling event.
questions.followup: Now charge one tick on every FILLED round trip and an additional 0.1 tick on EVERY posted opportunity, including unfilled orders. Calculate conditional net payoff given a fill and unconditional net payoff per opportunity. Which charges can be multiplied by the fill probability?
questions.followSolution: Conditional on a fill the net is −2−1−0.1=−3.1 ticks. On an unfilled path it is −0.1. The opportunity mean is 0.6(−3)−0.1=−1.9 ticks. Equivalently it is 0.6(−3.1)+0.4(−0.1). The filled-round-trip fee is multiplied by fill probability; the posting cost is not. Keeping filled-only and opportunity denominators separate prevents both omitted costs and double counting. Real fill probabilities and liquidation bids would require evidence beyond this declared finite model.
rubric: Compute −\(\frac{6}{5}\) per opportunity, distinguishing it from +\(\frac{6}{5}\) unconditional bid change.
Separate conditional fill payoff from the full opportunity target.
Charge each fee on its actual event and obtain −3.1 conditional and −1.9 unconditional.

questions.title: A changed mix can reverse the baseline comparison
questions.prompt: A model M and persistence baseline P predict the same binary targets with the same available information. On QUIET opportunities their correct-prediction probabilities are respectively 0.96 and 0.99; on ACTIVE opportunities they are 0.70 and 0.60. These four conditional probabilities remain exactly the same in both periods. Quiet opportunities comprise one half of period one and nine tenths of period two. Calculate both aggregate accuracies in both periods and their paired population accuracy differences. Derive the quiet share w at which M and P tie. Does the reversal establish deterioration of the model WITHIN a market state, overfitting, or a change in trading profit?
hints: Weight conditional accuracy by the population share, not by the number of states.
The conditional model-minus-baseline difference is −0.03 in quiet and +0.10 in active.
A changed population can reverse an aggregate comparison while all conditional quantities stay fixed.
questions.solution:
In period one M has accuracy 0.5(0.96)+0.5(0.70)=0.83, while P has 0.5(0.99)+0.5(0.60)=0.795: difference +0.035. In period two M has 0.9(0.96)+0.1(0.70)=0.934; P has 0.9(0.99)+0.1(0.60)=0.951: difference −0.017. The general difference is

\[\Delta(w)=-0.03w+0.10(1-w)=0.10-0.13w.\]

It vanishes at w=\(\frac{10}{13}\). The model’s own aggregate accuracy actually rises in the later period, even while its advantage over persistence becomes negative. By construction no within-state deterioration occurred. Reweighting the later conditional results to the original one-half quiet share would recover +0.035; this separates the mixture change in this stated model. It does not prove that a fitted regime definition was causal, that a real estimated conditional difference is precise, or that a selected strategy generalizes. Accuracy supplies no payoff sizes, fills or costs, so it cannot determine net profit.
questions.followup: In observed data rather than this declared model, what must be checked before treating reweighting as a diagnosis? Can subtracting the two marginal accuracies determine how many records M alone gets right?
questions.followSolution: State the regime definition and whether it was available at each decision; compare identical target records, account for missing observations, quantify conditional-sample uncertainty/dependence and disclose any regime selection after looking at outcomes. Reweighting requires relevant support: an absent state has no observed conditional performance to transport. The accuracy difference equals Pr(M right,P wrong)−Pr(M wrong,P right), but it does not identify either disagreement probability separately. Overlap counts require the paired record-level predictions. A pre-specified decomposition can diagnose a mixture contribution without ruling out implementation, search or execution problems elsewhere.
rubric: Calculate model versus baseline accuracy 0.83 versus 0.795, then 0.934 versus 0.951, with differences +0.035 and −0.017.
Derive w=\(\frac{10}{13}\) and distinguish aggregate mixture from within-state changes.
Identify causal regime definitions, support and conditional uncertainty as evidence obligations.
Explain why marginal accuracy differences cannot recover paired disagreement counts or profit.

questions.title: Selective observations do not identify a policy by themselves
questions.prompt:
Consider iid independent opportunities with observed context X. A fixed target policy \(\pi(X)\in\{0,1\}\) either takes a declared trade or stays flat. Let Y be the potential NET payoff of taking that trade, including zero/no-fill outcomes, all stated costs and complete terminal liquidation; staying flat has payoff zero. In this hypothetical model there is no market impact, interference, or inventory carried between opportunities, and implementing the target does not change Y. Historical action A is binary with KNOWN probability \(e(X)=P(A=1\mid X)\), and A is independent of Y conditional on X. Every opportunity and its A are recorded, but Y is observed only when A=1. On contexts where pi=1 assume e>0.

Prove unbiasedness for the target value \(v=E[\pi(X)Y]\) of the single-opportunity score \(Z=A\pi(X)Y/e(X)\), treating it as zero when pi=0. Derive its second moment and the variance of a mean of n independent scores, when those moments are finite. Then use two equally likely contexts: quiet with e=\(\frac{1}{4}\) and deterministic Y=+3 ticks, stressed with e=\(\frac{3}{4}\) and Y=−1 tick; pi=1 in both. Calculate v, the conditional mean payoff among historically traded opportunities, and Var(Z). Which assumptions would fail if your historical logger observed an unrecorded predictor of payoff?
hints: Condition on X and the potential payoff before averaging the randomized historical action.
The traded-only mean weights contexts by e(X), whereas the target population need not.
Use \(A^2=A\). The second moment contains one inverse propensity factor after averaging A, not two.
questions.solution:
For pi=1, conditional independence gives \(E[A\mid X,Y]=e(X)\). Thus \(E[Z\mid X,Y]=\pi(X)Y\); for pi=0 the target and score are both zero without dividing by a zero e. Averaging gives E[Z]=v. Squaring before conditioning yields

\[E[Z^2]=E\!\left[\frac{\pi(X)Y^2}{e(X)}\right],\]

where the integrand is defined as zero on pi=0. Hence \(\operatorname{Var}(\bar Z_n)=(E[Z^2]-v^2)/n\) for independent identically distributed scores with finite second moment. Very small logging probabilities can make that moment large or infinite even when Y is bounded unless positivity is bounded away from zero.

In the declared two-state example v=(3−1)/2=1 tick. Historical trade probability is (\(\frac{1}{4}\)+\(\frac{3}{4}\))/2=\(\frac{1}{2}\). Unnormalized traded payoff is (\(\frac{1}{2}\))(\(\frac{1}{4}\))3+(\(\frac{1}{2}\))(\(\frac{3}{4}\))(−1)=0, so the traded-only conditional mean is zero. Z takes value 12 with probability \(\frac{1}{8}\), −\(\frac{4}{3}\) with probability \(\frac{3}{8}\) and zero with remaining probability \(\frac{1}{2}\). Its second moment is 18+\(\frac{2}{3}\)=\(\frac{56}{3}\) and variance is \(\frac{53}{3}\). Historical selection changes the context mix; simply averaging observed trades answers the wrong policy question.

If the logger selects using an unrecorded predictor of Y, knowing the marginal e(X) does not ensure conditional independence. The key equality E[A|X,Y]=e(X) can fail. Weighting then need not identify the counterfactual policy. Likewise these assumptions deliberately exclude size-dependent execution, carry-over inventory and intervention-dependent market paths: a reweighted toy cannot certify a different strategy’s live economics.
questions.followup: In a DIFFERENT dataset quiet opportunities still have probability one half, but are NEVER traded (e=0), and their potential payoff is otherwise unknown in [−B,B], B≥1. Stressed opportunities have known payoff −1. With pi=1 everywhere, derive the sharp interval for v. Separately, under |Y|≤B and e≥epsilon>0 wherever pi=1, bound E[Z²]. Does clipping inverse weights retain exact unbiasedness?
questions.followSolution:
The stressed contribution is −\(\frac{1}{2}\) and the unobserved quiet contribution can be any number in [−B/2,B/2]. Thus

\[v\in\left[-\frac{B+1}{2},\frac{B-1}{2}\right].\]

Both endpoints are attainable by assigning every unobserved quiet trade payoff −B or +B; the logged observations are identical in those worlds. No reweighting recovers data where the action has zero support. Under the separate bounded-positivity assumptions, E[Z²]≤B²/epsilon, because E[pi Y²/e]≤B²/epsilon. Clipping at c replaces 1/e by min(1/e,c); conditional score mean becomes pi Y min(1,c e), generally changing the estimand/bias. It can reduce variance, but exact unbiasedness needs a new justification. Self-normalizing empirical weights also generally changes finite-sample unbiasedness. Choosing a policy after inspecting these same outcomes adds selection beyond the fixed-policy proof.
rubric: State fixed policy, conditional action independence, overlap and the net-payoff/no-interference accounting boundary.
Prove the first/second moments by conditioning and require finite moments for the iid variance formula.
Calculate target 1, traded-only mean 0 and score variance \(\frac{53}{3}\).
Identify unrecorded selection and zero action support as identification failures; derive sharp bounds and explain clipping bias.

questions.title: Count independently drawn pairs
questions.prompt: A simulation makes 512 function evaluations grouped into 256 pairs. Different pairs are independently sampled, while the two evaluations within a pair may be dependent. The 256 pair AVERAGES have sample variance 36 in squared payoff units. What is the estimated standard error of the mean of those pair averages? Use the usual sample-variance-over-independent-unit-count formula.
hints: The independent sample count is 256, not 512.
The standard deviation of pair averages is six.
questions.solution: The estimated variance of the mean is \(\frac{36}{256}\), so estimated standard error is \(\frac{6}{16}\)=\(\frac{3}{8}\) payoff unit. The covariance inside a pair has already influenced the variance of its average. Dividing that pair variance by 512 would pretend there were twice as many independently sampled pair averages. This is an estimated Monte Carlo precision for the chosen design; it does not certify the underlying model or the closeness of this one realized estimate.
questions.followup: Under the planning assumption that pair variance remains unchanged, how many independent pairs and function evaluations are needed to halve the standard error? Would copying each saved pair count as new sampling?
questions.followSolution: Standard error scales as the inverse square root of the independent pair count. Halving it needs four times the count: 1024 independent pairs and 2048 evaluations under the stated two-evaluation cost. Copies reuse the same randomness and do not reduce uncertainty. The future sample variance need not be exactly 36; the fourfold rule is the planning comparison under a stable variance assumption.
rubric: Identify 256 independent units and obtain \(\frac{3}{8}\) payoff unit.
Explain why within-pair dependence is incorporated before the count division.
Give 1024 pairs/2048 evaluations and reject duplicated records as new draws.

questions.title: Compare variance at the same evaluation cost
questions.prompt: Each output has the same mean theta and variance 4. A paired construction preserves both marginals and gives covariance −3 between its two outputs. Different pairs are independent. You can afford exactly 2000 function evaluations: either 1000 such pairs, averaged through their pair averages, or 2000 independent single outputs. What is the ratio of the PAIRED estimator variance to the independent estimator variance? Each evaluation has equal cost and pairing has no extra cost in this toy.
hints: The variance of (Y1+Y2)/2 contains twice the covariance before division by four.
Divide the pair variance by 1000 and the single-output variance by 2000.
questions.solution: One pair average has variance (4+4+2(−3))/4=\(\frac{1}{2}\) and mean theta. Across 1000 independent pair averages the estimator variance is \(\frac{1}{2000}\). Across 2000 independent singles it is \(\frac{4}{2000}\)=\(\frac{1}{500}\). The variance ratio is one quarter; the standard-error ratio is one half. Counting pairs as 2000 independent units would exaggerate the gain. Equal marginals preserve the target; the covariance and cost determine this comparison.
questions.followup: Keep each marginal variance at four but change the pair covariance to +4. What is the equal-cost variance ratio? Why does a negative covariance alone not settle a comparison with a differently priced algorithm?
questions.followSolution: At covariance +4 the two centered outputs coincide almost surely, because their difference has zero variance. The pair-average variance is four, giving \(\frac{4}{1000}\) compared with \(\frac{4}{2000}\) for singles: ratio two. Its second evaluation repeats the same noise. With unequal costs, compare estimator variance at a common total computational budget; an expensive construction can use fewer independent units. Covariance alone describes variance per pair, not variance per unit of time or money.
rubric: Compute pair variance \(\frac{1}{2}\) and budget-matched estimator variances.
Obtain variance ratio \(\frac{1}{4}\) and distinguish it from standard-error ratio \(\frac{1}{2}\).
Derive the positive-covariance ratio two and name the needed cost comparison.

questions.title: No rare-event hits is not zero uncertainty
questions.prompt: Before sampling, fix n independent Bernoulli simulation trials with unknown event probability p. You observe K=0 events. The empirical event rate and its plug-in standard error are both zero. Derive a one-sided 95-percent upper bound u_n from the probability of zero hits, and prove coverage of this complete confidence rule: report [0,u_n] when K=0, and [0,1] otherwise. Compute u_1000 approximately, and the smallest integer n for which u_n≤0.001. Use alpha=0.05; include the endpoints. This is a deliberately conservative rule for nonzero K, not a claim that the observed event probability has a posterior distribution.
hints: For a fixed n, \(P_p(K=0)=(1-p)^n\).
Invert the zero-hit probability at alpha, and check the event on which the interval misses the true p.
Take logarithms carefully: log(0.999) is negative.
questions.solution:
Solve (1−u_n)^n=alpha, giving

\[u_n=1-\alpha^{1/n}.\]

If p≤u_n, the reported interval always covers p. If p>u_n, the only possible miss is K=0, with probability (1−p)^n<alpha. Thus unconditional coverage is at least 95 percent at every p. Equality p=u_n is covered because the interval is closed. The statement concerns repetitions of the fixed-n procedure, not a 95-percent posterior probability after seeing zero.

For n=1000, u_n is approximately 0.00299125. The requirement u_n≤0.001 is equivalent to n≥log(0.05)/log(0.999), approximately 2994.234. Hence the smallest integer count is 2995. A zero sample variance reflects no observed variation in that finite sample; it does not rule out unobserved rare losses. Monte Carlo error, rare-event support and model error remain separate.
questions.followup: Instead inspect independent blocks of 2995 trials repeatedly until the FIRST all-zero block appears, then report the same upper bound. For a fixed p strictly between 0.001 and one, what is the chance that this procedure eventually reports an interval missing p? Would relabeling these dependent/adaptively selected trials as a fixed run repair coverage?
questions.followSolution: Each independent block is all-zero with positive probability (1−p)^2995. The probability of never seeing such a block after M blocks is [1−(1−p)^2995]^M, which tends to zero. Eventually an all-zero block appears almost surely, and its reported upper bound is below p. The eventual miscoverage probability is therefore one. A fixed sample count and one pre-specified inspection were part of the original coverage proof. Optional repetition/selection changes the reporting procedure; an appropriate sequential bound or a pre-specified error budget would require a new proof. Mere relabeling cannot make selected evidence fixed or independent.
rubric: Invert the fixed-n zero-hit tail to 1−alpha^(1/n).
Prove unconditional coverage for the stated complete rule, including boundary p=u_n.
Compute about 0.00299125 and minimum count 2995 without treating zero plug-in error as certainty.
Show almost-sure eventual miscoverage under repeated-block selection and explain which design assumption changed.
