questions.title: A coefficient fitted on two draws can bias the mean
questions.prompt: The control C is uniform on {0,1,2}, with KNOWN mean one; target output is Y=C² and target expectation is \(\frac{5}{3}\). Draw C1,C2 independently. If C1 differs from C2, fit the secant coefficient c=(C1²−C2²)/(C1−C2)=C1+C2; if they coincide, set c=0. Report \(T=(C_1^2+C_2^2)/2-c((C_1+C_2)/2-1)\) using THESE SAME two draws. What is E[T]? Decide whether the known control mean alone guarantees unbiasedness here. All nine ordered pairs are equally likely.
hints: Separate the equal-control branch from the secant-fit branch.
For unequal a,b, simplify the adjusted estimate to a+b−ab.
Average all nine ordered outcomes, retaining their multiplicities.
questions.solution:
The ordered-pair estimates, in row order C1=0,1,2 and column order C2=0,1,2, are

\[\begin{pmatrix}0&1&2\\1&1&1\\2&1&4\end{pmatrix}.\]

Their sum is 13, so E[T]=\(\frac{13}{9}\), with bias −\(\frac{2}{9}\) relative to \(\frac{5}{3}\). Although the control sample mean minus one has mean zero, the fitted c is dependent on it. One cannot factor E[c(Cbar−1)] into the product of means. The coefficient was chosen to fit the same random observations whose average is then corrected. The explicit equal-draw convention matters: silently dividing by zero or discarding that branch changes the procedure.
questions.followup: Fit c by the SAME rule on a separate independent two-draw pilot, then freeze it and use TWO fresh main draws. Derive the main estimator’s unconditional mean and variance. Compare that variance with using the fixed population-optimal coefficient. Does a random independent pilot require adding a separate variance of its conditional mean?
questions.followSolution:
Pilot c has probability \(\frac{1}{3}\) of zero and probability \(\frac{2}{9}\) each of one, two and three. Thus E[c]=\(\frac{4}{3}\) and E[c²]=\(\frac{28}{9}\). For the main law, Var(C)=\(\frac{2}{3}\), Var(Y)=\(\frac{26}{9}\) and Cov(C,Y)=\(\frac{4}{3}\). Conditional on the pilot, the adjusted MAIN mean is always \(\frac{5}{3}\). Total variance therefore averages the conditional main variance with no extra conditional-mean term:

\[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{Var}(T_{\mathrm{pilot}})&=\frac12\left(\frac{26}{9}+\frac{28}{9}\frac23-2\frac43\frac43\right)\\&=\frac{19}{27}.\end{aligned}\]

The fixed optimum is c*=2, giving one-output variance \(\frac{2}{9}\) and two-draw mean variance \(\frac{1}{9}\). The noisy pilot remains unbiased but has larger variance than that optimum. Its unconditional excess is (Var(C)/2)E[(c−2)²]=\(\frac{16}{27}\). There is no separate Var(E[T|pilot]) contribution here because that conditional expectation is the same constant \(\frac{5}{3}\) for every pilot. Conditional main-sample uncertainty still needs to use the actual adjusted outputs. This argument fixes the sampling design; selecting a coefficient or estimator by its flattering main result would be another procedure.
rubric: Retain all nine ordered pairs and the c=0 tie convention to obtain E[T]=\(\frac{13}{9}\).
Identify the forbidden factorization behind a false unbiasedness claim.
Condition on an independent pilot to restore mean \(\frac{5}{3}\).
Derive pilot moments and variance \(\frac{19}{27}\), compare optimum \(\frac{1}{9}\) and explain the zero conditional-mean variance term.

questions.title: Use the old mean and the new mean
questions.prompt: Three stored observations are [8,10,12]. Their count is n=3, mean m=10 and CENTRED squared-deviation sum M2=8. A new observation x=14 arrives. Update the mean, then use the old-mean deviation times the new-mean deviation to update M2. What is the NEW M2? Work in exact arithmetic; M2 is a sum, not an already-divided variance.
hints: The new mean is 11; the old-mean deviation is four.
Add (14−10)(14−11) to the old M2.
questions.solution: The new count is four and the new mean is 10+(14−10)/4=11. The M2 increment is (14−10)(14−11)=12, giving M2=20. Direct residuals around 11 are −3, −1, 1 and 3; their squares sum to 20. Using the old mean twice adds 16 and incorrectly gives 24. The update preserves a centred sum whose centre itself changes.
questions.followup: What are the descriptive variance and the usual sample-variance estimate? Which assumption lets you interpret the latter as unbiased for a population variance? Could an algorithm settle that assumption?
questions.followSolution: The descriptive variance is \(\frac{20}{4}\)=5. The usual sample variance is 20/(4−1)=\(\frac{20}{3}\). Under iid sampling from a population with a finite second moment, the latter is unbiased for that population variance. The arithmetic can compute both quantities for dependent observations, but their usual population interpretation does not follow from the update. A data-structure invariant is distinct from a sampling assumption.
rubric: Update the count/mean to four and 11 before the second deviation.
Obtain M2=20 and reject the old-mean-twice increment.
Separate 5 from \(\frac{20}{3}\) and state the iid finite-second-moment interpretation.

questions.title: A maximum value can hide a wrong tie rule
questions.prompt: values=[5,5,4,5] has indices 0,1,2,3. At index 3, consider the complete CURRENT-INCLUSIVE window of width k=3. Return the EARLIEST index attaining its maximum. What index should be returned? Explain which expired and tied observations remain eligible; values alone are insufficient for this contract.
hints: The final window contains indices 1,2,3, not 0,1,2.
The eligible maxima occur at indices one and three.
questions.solution: The eligible window is [1,2,3], containing [5,4,5]. Index zero is expired because it is ≤3−3. The earliest eligible maximum is index one. Replacing an older equal-valued candidate with index three preserves the maximum VALUE but violates the earliest-index answer. Store indices so equality and expiry remain distinguishable.
questions.followup: Which back-removal comparison should a monotone deque use for earliest ties? Which should it use for newest ties? If value zero arrives at index four, what becomes the earliest maximum in the new window?
questions.followSolution: For earliest ties, remove older candidates only when their values are STRICTLY smaller than the new value; retain equal values in increasing index order. For newest ties, remove smaller-or-equal values. At index four the window is [2,3,4], so index one expires and index three is the earliest maximum. Tie handling and expiry are independent obligations; keeping all equal candidates can use k entries for a constant window.
rubric: Use the final current-inclusive window [1,2,3] and return index one.
Explain why the same maximum value does not certify a tie-index contract.
Distinguish < from ≤ back-removal and derive index three after the next arrival.

questions.title: Merge statistics without mixing up within and between
questions.prompt: Two DISJOINT batches contain finite real observations. Each is summarised by count n, arithmetic mean m and CENTRED sum \(M_2=\sum_i(x_i-m)^2\), with no variance denominator applied. Derive a constant-arithmetic-work merge of two nonempty summaries that equals recomputing these three summaries on the concatenated data in exact arithmetic. Evaluate it for batch A=[0,2] and batch B=[8,10,12]. Include an empty-batch identity, the descriptive/sample variance conventions and whether exact associativity implies bit-for-bit floating associativity.
hints: The combined mean is weighted by batch counts, not by number of batches.
Expand each batch’s residuals around the combined mean; its residual sum around its own mean is zero.
Different batch means create a between-batch term even if both within-batch variances vanish.
questions.solution:
Let n=n_A+n_B and delta=m_B−m_A. For nonempty batches,

\[\begin{aligned}m&=m_A+\frac{n_B}{n}\delta,\\M_2&=M_{2,A}+M_{2,B}+\frac{n_A n_B}{n}\delta^2.\end{aligned}\]

Within each batch, expanding x−m=(x−m_batch)+(m_batch−m) makes its cross term zero. Thus its contribution is its old M2 plus n_batch(m_batch−m)². The two mean-shift terms simplify to n_A n_B delta²/n. Counts, not batches, supply the weights. For A, (n,m,M2)=(2,1,2); for B, (3,10,8). Their union has n=5, mean \(\frac{32}{5}\) and M2=10+(\(\frac{6}{5}\))81=\(\frac{536}{5}\). Descriptive variance is \(\frac{536}{25}\); sample variance is \(\frac{134}{5}\). Simply averaging 1 and 10, or averaging the within variances, answers a different question.

An empty summary has count zero with undefined mean and zero centred sum; merging it returns the other summary without subtracting an undefined mean. Two empty batches stay empty. For count one, descriptive variance is zero and sample variance is undefined. Since concatenation determines the exact sufficient summaries, the exact merge is associative and commutative. Floating addition/multiplication round at each operation, so different merge trees can produce different final bits; exact associativity is not a reproducibility or numerical-accuracy guarantee.
questions.followup: A colleague proposes averaging worker variances by their observation counts, omitting the between-worker term. Give a two-worker example where every worker variance is zero but the combined variance is positive. What changes if batches overlap or worker outputs have already been divided by \(n-1\)?
questions.followSolution: Workers containing [0,0] and [10,10] each have M2=0 and descriptive variance zero. Their union has mean five and M2=100, descriptive variance 25. The missing quantity is variability between worker means. For disjoint nonempty batches, a supplied sample variance must first be converted to M2=(\(n-1\))s²; an empty/singleton convention is needed when that variance is undefined. Overlapping batches duplicate observations if treated as disjoint; the formulas then describe the multiset with those repetitions, not the intended unique dataset. Counts and moment summaries alone generally cannot identify which records overlap.
rubric: Derive both count-weighted mean and between-batch centred-sum term.
Compute n=5, m=\(\frac{32}{5}\), M2=\(\frac{536}{5}\) and the two variance conventions.
Handle empty/singleton summaries without undefined operations.
Separate exact associativity from floating reproducibility and disjointness from duplicated records.

checks.prompt: What is the merged centered sum M2 for the two given batches?
checks.explanation: Within sums are 2 and 8; the between-batch correction is (2×\(\frac{3}{5}\))×9²=97.2.

checks.prompt: Which merge rules are valid?

options.text: Merged \(M_2=M_{2,A}+M_{2,B}+\delta^2 n_A n_B/(n_A+n_B)\).
options.explanation: Expand each observation around the merged mean.
options.label: Merged M two is both within-batch M two sums plus delta squared times both batch counts divided by total count.

options.text: An empty batch acts as identity; sample variance requires n>1, and exact associativity need not be bitwise floating associativity.
options.explanation: Rounding depends on arithmetic order.
options.label: An empty batch acts as identity; sample variance requires n>1, and exact associativity need not be bitwise floating associativity.

options.text: For \(\delta=m_B-m_A\), merged mean is \(m_A+\delta n_B/(n_A+n_B)\).
options.explanation: It is the weighted batch mean.
options.label: For delta equal to batch B mean minus batch A mean, merged mean is batch A mean plus delta times batch B count divided by total count.

options.text: Merged M2 is simply M2_A+M2_B.
options.explanation: This loses between-batch mean differences.
options.label: Merged M2 is simply M2_A+M2_B.

options.text: The centered sum M2 already contains the unbiased variance divisor.
options.explanation: It is a sum; denominator conventions are separate.
options.label: The centered sum M2 already contains the unbiased variance divisor.

questions.title: A rolling statistic must remember what leaves
questions.prompt: A streaming monitor reports the mean and centred squared-deviation sum M2 for the latest FULL window of width k≥2. An insertion-only Welford implementation retains just (k,m,M2). Derive an exact-arithmetic REMOVE-THEN-ADD update when the departing oldest value y is known and a new value x arrives. Can (k,m,M2) plus x alone determine the new window statistics for every ordered history? Give an explicit indistinguishable-summary counterexample. State the needed data structure and arithmetic/storage costs. Discuss the k=1 boundary and numerical risks separately from the exact derivation.
hints: Invert a Welford insertion to obtain the mean and M2 after removing y.
Compare ordered windows [0,1,2] and [2,1,0], then append three.
A streaming source does not necessarily let you reread the value from k arrivals ago.
questions.solution:
Remove y from k observations. The remaining k−1 observations have

\[\begin{aligned}m_-&=m+\frac{m-y}{k-1},\\M_{2,-}&=M_2-(y-m)(y-m_-).\end{aligned}\]

The mean follows from km−y; the M2 formula inverts the centred insertion identity. Now add x:

\[\begin{aligned}m_+&=m_-+\frac{x-m_-}{k},\\M_{2,+}&=M_{2,-}+(x-m_-)(x-m_+).\end{aligned}\]

Both [0,1,2] and [2,1,0] have k=3, m=1 and M2=2. Appending three removes zero from the first and two from the second. Their new windows are [1,2,3] with mean two/M2 two, and [1,0,3] with mean 4/3/M2 \(\frac{14}{3}\). Identical retained summaries plus identical arrival require different answers, so the proposed state is insufficient. In a one-pass source, a FIFO queue or ring buffer of the k recent values supplies y. Updates use O(1) arithmetic and \(O(k)\) value storage, excluding output; a batch array can instead supply y by index, but that array is still retained history.

For k=1 replace the only observation: mean x, M2 zero, descriptive variance zero, no sample variance. Do not divide by k−1. The formulas are exact identities, not floating stability theorems. Repeated subtract/add updates can accumulate rounding and a slightly negative M2. Blindly clamping all negatives can conceal an indexing error or a materially wrong statistic. Validate against centred recomputation and a scale-aware numerical tolerance; rebasing every k replacements costs \(O(k)\) per rebase and \(O(n)\) total work over n replacements, but still supplies no universal error guarantee for arbitrary inputs or rounded observations.
questions.followup: For binary observations, justify an information lower bound for a state that can report the current exact k-window sum and continue under arbitrary next arrivals. Does this prove that every implementation needs k Python objects or k machine words? Could storing one unbounded integer evade the bound?
questions.followSolution:
There are \(2^k\) ordered binary windows, written \(b_1,\ldots,b_k\). Query the current sum \(s_0\), then append k zeros and query each resulting sum \(s_1,\ldots,s_k=0\):

\[\begin{aligned}s_t&=\sum_{j=t+1}^k b_j,\\b_t&=s_{t-1}-s_t\quad(1\leq t\leq k).\end{aligned}\]

The differences recover the original observations in order. Therefore two different binary windows cannot share the same state under this query/continuation contract: at least \(2^k\) distinguishable states, or k bits, are necessary. This is a BIT lower bound; it does not assert k objects or words. Bit-packing can compress a binary ring buffer, and one unbounded integer could encode the whole window, but that integer still occupies \(\Omega(k)\) bits and its arithmetic is not a constant-cost fixed-width-word operation. Exact means reveal sums by multiplying by k. This argument fixes the reporting/window contract and does not claim that one approximate variance estimate requires the same state.
rubric: Derive removal and insertion identities with old/new means in the correct factors.
Use two ordered histories with equal retained summaries and different departing values.
Separate O(1) arithmetic from \(O(k)\) retained values and handle k=1 explicitly.
Discuss floating drift/rebasing without silently certifying accuracy.
Prove the binary k-bit lower bound and distinguish bits from objects/words.

checks.prompt: From window [0,2,4], remove the oldest 0 and append 6. What is the new M2?
checks.explanation: The new window [2,4,6] has mean 4 and squared deviations 4+0+4.

questions.title: Correct heap maxima with an incorrect space claim
questions.prompt: For a current-inclusive rolling maximum of width k, an implementation pushes (−value,index) into an ordinary binary min-heap at each arrival. Before reporting, it removes heap ROOTS whose indices are ≤i−k. Python tuple ties choose the smaller index, so the intended returned index is the earliest maximum. The author claims O(n log k) total time and \(O(k)\) auxiliary memory because every active window has at most k values. Audit correctness and the cost claim. Exhibit a fixed-small-k stream with unbounded retained heap size, then design and prove an \(O(n)\)-total-time/\(O(k)\)-auxiliary deque algorithm that returns the earliest maximum index. Separate worst-case single-update cost, amortised cost and result storage.
hints: An expired item can remain buried below a better current maximum.
At k=2, consider a strictly increasing input stream.
For earliest ties, equal old candidates must survive back dominance.
questions.solution:
Root eviction yields a correct answer once the root is eligible: if the root were expired it would be removed; among surviving entries the heap orders by greatest value and then earliest index, so no eligible entry is better. But eligibility of the root does not bound all retained entries. For k=2 and a strictly increasing stream, each new value is the global maximum at the root. Old expired smaller values stay buried and are never popped. After n arrivals the heap contains n entries. Its space is Θ(n) on this input and pushing successive new minima in the negated-key heap can require Θ(log i) swaps, hence Θ(n log n) total work; a log-k/\(O(k)\) claim is false.

Store a deque of increasing candidate indices with NONINCREASING values. At arrival i: remove front indices ≤i−k; remove back indices whose values are STRICTLY smaller than values[i]; append i. An older strictly smaller value is dominated: any future right-moving fixed-width window containing it also contains the newer larger value, which expires later. Equal values are retained because the earlier index wins the declared tie. Thus the front is the earliest eligible maximum. A complete window exists only when i≥k−1.

Each index enters once and leaves at most once, by expiry or dominance, so there are at most n pushes and n total pops. Deque end operations give \(O(n)\) total work and O(min(k,n)) auxiliary entries; result storage is separately O(max(n−k+1,0)). One arrival can still pop Θ(k) candidates: build a decreasing full window, then insert a value larger than all of them. Constant AMORTISED update cost does not mean every update finishes in constant worst-case work.
questions.followup: Now allow a query to move its left boundary BACKWARD after indices have been evicted. Does the same dominance/expiry proof survive? Give a concrete example. Could a bounded-size heap fix its storage just by dropping any expired item while still supporting such re-expansion?
questions.followSolution: It does not survive. With [10,1,2] processed using width one, only index two/value two is retained. Re-expanding the query to [0,2] needs the discarded value ten. The proof depended on a left boundary that never moves backward and on newer dominators remaining in every relevant future window. Expired does not mean permanently irrelevant when re-expansion is permitted. A heap that permanently drops those records loses the same information. Retain a history with a suitable range-query structure, or restrict the query contract; neither is the same \(O(k)\) fixed-window streaming promise. Handling out-of-order arrivals likewise requires a defined reordering/late-data policy before reusing the chronological proof.
rubric: Prove root-answer correctness separately from the size/cost claim.
Construct increasing input at fixed k=2 with n retained heap entries and logarithmic pushes.
Give the earliest-tie deque invariant, strict dominance proof and independent expiry rule.
Prove aggregate \(O(n)\), bound auxiliary/output storage and exhibit a costly individual update.
Explain why backward re-expansion invalidates permanent discards.

checks.prompt: For k=2 and strictly increasing values 1 through 100, how many entries remain in the described lazy heap after the last arrival?
checks.explanation: The newest, valid maximum is always at the root; expired smaller entries never reach the cleanup root.

options.explanation: Expired entries can remain hidden below the root.
options.label: The heap necessarily uses O(k) space because only k timestamps are active.

options.label: For earliest ties the deque should pop tail values equal to the new value.

options.text: The deque has \(O(n)\) total operations and \(O(k)\) auxiliary space, but one update can still remove \(O(k)\) entries.

options.explanation: Each index is pushed once and removed at most once.
options.label: A decreasing deque removes expired front indices and pops strictly smaller tail values; retaining equal values preserves the earliest tie.

options.text: The root cleanup can report a correct maximum while retaining arbitrarily many expired entries.

options.label: The lazy heap’s total work is O(n log k) on every stream, even if its retained size grows to n.

questions.title: A settlement edge is not an early-exit profit
questions.prompt: A contract has conditional expected terminal cash payment 106. A dealer’s executable bid / ask is 104 / 105. You BUY one contract now; a purchase costs an additional 0.25 and there is no settlement fee. Interest is zero. Under expected-cash-profit preferences, what is the expected NET profit if you hold to settlement? Your quote is guaranteed executable and carries no extra information about the payment. An alternative plan is to sell before settlement at a guaranteed executable bid 104.5, paying another 0.25 sale fee. Explain why the two plans have different answers. Prices already contain the spread.
hints: A taker buys at the dealer’s ask, not its bid or midpoint.
For holding, subtract 105 and the one applicable fee from 106.
questions.solution: Holding gives expected net profit 106−105−0.25=0.75. The early exit instead gives cash profit 104.5−105−0.25−0.25=−1.00. Its exit payment is the bid you receive, not the still-uncertain terminal payment you no longer own. Do not subtract an extra bid–ask spread: the entry ask and exit bid already account for it. A positive settlement expectation is not a promise about an executable early exit, nor a guarantee of a gain at settlement.
questions.followup: If you instead SELL short one contract at the original bid and hold it to settlement, what is expected net profit when the sale fee is 0.25? If a second identical contract settles on the SAME underlying outcome, do two contracts remove the risk?
questions.followSolution: The short receives 104, pays 0.25 to trade and owes the terminal payment: expected net profit 104−0.25−106=−2.25. Two identical contracts on the same outcome double the random cash profit or loss; they do not make independent trials or diversify that exposure. Cash-flow signs, number of fees and the actual exit/settlement objective must be specified separately.
rubric: Buy at ask 105 and get 0.75 after the stated purchase fee.
Use exit bid 104.5 and two fees to obtain −1, without subtracting spread twice.
Obtain short edge −2.25 and identify shared, rather than independent, settlement risk.

questions.title: A signal about one component moves both
questions.prompt: A contract pays V=A+B. The joint probabilities for (A,B)=(0,0),(0,10),(10,0),(10,10) are 0.4,0.1,0.1,0.4. A binary signal H/L is conditionally independent of B GIVEN A, with P(H|A=10)=\(\frac{3}{4}\) and P(H|A=0)=\(\frac{1}{4}\). You see H before acting. Derive the posterior weights and E[V|H]; explain whether updating A but leaving E[B]=5 is justified. A still-executable dealer quote is bid 12 / ask 14.5; either trade costs 0.25, interest is zero, shorting is allowed and the objective is expected cash profit at settlement. Should you buy, sell or abstain? Quote availability adds no further information.
hints: Weight each JOINT record by its signal likelihood before normalising.
The denominator is P(H), not the probability of the high A state.
Conditional independence given A does not make A and B independent.
questions.solution:
The unnormalised H weights are 0.1,0.025,0.075,0.3. They sum to P(H)=\(\frac{1}{2}\); posterior weights are \(\frac{1}{5}\),\(\frac{1}{20}\),\(\frac{3}{20}\),\(\frac{3}{5}\). Thus

\[\begin{aligned}E[A\mid H]&=10(3/20+3/5)=15/2,\\E[B\mid H]&=10(1/20+3/5)=13/2,\\E[V\mid H]&=14.\end{aligned}\]

Learning about A also moves B because their joint distribution is dependent. Updating only A gives the incorrect value 12.5; treating H as a perfect reveal gives another incorrect value 15. The actual net buy edge is 14−14.5−0.25=−0.75 and sell edge is 12−14−0.25=−2.25. Abstain. The posterior is about specified payments, not a midpoint or a realised payout.
questions.followup: Now you also learn that B=10. What is E[V|H,B=10]? Separately compute E[V|L] and check that averaging over H/L recovers the prior E[V]. Does “the conditional means average back” imply no benefit from choosing an action after a signal?
questions.followSolution: Among the B=10 records after H, the weights are \(\frac{1}{20}\) and \(\frac{3}{5}\). The probability A=10 is (\(\frac{3}{5}\))/(\(\frac{13}{20}\))=\(\frac{12}{13}\), so E[V|H,B=10]=10+\(\frac{120}{13}\)=\(\frac{250}{13}\). For L the posterior weights are \(\frac{3}{5}\),\(\frac{3}{20}\),\(\frac{1}{20}\),\(\frac{1}{5}\), giving E[V|L]=6. Hence (\(\frac{1}{2}\))14+(\(\frac{1}{2}\))6=10, equal to the prior mean. This is the tower property for one specified payment. Optimising a buy/sell/abstain action AFTER a signal applies a maximum to conditional edges; a maximum does not commute with averaging. Information can change the chosen action even when mean payoff averages back, provided that those actions/prices remain available.
rubric: Normalise the four joint H weights by \(\frac{1}{2}\) and obtain means 7.5, 6.5 and 14.
Explain how dependence updates B despite conditional independence of the signal given A.
Use the correct executable sides/costs and abstain on edges −0.75 and −2.25.
Derive \(\frac{250}{13}\) after both observations and verify L mean six and the tower identity.
Separate the expected payment from the value of an information-dependent action.

checks.prompt: Compute E[V|H].
checks.explanation: Posterior cells are 0.2,0.05,0.15,0.6.

options.explanation: Compare updated fair value with executable ask and costs.
options.label: Buying is profitable merely because the signal raises fair value above its prior mean.

options.explanation: Buy edge is −0.75 and sell edge is −2.25.
options.label: Both buy and sell have negative expected net edge at the given quote; abstaining is optimal.

options.explanation: Marginal independence does not follow.
options.label: Conditional independence of H and B given A lets E[B] remain at 5 after H.

options.explanation: The signal updates B through its dependence on A.
options.label: After H, E[A]=7.5 and E[B]=6.5.

questions.title: A physical expectation and a replicated price
questions.prompt: In a one-period, frictionless two-state market, cash has gross return one. A traded asset costs S0=5 and pays 2 in the low state or 8 in the high state. Both states are possible; your physical probability of high is \(\frac{3}{4}\). A new claim pays 1 in low and 13 in high. Fractional holdings, borrowing and shorting at these prices are allowed. Find the claim’s physical expected payoff and the cost of a portfolio that replicates its payment in BOTH states. Derive the no-arbitrage claim price and its risk-neutral weighting. Explain why replacing that weighting with your physical probability is not a replication argument.
hints: Match the high-minus-low claim payment using units of the traded asset.
Use the low state to determine the cash holding; it may be negative.
A risk-neutral high weight makes the asset’s weighted payoff equal its current price.
questions.solution:
The physical expected payment is (\(\frac{1}{4}\))1+(\(\frac{3}{4}\))13=10. Matching the claim’s payoff difference gives delta=(13−1)/(8−2)=2 asset units. The cash holding is 1−2×2=−3: borrow three. Portfolio payment is two times the asset payment minus three, namely one or thirteen, and current cost is 2×5−3=7. An independently tradable claim must have price seven in this ideal market: if it trades above seven, sell it and buy the replicator; if below, buy it and sell the replicator. Either mismatch releases positive initial cash with exactly offsetting terminal payments.

The risk-neutral high weight q solves 2(1−q)+8q=5, hence q=\(\frac{1}{2}\). Weighting the claim gives (\(\frac{1}{2}\))1+(\(\frac{1}{2}\))13=7. This q is inferred from traded prices and replication, not a forecast that high occurs half the time. Physical mean ten and replicated price seven answer different questions; neither calculation contradicts the other.
questions.followup: Suppose the claim has executable bid 6 / ask 8. Under your physical probabilities, buying at eight has positive expected profit. Is that an arbitrage? Can the physical probability change the replicating cost? What fails if borrowing/shorting is prohibited or a third state is added?
questions.followSolution: Buying at eight has expected profit 10−8=2 but loses seven in low, so it is not an arbitrage. The replicated value seven lies inside 6 / 8: buying the claim for eight or selling it for six does not lock in an arbitrage against the cost-seven replicator. If replication remains feasible, obtaining the same terminal payment through the cost-seven portfolio improves the physical expected profit, but it still has state risk when financed. Altering physical probabilities changes predicted profit, not the two state-matching equations or cost. Constraints can prevent the offsetting arbitrage portfolios; a third state generally adds a third payment equation with only two holdings, so arbitrary claims may cease to be replicable. Uniqueness here depends on the declared complete, frictionless two-state market.
rubric: Compute physical mean ten separately from delta two, cash −3 and replicating cost seven.
Explain both directions of a price-mismatch arbitrage with offset terminal payments.
Derive risk-neutral q=\(\frac{1}{2}\) from the traded asset price, without calling it the physical probability.
Separate positive physical expectation from arbitrage and explain the spread/constraint/third-state limits.

checks.prompt: What is the replication cost?
checks.explanation: Hold two units of stock and minus three units of cash.

checks.prompt: What is the physical expected payoff?
Which pricing arguments are valid?

options.explanation: That conflicts with its state-by-state replication cost.
options.label: Use the physical high-state probability to price the replicated claim at 10.

options.text: Risk-neutral weights are one half in each state, determined by the traded stock and cash.
options.label: Risk-neutral weights are one half in each state, determined by the traded stock and cash.

options.label: A different claim price from 7 creates an arbitrage by taking opposite claim and replicating positions.

options.label: The risk-neutral weights assert that high occurs half the time physically.

questions.title: The value of a signal depends on the actions left open
questions.prompt: A contract pays zero or ten with equal prior probabilities. You may take AT MOST one action: buy one at ask six, sell one at bid four, or abstain. A trade costs an extra \(\frac{1}{2}\); settlement and financing cost nothing. A binary H/L signal has P(H|V=10)=\(\frac{4}{5}\) and P(H|V=0)=\(\frac{1}{5}\). Its acquisition fee f is paid once, whether you trade or abstain. First assume the quote is guaranteed to stay available after the signal and adds no other information. Derive the optimal signal-dependent policy, expected profit BEFORE its acquisition fee and the largest break-even f. Then prove why cost-free additional information cannot reduce the optimal expected profit under fixed available actions. State the exact assumptions needed; the payoff mean itself averages back.
hints: For conditional mean m, optimise g(m)=max(0,m−6.5,3.5−m).
Compute both signal probabilities and posterior means; do not pay the acquisition fee only when trading.
A maximum of affine functions is convex, or you may imitate the old action after every signal.
questions.solution:
Before information the mean is five, giving buy and sell edge −1.5; abstain for zero. P(H)=P(L)=\(\frac{1}{2}\), posterior means are eight and two. After H buy for expected net trading profit 8−6−0.5=1.5; after L sell for 4−2−0.5=1.5. Expected trading profit is 1.5, so total expected profit is 1.5−f. Break-even is f=1.5 (indifferent to not acquiring); strictly preferable when f<1.5. Costs already incurred to obtain information are common to the later actions and must not be charged only on fills.

For a generic available signal S and finite payoff expectation, let \(m_S=E[V\mid S]\). Fixed executable prices and fees give

\[g(m)=\max\{0,m-a-c_b,b-m-c_s\}.\]

The no-trade option has zero; the other terms are affine. Consequently g is convex and

\[E[g(m_S)]\geq g(E[m_S])=g(E[V]).\]

Equivalently, after observing S you could ignore it and use the old action; maximising cannot do worse than that feasible baseline. This requires unchanged feasible actions and prices, expected-cash-profit evaluation, and the signal as the only new conditioning information relevant to those executions. It is a statement about gross information value before its acquisition cost. It is not a claim that every signal makes money, or that the average conditional payment rises.
questions.followup: Now the dealer sees the same signal and replaces its quote by bid \(m_S-1\) / ask \(m_S+1\) before you can act; trading still costs \(\frac{1}{2}\). What is the value of buying the signal for f=1? Compare with a PERFECT signal when the original quote stays fixed. Can a positive expected information value guarantee a realised profit?
questions.followSolution: With the updated quote, either trade loses 1.5 in conditional expectation; abstain. Acquiring for f=1 produces −1, so do not acquire. The fixed-action proof never promised that a dealer would leave a stale price executable. With perfect information and the original quote, buy at V=10 for net trading profit 3.5 or sell at V=0 for 3.5, so gross information value is 3.5, two more than the noisy signal. With the noisy signal, H can occur in the zero state (conditional probability \(\frac{1}{5}\)), causing buy loss 6.5 before acquisition cost. L can occur in the ten state, causing sell loss 6.5. Positive expected information value under a model is compatible with an actual loss. Acquisition cost and loss tolerance are separate decisions.
rubric: Derive both posterior means and signal weights, and choose buy after H/sell after L.
Average the optimised conditional edges to 1.5 and charge f on every signal acquisition.
Prove the inequality by convexity/tower property or by feasibility of the old action.
State the fixed executable action set and expected-profit assumptions explicitly.
Reject signal purchase after quote updating, compute perfect-information value 3.5 and exhibit a noisy-signal loss.

checks.prompt: What is the largest break-even acquisition fee f?
checks.explanation: Buy after H and sell after L; each conditional net edge is 1.5, so expected pre-fee gain is 1.5.

options.explanation: It improves action selection before averaging payoffs.
options.label: The value of information must be zero because posterior means average back to the prior.

options.text: The same guarantee applies unchanged when observing the signal causes the quote to disappear.
options.explanation: That changes the available actions.
options.label: The same guarantee applies unchanged when observing the signal causes the quote to disappear.

options.text: The posterior means are 8 after H and 2 after L; their average is still 5.
options.explanation: Information does not increase the unconditional payoff mean.
options.label: The posterior means are 8 after H and 2 after L; their average is still 5.

options.text: With fixed available actions and zero acquisition cost, the informed decision maker can always imitate the old policy.
options.explanation: The larger policy set cannot reduce the optimum.
options.label: With fixed available actions and zero acquisition cost, the informed decision maker can always imitate the old policy.

questions.title: A set of models is not a mixture of models
questions.prompt: A contract pays V=12 or zero. The prior high-state probability p is only known to lie in [\(\frac{1}{4}\),\(\frac{3}{4}\)]; this is a SET of possible priors, not a probability distribution over p. A signal H has P(H|V=12)=\(\frac{3}{4}\) and P(H|V=0)=\(\frac{1}{4}\) under every model. You observe H, then may buy one at ask nine, sell one at bid eight, or abstain; either trade costs \(\frac{1}{4}\). Quotes are still executable and add no information, interest is zero and the objective is worst-case CONDITIONAL expected cash profit across the model set. Derive the posterior fair-value interval, worst-case buy/sell edges and optimal robust action. Could randomising between buy, sell and abstain strictly improve that minimax value? Do not average posterior endpoints as if ambiguity supplied probabilities.
hints: Normalising a likelihood-weighted prior produces a ratio in p.
A buy is hurt by the LOWEST conditional mean, a sale by the HIGHEST.
To rule out randomisation, look for one allowed model that hurts both trading actions simultaneously.
questions.solution:
For any fixed allowed p, P(H)=(1+2p)/4 is positive, and

\[m(p)=E[V\mid H,p]=\frac{36p}{1+2p}.\]

Its derivative is 36/(1+2p)²>0. Endpoints give m(\(\frac{1}{4}\))=6 and m(\(\frac{3}{4}\))=\(\frac{54}{5}\), so the conditional value interval is [6,10.8]. Net buy edge is m−\(\frac{37}{4}\), with worst case 6−\(\frac{37}{4}\)=−\(\frac{13}{4}\). Sell edge is \(\frac{31}{4}\)−m, with worst case \(\frac{31}{4}\)−\(\frac{54}{5}\)=−\(\frac{61}{20}\). Abstention has worst-case profit zero and is optimal among deterministic actions.

One must not simply mix the TWO DIFFERENT worst-case endpoints to assess a randomised policy: one model governs its average payoff. At the allowed p=\(\frac{1}{2}\), m=9, buy edge is −\(\frac{1}{4}\) and sell edge −\(\frac{5}{4}\). Any mixture with positive trading probability has negative conditional expected profit in this single model; its worst case is therefore negative. Pure abstention attains zero. This common adverse model proves that randomisation cannot strictly improve the minimax value.
questions.followup: Change the interpretation: before any signal, a hidden model is p=\(\frac{1}{4}\) or p=\(\frac{3}{4}\) with equal probability, then V and H are drawn from that model. Compute the model probabilities AFTER H and the mixture E[V|H]. Why is the average of the two posterior values with equal weights incorrect? Does this new answer remove the original ambiguity?
questions.followSolution: The signal probabilities under the low/high models are \(\frac{3}{8}\) and \(\frac{5}{8}\). With equal PRIOR model weights, posterior model weights become \(\frac{3}{8}\) and \(\frac{5}{8}\) (their normalising signal probability is \(\frac{1}{2}\)). Thus mixture value is (\(\frac{3}{8}\))6+(\(\frac{5}{8}\))(\(\frac{54}{5}\))=9, also obtained by first marginalising to prior high probability \(\frac{1}{2}\) and then applying Bayes. The naive equal average of posterior values is \(\frac{42}{5}\)=8.4; it failed to update model weights after observing H. This hierarchy is an additional modelling choice with assigned model probabilities. It does not turn the earlier set-valued uncertainty into an empirical fact or change its minimax answer. Within-model conditioning, across-model mixing and worst-case optimisation are three distinct operations.
rubric: Derive and normalise m(p), prove monotonicity and obtain interval [6,\(\frac{54}{5}\)].
Compute worst-case buy −\(\frac{13}{4}\), sell −\(\frac{61}{20}\) and choose abstention.
Rule out randomisation using one allowed p=\(\frac{1}{2}\), rather than mixing incompatible adverse models.
Update hierarchical model weights to \(\frac{3}{8}\) and \(\frac{5}{8}\) and compute mixture value nine.
Explain why equal posterior averaging gives 8.4 and why a model mixture differs from a prior set.

questions.title: A fill rate is part of the profit calculation
questions.prompt: A dealer starts with no inventory and offers one contract at ask 75. The probability of a sale during this single opportunity is \(\frac{1}{5}\). CONDITIONAL ON that sale, the contract’s expected terminal cash payment is 80. A filled sale incurs one unit of fees; no sale incurs no fee and creates no position. Interest is zero. What is expected net profit PER OPPORTUNITY? Also identify expected profit per fill and why using a prior value of 70 would answer the wrong question.
hints: The dealer receives the ask and owes the payment after a sale.
Multiply the conditional net edge by the probability of a sale; no sale contributes zero.
questions.solution: Expected net profit per filled sale is 75−80−1=−6. Since an opportunity fills with probability \(\frac{1}{5}\) and otherwise contributes zero, expected net profit per opportunity is −\(\frac{6}{5}\)=−1.2. The prior value 70 describes the unselected population, while the liability on sold contracts has conditional mean 80. The quoted positive prior edge 75−70 is not the expected edge among executions. There is no additional spread to subtract when the entry ask and settlement payment are already specified.
questions.followup: An alternative quote earns a conditional net profit of two per sale but fills only with probability \(\frac{1}{100}\). What is its profit per opportunity? Can comparing only per-fill edge decide between quotes, or justify scaling quantity on one common settlement?
questions.followSolution: The alternative gives \(\frac{2}{100}\)=\(\frac{1}{50}\) per opportunity, positive under its declared model. Per-fill edge alone omits how often the action occurs: a rarer, larger edge can earn less per opportunity than a smaller frequent one. Multiplying contracts on the SAME settlement scales that common exposure; it does not create independent trials. Quote choice and permitted quantity also require costs, information, inventory and constraints to be specified.
rubric: Use sale cash-flow signs and one fee to obtain −6 per fill.
Include no-fill mass to obtain −\(\frac{6}{5}\) per opportunity.
Reject the prior-mean substitution and separate frequency from conditional edge and shared risk.

questions.title: Whose buy changes whose inventory?
questions.prompt: A dealer’s signed inventory q=2 means it owns two contracts; negative inventory means a settlement liability. A CUSTOMER buys one contract from the dealer, with no other transaction. What is the dealer’s new q? Separately, its stated terminal inventory penalty is three times q squared. Compute the change in that penalty and contrast a customer SALE to the dealer. This is an accounting exercise, not an optimal-quote claim.
hints: The customer takes a unit OUT of the dealer’s position.
Compare the penalty at the resulting inventory with the penalty at two.
questions.solution: A customer buy is a dealer sale, so q changes from two to one. The penalty changes from 3×2²=12 to 3×1²=3, a reduction of nine. A customer sale is a dealer purchase: q becomes three and the penalty becomes 27, an increase of fifteen. Cash direction and inventory direction must be stated from the same party’s perspective. A quoted bid is the dealer’s buying price; an ask is its selling price.
questions.followup: If a filled dealer sale has zero expected cash trading edge under the CURRENT conditional payoff distribution, how does that nine-unit penalty reduction affect the change in the specified objective? Does this establish that lowering the ask is always optimal?
questions.followSolution: For expected cash trading profit MINUS the declared inventory penalty, zero trading edge plus a nine-unit penalty reduction gives an objective improvement of nine, when comparing the position change under the same current conditional information. This is an explicit preference/model, not free cash earned. It does not establish a quote optimum: changing ask can change fill probability, conditional payoff, feasible actions and information about existing inventory. Compare full action-dependent outcomes and limits before recommending a skew.
rubric: Translate customer buy into dealer sale and new inventory one.
Compute penalty changes −9 on a sale and +15 on a purchase.
Separate an objective improvement from cash profit and from an unspecified optimal quote.

questions.title: The missing order is an observation too
questions.prompt: A SINGLE terminal contract value V is zero or 100, with prior probabilities one half each. During each opportunity a customer buys with probability \(\frac{3}{4}\) if V=100 and \(\frac{1}{4}\) if V=0; otherwise no order occurs. Opportunities are conditionally independent GIVEN this same V. You observe Buy, No order, Buy in that order. Derive the posterior value, including the no-order likelihood. Then you post an executable ask 80 for the NEXT opportunity under the same rule, with no fees or financing. Compute the dealer’s expected profit per NEXT fill and per NEXT opportunity. Do not treat posting as execution or reset the prior for each order.
hints: Multiply the three history likelihoods within each fixed state.
The next fill selects AGAIN from the posterior reached after the history.
Next-fill conditional value and current posterior value are different quantities.
questions.solution:
The history likelihood is (\(\frac{3}{4}\))(\(\frac{1}{4}\))(\(\frac{3}{4}\))=\(\frac{9}{64}\) in high and (\(\frac{1}{4}\))(\(\frac{3}{4}\))(\(\frac{1}{4}\))=\(\frac{3}{64}\) in low. Equal prior weights give posterior high probability \(\frac{3}{4}\) and current mean 75. Ignoring the no-order event would instead use two buys and get high probability \(\frac{9}{10}\).

For the NEXT buy, joint high-and-buy mass is (\(\frac{3}{4}\))(\(\frac{3}{4}\))=\(\frac{9}{16}\); low-and-buy mass is (\(\frac{1}{4}\))(\(\frac{1}{4}\))=\(\frac{1}{16}\). Hence next fill probability is \(\frac{5}{8}\) and next-fill mean is 90. Selling at ask 80 gives −10 per fill and −\(\frac{25}{4}\) per opportunity. Comparing the ask only with current mean 75 misses the next execution’s selection. These results hold because the stated likelihoods remain unchanged at ask 80.
questions.followup: Derive posterior odds after b buys and n no-order events under these assumptions. What breaks if repeated orders come from a single counterparty whose hidden type persists? Can an unfilled order be ignored simply because it produces no trade cash flow?
questions.followSolution: With prior odds one, each buy multiplies odds by three and each no-order observation divides them by three. Posterior odds are \(3^{b-n}\); normalise odds o to high probability o/(1+o). No-order cash flow is zero but its state likelihood is informative. A persistent counterparty type can make observations dependent even conditional on V; the product likelihood then needs the joint process or a state that also tracks that type. The finite experiment’s conditional-independence assumption is essential, not a conclusion from observing a sequence.
rubric: Use all three state-specific history likelihoods and obtain current mean 75.
Recondition on the next fill to obtain mean 90 and fill rate \(\frac{5}{8}\).
Separate next-fill profit −10 from next-opportunity profit −\(\frac{25}{4}\).
Derive the odds update and identify conditional independence/persistent-type limits.

checks.prompt: What is the expected dealer profit per next opportunity at ask 80?
checks.explanation: Next fill probability is \(\frac{5}{8}\), and fill-conditioned value is 90, giving −10 per fill.

questions.title: Raising the ask changes who accepts it
questions.prompt: V is zero or 100 with equal priors. A customer is independently informed with probability \(\frac{1}{2}\); an informed customer buys only when V STRICTLY exceeds the ask. An uninformed customer buys only at asks ≤60. The dealer may post ONE ask from {55,60,70,100} for one opportunity, or refrain from quoting. Each filled sale costs a fee of one; no trade costs zero. Interest is zero and inventory initially zero. For each quote, compute fill probability, conditional payment when defined, and expected net profit per opportunity. Choose an action using these quantities. Explain why keeping the posterior calculated at ask 55 while evaluating ask 70 is incorrect.
hints: At 55 and 60 both uninformed branches and the informed high branch buy.
At 70 only informed high buys; at 100 informed high is indifferent and DOES NOT buy under the stipulated strict rule.
An empty fill event has no conditional mean but still gives zero per-opportunity profit.
questions.solution: At 55 or 60 the fill probability is \(\frac{3}{4}\) and conditional value \(\frac{200}{3}\). Net profits per opportunity are (\(\frac{3}{4}\))(55−1−\(\frac{200}{3}\))=−\(\frac{19}{2}\) and (\(\frac{3}{4}\))(60−1−\(\frac{200}{3}\))=−\(\frac{23}{4}\). At 70 only the informed high branch fills, so fill probability \(\frac{1}{4}\), conditional value 100, and profit (\(\frac{1}{4}\))(70−1−100)=−\(\frac{31}{4}\). At 100 nobody buys: fill probability zero, conditional value undefined, opportunity profit zero. Refrain from quoting; an unfilled ask 100 ties at zero. Among quotes that can fill, 60 loses least, but it still loses. The likelihood changed at the uninformed participation threshold, so an old posterior cannot be transferred to a new quote.
questions.followup: Keep these behavioural rules but replace the informed fraction by α in [0,1]. At ask 60 with the same fee, derive net expected profit and the largest α for nonnegative profit. What does this say about claiming that no dealer can profit in general?
questions.followSolution:
At ask 60, the high branch buys with total probability \(\frac{1}{2}\), and low buys with probability (1−α)/2. The fee-adjusted cash received per fill is 59. Expected profit is

\[59(1-\alpha/2)-50=9-\frac{59}{2}\alpha.\]

It is nonnegative exactly when \(\alpha\leq18/59\). For α=\(\frac{1}{2}\) this agrees with −\(\frac{23}{4}\). The original no-positive-profit menu result belongs to its stated informed fraction, participation threshold and cost convention. It is not a universal impossibility theorem for real market making or a fitted demand model.
rubric: Recompute each quote’s eligible branches and distinguish zero fill from a defined conditional mean.
Obtain per-opportunity profits −\(\frac{19}{2}\), −\(\frac{23}{4}\), −\(\frac{31}{4}\) and zero.
Choose refraining and reject a price-invariant posterior.
Derive 9−59α/2 and threshold \(\frac{18}{59}\) without generalising the toy demand model.

questions.title: The best immediate edge can be the wrong first action
questions.prompt: A fixed terminal V is zero or 12 with equal priors. A dealer starts at q=0 with zero cash and must always keep signed inventory in \([-1,1]\). There are TWO customer opportunities, followed by settlement of all remaining inventory at V. No fees, interest or risk penalty apply. At each opportunity the dealer can skip (no observation), post quote A, or post quote B. Under A the customer buys ONE from the dealer at ask 12 if V=12 and sends NO ORDER if V=0. Under B the customer SELLS ONE to the dealer at bid two in either state. These behaviours, including accepting at V=ask, are STIPULATED and remain available in the second opportunity. You observe the actual order or no-order event before choosing again. A whole quote is infeasible if any positive-probability resulting inventory would breach the limit; you cannot reject a filled branch retroactively. Derive the optimal first action and conditional second actions, with expected final cash-plus-inventory value. Compare an immediate-edge strategy that chooses B first. Explain which observations and state variables the optimal policy needs.
hints: A has zero immediate expected trading edge, but its buy/no-order observations identify V.
After B first the dealer is long one; another B is infeasible.
Settle terminal inventory along each complete path before averaging.
questions.solution:
With one opportunity left at prior beliefs/q=0, B has expected edge six minus two = four; A has zero edge. With TWO opportunities, A first is better. If its customer buys, V=12 is known, dealer cash is +12 and q=−1. Choose B next, paying two and returning q to zero; final value is ten. If A produces no order, V=0 is known, q=0/cash=0; skip because B would lose two and A again produces no order. The expected final value is (\(\frac{1}{2}\))10+(\(\frac{1}{2}\))0=5.

B first pays two and sets q=1 without changing the prior. A second is feasible: high sells the unit for twelve, ending at q=0/cash=10; low produces no order, leaving q=1 worth zero and cash −2. Average final value is four. Skipping after B gives the same four. A second cannot improve B’s expectation because its high-state sale is at the exact value. Another B is prohibited. Skipping FIRST leaves only one opportunity and value four. Thus A first attains five and beats immediate-edge B and skipping. Enumerating these available first actions and optimal continuations proves optimality in this finite game.
questions.followup: Write the form of a Bellman state and terminal value for a general finite quote menu with state-dependent customer buy/sell/no-order probabilities, a quadratic terminal penalty \(\lambda q^2\), and h opportunities remaining. Why may past cash be left out of the state? Why must no-order branches and quote feasibility be included BEFORE optimisation?
questions.followSolution:
Let \(v_0<v_1\) be the two possible terminal payments, \(p\) the current high-state posterior, \(q\) the signed inventory and \(h\) the remaining horizon. Here \(\lambda\) is the nonnegative terminal-penalty coefficient. Terminal expected marked value minus penalty is

\[F_0(p,q)=q[(1-p)v_0+pv_1]-\lambda q^2.\]

For each reachable event e, let \(p_e\) be its updated high-state posterior and \(\delta_e\) its signed inventory change. For each feasible quote, average immediate dealer cash \(c_e\) plus continuation \(F_{h-1}(p_e,q+\delta_e)\) over its reachable events e; compare with skip, which supplies no observation. Bayes updates \(p_e\) with that quote’s event likelihood, including no order. A customer buy has delta −1/cash ask−fee; a customer sale has delta +1/cash −bid−fee; no order has delta zero/cash zero. Past cash is additive and does not affect later choices under this expected-cash objective and these inventory-only constraints; wealth-dependent utility/capital rules could invalidate that reduction. A quote that might breach limits is excluded in full before selecting it. Deleting its bad branch afterwards would describe a different execution model and invent profit.
rubric: Compute A’s complete high/low paths with final values ten/zero and expectation five.
Show B-first value four, its forbidden second purchase and feasible A continuation.
Compare skip-first and prove optimality across the actual finite first-action set.
Specify posterior, signed inventory and remaining horizon, with terminal marked value/penalty.
Explain additive cash, informative no-order events and ex-ante quote feasibility; avoid clairvoyant or retroactively rejected branches.

questions.title: Keep the payment or buy the remaining choice
questions.prompt: You currently may keep payment four. Alternatively, pay a fee of 1.5 and take a compulsory fresh payment: two or eight, each with probability one half. The fresh outcome is independent of your current observation. Maximise expected cash payment MINUS any fee paid now; there are no further options, capital constraints or financing costs. What is the optimal conditional expected NET payment, and which action obtains it? A fee is charged only if you continue; no past cost is included.
hints: The fresh payment has mean five, before its fee.
Compare four with five minus 1.5, rather than with the largest possible payment.
questions.solution: Continuing gives expected net payment (2+8)/2−1.5=3.5. Keeping gives four, so keep and obtain optimal conditional value four. Eight being possible does not make the remaining action worth eight. Subtracting the fee from the kept payment would impose a cost that the stated action never incurs.
questions.followup: If the fee is instead 0.5, which action is optimal and what is its expected net payment? If it subsequently pays two, does that establish that the choice was wrong? What if the fee is one and the convention is to keep at an exact tie?
questions.followSolution: With fee 0.5, continue for expected net value 4.5. The realised low outcome gives 1.5, worse than keeping four, but it occurs within the model used to choose; it does not retroactively replace expected value with hindsight. At fee one both actions have expected value four, and the declared tie convention keeps. Decision quality depends on the information, objective and feasible alternatives at the time, not just the realised outcome.
rubric: Use the full fresh distribution and subtract the fee only on continuation.
Compare continuation 3.5 with keeping four.
Derive 4.5 at the changed fee, separate hindsight from decision quality and keep on the specified tie.

questions.title: One win and one loss do not cancel percentages
questions.prompt: Initial wealth is 100. In each of TWO even-money rounds you stake exactly one quarter of CURRENT wealth. There are no fees, withdrawals or borrowing. One round wins and the other loses. What is final wealth? Explain whether order changes it for this fixed-fraction policy; do not treat both stakes as 25 cash units.
hints: A win multiplies current wealth by 1.25; a loss by 0.75.
The product is 1−f², not one.
questions.solution: Final wealth is 100×1.25×0.75=93.75, a loss of 6.25. Win first: wealth becomes 125, then the loss is 31.25. Lose first: wealth becomes 75, then the gain is 18.75. The product of these fixed multipliers commutes, so either order gives the same answer. Constant-dollar stakes would describe a different policy.
questions.followup: If independent wins each have probability 0.6, what is expected wealth after the two rounds at this same fraction? Does the result above contradict that expectation? Does order remain irrelevant if the next fraction depends on the previous outcome?
questions.followSolution: The expected multiplier is 0.6×1.25+0.4×0.75=1.05. Independent rounds and a fixed fraction give expected final wealth 100×1.05²=110.25. Explicitly, two wins have probability 0.36 and wealth 156.25; mixed outcomes total probability 0.48 and wealth 93.75; two losses have probability 0.16 and wealth 56.25. Weighting them gives 110.25. A losing mixed path does not contradict positive arithmetic expectation. With a history-dependent policy order can matter: use f=\(\frac{1}{4}\) first, then f=\(\frac{1}{2}\) after a win or zero after a loss. Win-then-loss gives 62.5; loss-then-win gives 75. The fixed-fraction commutativity argument no longer applies.
rubric: Compound current-wealth multipliers to 93.75 in either order.
Distinguish proportional stakes from constant-dollar stakes.
Compute two-round expected wealth 110.25 under independence and retain the losing-path possibility.
Give the changed-policy order counterexample 62.5 versus 75.

questions.title: The order of optional fees changes continuation value
questions.prompt: Roll independent fair six-sided dice. After the first observation you may stop and keep it, or pay the FIRST listed fee to discard it and roll again. After that observation you may stop, or pay the SECOND fee to discard it and take one last compulsory roll. Fees are subtracted from the final numerical payment only when their reroll is taken; no financing or capital constraint. Maximise expected net cash payment BEFORE seeing the first roll. Compare fee schedules [1,0] and [0,1]. They have the same sum of listed fees. Derive each continuation threshold and expected value by backward induction, and explain why subtracting that sum from every path is wrong. At exact ties keep.
hints: Begin with the final compulsory roll of mean 3.5.
The expected fresh roll WITH its remaining option is not generally 3.5.
The first fee is subtracted from the value of the next roll WITH the second option.
questions.solution:
For [1,0], the second decision has free continuation 3.5, so a fresh second roll with its option is worth \(\frac{17}{4}\). At the first observation, reroll continuation is \(\frac{17}{4}\)−1=\(\frac{13}{4}\). Reroll 1,2,3 and keep 4,5,6. Initial value is

\[\frac{3(13/4)+4+5+6}{6}=\frac{33}{8}.\]

For [0,1], the second decision has continuation 3.5−1=2.5; a fresh second roll with that option is worth \(\frac{23}{6}\). The first fee is zero, so its continuation threshold is \(\frac{23}{6}\). Again reroll 1,2,3 and keep 4,5,6, but initial value is

\[\frac{3(23/6)+4+5+6}{6}=\frac{53}{12}.\]

The policies’ first kept values coincide while their continuation values differ. The expensive early option must be paid whenever it is used; an expensive later option is paid only when the later observation warrants it. A listed fee is not an unavoidable cost on every branch. Past fees are sunk/additive under this cash objective and do not enter the remaining comparison again.
questions.followup: Two possible fresh-roll laws both have mean three: A pays three certainly; B pays zero or six with equal probabilities. You know which law applies, and fresh draws are iid under that law. A fresh draw comes with ONE free additional redraw option. What are the two continuation values? If you currently can keep four, can a common raw mean of three justify the same decision for both laws?
questions.followSolution: Under A, a fresh draw and any redraw always pay three, so its optional value is three. Under B, the redraw mean is three; a first zero is redrawn and a six is kept, giving optional value (3+6)/2=4.5. Currently keeping four beats continuing under A but loses to continuing under B. The raw means agree; the distributions of observed payments inside the maximum do not. If a signal/history determines which law applies, that information belongs in the state. Do not substitute the mean of a compulsory draw for the value of a draw with remaining options.
rubric: Work backward from compulsory mean 3.5 and charge only the applicable reroll fee.
Derive first thresholds \(\frac{13}{4}\) and \(\frac{23}{6}\), and values \(\frac{33}{8}\) and \(\frac{53}{12}\).
Explain optional branch costs and why sunk past fees do not change the remaining comparison.
Compute optional values three under A and 4.5 under B under equal raw means and opposite decisions at current value four.

questions.title: Bayesian uncertainty is not a worst-case probability
questions.prompt: A single hidden coin parameter P is 0.55 or 0.65 with equal PRIOR model probabilities. Conditional on P, outcomes are iid; P stays fixed. Before ONE even-money round choose 0≤f<1 of positive wealth W; wealth multiplier is 1+f on a win and 1−f on a loss. No fees, other outcomes or capital rules apply. Maximise BAYESIAN expected log final wealth, averaging over the stated model probabilities. Derive the optimal fraction and explain whether uncertainty about P alone forces a fraction below 0.2 for this objective. Separately replace those model probabilities by an AMBIGUITY SET p∈[0.55,0.65], with a worst-case expected-log objective; derive its fraction. These are toy criteria, not a real-money recommendation.
hints: Expected one-round log growth is affine in p for a fixed fraction.
Averaging over model probabilities differs from minimising over a set.
For f≥0, log(1+f) exceeds log(1−f), so identify the worst p.
questions.solution:
Define the conditional growth \(g_p(f)=p\log(1+f)+(1-p)\log(1-f)\) for a fixed coin probability p. For a fixed fraction, Bayesian expected log growth is

\[\begin{aligned}E[g_P(f)]&=\bar p\log(1+f)\\&\quad +(1-\bar p)\log(1-f),\end{aligned}\]

where the current predictive probability is \(\bar p=E[P]=0.6\). Strict concavity and derivative zero give \(f=2\bar p-1=0.2\). Probability uncertainty alone does not introduce a separate variance penalty into this ONE-round expected-log expression. A different utility, ambiguity objective, drawdown constraint, cost or tail model could change the answer; none is stipulated here.

Under the ambiguity SET and f≥0, growth is increasing in p because its slope in p is \(\log((1+f)/(1-f))\geq0\). The worst case is p=0.55. Maximising that concave growth function gives f=0.10. Equal model weights and a worst-case model are distinct assumptions; they are not interchangeable interpretations of “uncertain”. At f approaching one any model has positive loss probability, making expected log wealth tend to minus infinity.
questions.followup: Extend the Bayesian problem to TWO rounds, allowing the second fraction to depend on the observed first outcome. The coin outcome is observed even if f=0; its distribution and future information do NOT depend on your fraction. All constraints remain proportional and unchanged. Compute the posterior model weights, second predictive win probabilities and optimal second fractions after win/loss. Prove whether a non-myopic first fraction improves on 0.2 under terminal expected log wealth.
questions.followSolution:
After a win, the high-p model has weight 0.65/(0.55+0.65)=\(\frac{13}{24}\) and the low model \(\frac{11}{24}\). Next predictive win probability is \(\frac{29}{48}\), giving second fraction \(\frac{5}{24}\). After a loss, model weights are \(\frac{7}{16}\) high and \(\frac{9}{16}\) low; next predictive probability \(\frac{19}{32}\) gives fraction \(\frac{3}{16}\). Their predictive probabilities average back to 0.6 under first-outcome probability 0.6 for a win and 0.4 for a loss.

Write terminal log wealth as current log W plus first-round log multiplier plus second-round log multiplier. The distribution of posterior information and the optimal continuation term is INDEPENDENT of the first fraction under the stated observation rule. Hence only the first expected log multiplier depends on that fraction, and its unique optimum remains 0.2. The same separation proves posterior-predictive myopic fractions optimal at any finite horizon in this particular model. Learning occurs, but no stake is needed to cause it. Action-dependent information, wealth-dependent feasible sets or nonlinear costs would invalidate this separation. Unconditionally the outcomes are correlated through the persistent P; the finite conditional-expectation argument does not assume unconditional iid outcomes.
rubric: Average one-round growth over the stated model weights to predictive p=0.6 and fraction 0.2.
Derive the distinct worst-case p=0.55/fraction 0.1 and check the positive-wealth domain.
Update model probabilities after win/loss and derive predictive \(\frac{29}{48}\) and \(\frac{19}{32}\), fractions \(\frac{5}{24}\) and \(\frac{3}{16}\).
Separate the first growth term from action-independent information/continuation; prove first fraction 0.2 remains optimal.
State the observation/feasibility assumptions and persistent-model dependence; do not claim uncertainty universally requires fractional sizing.

questions.title: A rare third outcome invalidates the binary formula
questions.prompt: Positive wealth W becomes W(1+fR) after a round. The NET return R is +1 with probability 0.60, −1 with probability 0.39 and −9 with probability 0.01. Exposure f is nonnegative; every possible wealth multiplier must be strictly positive. No fees or further constraints apply. Derive the admissible domain and maximise expected natural-log wealth growth. Is the binary even-money formula f=2(0.60)−1=0.20 even admissible? Show strict concavity and select the correct root, rather than applying an even-money formula to a three-outcome return. Expected one-round cash return and log growth are different objectives.
hints: The largest possible loss is nine times exposure, not one.
Differentiate the three weighted logarithms within the positive-multiplier domain.
Multiply by the positive common denominator to obtain a quadratic; check which root stays admissible.
questions.solution:
The domain is \(0\leq f<1/9\); \(f=0.2\) gives catastrophe multiplier −0.8 and is inadmissible. Expected net return is 0.6−0.39−9(0.01)=0.12, so growth initially increases. The objective and derivative are

\[\begin{aligned}g(f)&=.60\log(1+f)\\&\quad+.39\log(1-f)\\&\quad+.01\log(1-9f),\end{aligned}\]

\[g^{\prime}(f)=\frac{.60}{1+f}-\frac{.39}{1-f}-\frac{.09}{1-9f}.\]

An outcome with probability p and net return r contributes second derivative \(-pr^2/(1+fr)^2\). Each nonzero return therefore contributes negative curvature, so g is strictly concave. Its derivative starts at 0.12 and tends to minus infinity at \(\frac{1}{9}\). Multiplying by the positive denominator gives \(9f^2-2.88f+.12=0\), equivalently \(75f^2-24f+1=0\). Only

\[f_* =\frac{12-\sqrt{69}}{75}\approx0.049245\]

is admissible; the other root exceeds \(\frac{1}{9}\). This is the unique maximum, with growth about 0.00329237 per round. The lower fraction comes from the specified third outcome/domain, not from changing the probability of the original binary game while pretending its loss sizes stayed fixed.
questions.followup: Keep the win probability 0.60, but let catastrophe probability ε be only known to lie in [0,0.02], taken from the ordinary loss probability so it becomes 0.40−ε. Choose one exposure before knowing ε to maximise WORST-CASE expected log growth. Locate the adverse ε and derive the admissible optimum. Does putting equal weights on ε endpoints describe the same objective?
questions.followSolution:
For positive f<\(\frac{1}{9}\), shifting probability from R=−1 to R=−9 decreases growth by \(\log(1-9f)-\log(1-f)<0\). The worst ε is 0.02; at f=0 all models tie at zero. Feasibility must cover the possible catastrophic state, so the robust domain still ends at \(\frac{1}{9}\) even though ε=0 is allowed. The worst-model derivative has numerator \(9f^2-2.96f+.04\), giving

\[f_*^{\rm robust}=\frac{37-\sqrt{1144}}{225}\approx0.0141197.\]

Its derivative at zero is 0.04>0, and strict concavity plus the boundary identify the smaller root as the unique optimum. Equal PRIOR weights on the two ε endpoints would instead create predictive ε=0.01 for this one-round log objective and give the earlier 0.049245 result. That mixture is a different model choice from an ambiguity set. Neither objective supplies a guarantee for an individual realised wealth path.
rubric: Enforce 0≤f<\(\frac{1}{9}\) and reject fraction 0.2 before evaluating any logarithm.
Derive all three derivative terms and strict concavity.
Obtain quadratic 75f²−24f+1 and its unique admissible smaller root.
Identify worst ε=0.02 and derive the robust root/domain, including the zero-fraction tie.
Separate expected cash, a Bayesian model mixture, a worst-case model and realised outcomes.
