questions.title: A factor-neutral hedge still moves
questions.prompt: Centred unit cash payoffs are X=2F+ε₁ and Y=3F+ε₂. The factor has variance nine; residual variances are four for ε₁ and nine for ε₂. F, ε₁ and ε₂ are pairwise uncorrelated with finite second moments. Take one unit of X and SHORT two thirds of a unit of Y, fixed before outcomes: H=X−(\(\frac{2}{3}\))Y. What is Var(H)? Explain what was neutralised and what remains. These are position quantities, not fully allocated capital-fraction weights; no costs or other risks are included.
hints: Combine factor loadings before measuring their variance.
The short residual coefficient is −\(\frac{2}{3}\); square it before multiplying by residual variance nine.
questions.solution: The factor coefficient is 2−(\(\frac{2}{3}\))·3=0, so H=ε₁−(\(\frac{2}{3}\))ε₂. Residual covariance is zero and \(\operatorname{Var}(H)=4+(2/3)^2\cdot9=8\). Only the specified common factor is neutralised. Gross position quantity is \(\frac{5}{3}\), net quantity \(\frac{1}{3}\); neither is the remaining variance. Independence or normality is unnecessary for this calculation.
questions.followup: The second factor loading changes from three to 2.5, while all stated variances and uncorrelated-residual assumptions remain. Keep the same positions. What is the new factor loading and total variance? Does setting net position quantity to zero by shorting one whole Y instead solve the problem?
questions.followSolution: The old hedge now has factor loading 2−(\(\frac{2}{3}\))·2.5=\(\frac{1}{3}\), giving factor variance (\(\frac{1}{3}\))²·9=1 and total variance nine. A whole-unit short has net quantity zero but factor loading 2−2.5=−\(\frac{1}{2}\); variance is (\(\frac{1}{2}\))²·9+4+9=\(\frac{61}{4}\). Net units and net factor exposure are different. An estimated model hedge is sensitive to changed loadings and does not eliminate residual, funding or execution risk.
rubric: Cancel the factor coefficient before squaring and obtain residual variance eight.
Separate quantities, factor loading and remaining risk.
Derive changed loading one third, total variance nine and reject net-unit neutrality as a substitute.

questions.title: Joint stress changes variance and volatility differently
questions.prompt: Two same-horizon returns are measured in percentage points. Fixed capital weights are one half each. Baseline standard deviations are two percentage points each, with correlation 0.5. A specified stress increases the FIRST standard deviation to four, keeps the SECOND at two, and raises correlation to one. What is the ratio of stressed portfolio STANDARD DEVIATION to baseline portfolio standard deviation? Derive both variances; do not report their ratio as the volatility ratio. The stress is a specified joint model, not a probability forecast.
hints: Baseline covariance is 0.5×2×2.
Standard deviation is the square root of variance.
questions.solution: Baseline variance is (\(\frac{1}{4}\))·4+(\(\frac{1}{4}\))·4+2(\(\frac{1}{4}\))·2=3. Stress covariance is 4·2=8, so stressed variance is (\(\frac{1}{4}\))·16+(\(\frac{1}{4}\))·4+2(\(\frac{1}{4}\))·8=9. Standard deviations are √3 and three percentage points; the ratio is 3/√3=√3. Variance triples, but standard deviation does not. Variance units are squared percentage points.
questions.followup: Now use standard deviations two and three, and correlation −1. Do equal weights cancel risk? Which long-only weights summing to one do cancel the centred linear fluctuations in this exact model? Does zero variance imply zero mean return?
questions.followSolution: Equal-weight variance is (2−3)²/4=\(\frac{1}{4}\). Perfect anticorrelation relates standardised centred fluctuations, not raw returns with different scales. Cancellation needs 2w₁=3w₂, hence w₁=\(\frac{3}{5}\) and w₂=\(\frac{2}{5}\). The centred portfolio is then zero almost surely, while its raw return equals its weighted mean, which need not be zero. This is an exact specified relationship, not a claim that estimated correlation stays −1.
rubric: Compute variances three and nine in consistent units.
Return the standard-deviation ratio √3 rather than three.
Handle unequal-volatility anticorrelation and distinguish a constant level from a zero mean.

questions.title: More names cannot diversify away the shared shock
questions.prompt: For each positive integer n, consider n centred same-horizon returns Rᵢ=F+εᵢ and weights 1/n. Var(F)=1 and Var(εᵢ)=4; residuals are mutually uncorrelated and uncorrelated with F, with finite second moments. No rebalancing or costs. What is the SMALLEST n for portfolio variance at most 1.1? Derive the variance rather than dividing the entire single-name variance by n.
hints: The portfolio factor loading stays one.
Only the independent or uncorrelated residual part scales down with the number of names.
questions.solution: The average is \(F+n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\varepsilon_i\). Its variance is 1+4/n, so 4/n≤0.1 requires n≥40. At n=40 variance equals 1.1; n=39 fails. The single-name variance five cannot simply be divided by n because every name contains the SAME factor. Mutually uncorrelated residuals suffice; independence is not required.
questions.followup: Instead every distinct residual pair has correlation 0.05, while residual variances remain four and all residuals stay uncorrelated with F. Derive the variance for general n and decide whether ANY finite n can achieve 1.1. Give a coherent construction for these residuals, rather than assuming arbitrary pairwise stress numbers form a valid matrix.
questions.followSolution: Each residual pair now has covariance 0.2. The average residual variance is 4/n+0.2(\(n-1\))/n=0.2+3.8/n. Total variance is 1.2+3.8/n, exceeding 1.2 for every finite n; the target 1.1 is impossible. A coherent construction is εᵢ=√0.2·G+√3.8·Zᵢ, where G and all Zᵢ are centred, variance one, mutually uncorrelated and uncorrelated with F. The common residual component creates another nondiversifying exposure. A common correlation assumption should be checked collectively, not merely cell by cell.
rubric: Derive the factor floor and residual term 1+4/n; identify n=40 with the boundary.
Include all residual cross terms under the changed model.
Prove the unattainable target and exhibit a valid shared-residual construction.

questions.title: The same covariance matrix hides different joint crashes
questions.prompt: Three binary crash indicators X₁,X₂,X₃ each satisfy P(Xᵢ=1)=\(\frac{1}{2}\). Every distinct pair is INDEPENDENT, but joint independence is not assumed. Unit cash payoffs are Yᵢ=1−2Xᵢ and the fixed equal-weight payoff is H=(Y₁+Y₂+Y₃)/3. Derive the SHARP possible interval for P(H<−\(\frac{2}{3}\)) over all joint distributions consistent with these assumptions. Construct distributions attaining both endpoints, and verify they have the SAME payoff means and covariance matrix. A covariance-only calculation must not invent a joint crash probability.
hints: The strict loss threshold occurs exactly when all three indicators are one.
Write all eight cell probabilities in terms of q=P(1,1,1), using the marginal and pair constraints.
Nonnegativity of every cell gives bounds; explicit endpoint tables prove sharpness.
questions.solution:
Let q=P(X₁=X₂=X₃=1). Pair independence gives each double-one marginal probability \(\frac{1}{4}\). Consequently each EXACTLY-two-one cell has mass \(\frac{1}{4}\)−q. The individual one-margins then force each EXACTLY-one-one cell to have mass q; total mass forces P(0,0,0)=\(\frac{1}{4}\)−q. Nonnegativity is equivalent to \(0\leq q\leq1/4\). Since H=1−(\(\frac{2}{3}\))(X₁+X₂+X₃), the strict event H<−\(\frac{2}{3}\) is exactly the all-one cell.

At q=0 use equal probability \(\frac{1}{4}\) on 000,011,101,110. At q=\(\frac{1}{4}\) use equal probability \(\frac{1}{4}\) on 001,010,100,111. Every indicator is fair and every two-indicator table is uniform in both constructions. Each Yᵢ has mean zero/variance one, and each payoff pair has covariance zero. Therefore both give the same covariance matrix I and Var(H)=\(\frac{1}{3}\), yet their joint crash probabilities are zero and \(\frac{1}{4}\). Every intermediate q is attained by mixing the two tables; the full interval is sharp. Jointly independent indicators would give \(\frac{1}{8}\), which is only one permitted value.
questions.followup: Can you reject the high-crash construction by calling its zero covariances evidence of three independent risks? If instead the requirement was full JOINT independence, what happens to the interval and the distribution of H? What additional evidence would a risk report need beyond second moments?
questions.followSolution: Zero payoff covariance, even paired with pairwise indicator independence, does not imply mutual independence. Under full joint independence all eight cells have probability \(\frac{1}{8}\), so the crash probability is fixed at \(\frac{1}{8}\). The crash count is then Binomial(3,\(\frac{1}{2}\)) and H has values 1,\(\frac{1}{3}\),−\(\frac{1}{3}\),−1 with probabilities \(\frac{1}{8}\),\(\frac{3}{8}\),\(\frac{3}{8}\),\(\frac{1}{8}\). A report about the joint downside needs a specified or estimated joint law, including higher-order dependence and appropriate support/horizon, plus uncertainty and executable loss assumptions. The identical mean/variance alone do not determine it.
rubric: Translate the strict portfolio event to the all-one cell.
Derive all eight masses and prove 0≤q≤\(\frac{1}{4}\) from their nonnegativity.
Construct both endpoints, verify pairwise independence and the identical covariance I/portfolio variance \(\frac{1}{3}\).
Distinguish pairwise from joint independence and compute the independent case \(\frac{1}{8}\).

checks.prompt: What is the largest possible probability of H<−\(\frac{2}{3}\)?
checks.explanation: The event is exactly X1=X2=X3=1; nonnegative cell masses bound q at \(\frac{1}{4}\).

options.explanation: It has the same one- and two-dimensional margins.

options.explanation: That requires joint independence.

options.explanation: All fixed marginal constraints are linear.
options.label: Mixing the endpoint tables attains every value in [0,1/4].

options.explanation: Every pair remains independent and fair.
options.label: Uniform mass on 000,011,101,110 gives joint crash probability zero.

questions.title: A hedge chosen before uncertain loadings are known
questions.prompt: In each specified model, centred payoffs are X=F+ε₁ and Y=bF+ε₂, with Var(F)=4, Var(ε₁)=Var(ε₂)=1 and all three components pairwise uncorrelated. The loading b is an unknown FIXED model parameter in [1,3], with no probability distribution assigned. Choose a fixed nonnegative short quantity h before knowing b: H=X−hY. Minimise the WORST-MODEL variance over that interval. Derive the globally optimal h and value, including where the active stress model changes. Do not replace the ambiguity set by its midpoint or choose h separately after learning b.
hints: For fixed h, the variance is convex in b, so its maximum on the interval occurs at an endpoint.
Compare the two endpoint squared factor loadings; the active one switches at h=\(\frac{1}{2}\).
Check derivatives on both sides of the switch, rather than averaging endpoint models.
questions.solution:
The specified variance is \(v_b(h)=4(1-bh)^2+1+h^2\). For fixed h its maximum in b is at 1 or 3. Their difference is \(v_1(h)-v_3(h)=16h(1-2h)\). Thus the worst-model envelope is

\[v(h)=\begin{cases}5-8h+5h^2,&0\leq h\leq1/2,\\5-24h+37h^2,&h\geq1/2.\end{cases}\]

The left derivative −8+10h stays negative up to the switch, where it is −3. The right derivative −24+74h is positive from the switch onward, starting at 13. The unique global minimum is therefore h=\(\frac{1}{2}\), with worst variance \(\frac{9}{4}\). Both endpoint models are active there; no single smooth derivative is zero at this kink. The midpoint model alone has minimiser \(\frac{8}{17}\), which gives worse worst-case variance \(\frac{677}{289}\). Averaging endpoint variances also describes another objective, not the model-set maximum.
questions.followup: Now the hedge residual variance is a known d≥0 instead of one, while the primary residual variance remains one. Derive the optimal robust hedge for ALL d, not just the original case. Explain why a factor-balanced hedge can become too costly in residual risk.
questions.followSolution: The factor comparison and switch at \(\frac{1}{2}\) are unchanged. The left branch is 5−8h+(4+d)h², whose unconstrained minimum is 4/(4+d); the right derivative at the switch is 12+d>0 and increases thereafter. Thus h*=min(\(\frac{1}{2}\),4/(4+d)). For 0≤d≤4 the minimum is at the kink, with variance 2+d/4. For d≥4 it is on the low-loading branch, with variance 5−16/(4+d); the two formulas agree at d=4. At d=12, h*=\(\frac{1}{4}\) and variance four, whereas the factor-balanced \(\frac{1}{2}\) hedge gives variance five. A hedge can reduce factor uncertainty while adding enough residual risk that a smaller position is preferable. Costs, means and funding rules could further change the action set/objective; none is included in this variance problem.
rubric: Derive each model variance with squared signed loadings and residual exposures.
Justify the endpoint worst case and active-model switch.
Use both one-sided derivatives to prove h=1/2/variance \(\frac{9}{4}\) is globally optimal.
Derive the d-dependent minimum, its boundary d=4 and d=12 counterexample.

questions.title: Contract quantities change the synthetic payoff
questions.prompt: European calls and puts have the same strike 100, underlying and maturity; each pays per one underlying unit. Hold TWO long calls and ONE short put. At terminal underlying price 120, what is the combined cash payoff? This asks terminal payment, not profit after an initial premium. Does the usual one-call-minus-one-put identity turn this whole position into one unit of a forward?
hints: Apply the signed contract quantities to max(S−100,0) and max(100−S,0).
One copy of call-minus-put leaves another long call.
questions.solution:
Each call pays twenty and the short put pays zero, so the combined payment is forty. The unit identity applies to ONE call and ONE short put. Write H(S) for this combined payoff at terminal price S. Its exact decomposition is

\[\begin{aligned}H(S)&=2(S-100)^+\\&\quad-(100-S)^+\\&=(S-100)+(S-100)^+.\end{aligned}\]

The extra call changes the upside slope; multiplying a remembered parity expression by an unrelated net contract count would lose that payment.
questions.followup: What is the payment at terminal price ninety? Derive the whole piecewise payoff and explain why a fixed stock-and-cash position alone cannot replicate it for every nonnegative terminal price. Give an exact decomposition using one call as well as stock/cash, assuming no dividends and zero interest.
questions.followSolution: At ninety the two calls pay zero and the short put pays minus ten. Below one hundred the payoff is S−100; above it the payoff is 2(S−100), with continuity and zero payment at the strike. A fixed stock/cash payoff aS+b has one constant slope, so it cannot match both slopes one and two. Exactly one long call plus one underlying unit and a terminal cash liability of one hundred does replicate it. Under zero interest/no dividends the liability can be financed by borrowing one hundred initially. This is state-by-state matching, not an expectation or a claim that the initial portfolio cost is zero.
rubric: Use both long calls and the negative put quantity to obtain forty.
Distinguish terminal payment from net profit or an initial price.
Derive both slopes, the payment minus ten at ninety, and the stock/cash/extra-call decomposition.

questions.title: Finance the strike and the dividend separately
questions.prompt: A European call and put share strike 100, maturity and underlying. Spot is 108. A risk-free claim paying the strike at maturity costs 95 today. A known cash dividend before maturity has present value three. The call costs fourteen. Assume frictionless matched borrowing/lending, available shorting and no other dividends. What put price is forced by exact replication? The present value of the dividend is not a change to the contractual strike.
hints: The stock position delivers both the terminal stock and the earlier dividend.
Subtract the dividend present value and the present value of the strike from spot to match call-minus-put.
questions.solution: Put-call replication gives \(C-P\)=108−3−95=10. Therefore P=14−10=4. Ignoring the dividend would produce one, and subtracting the undiscounted strike in place of its present value would produce nine. The financing prices and dividend timing are part of the matching argument; neither volatility nor a physical expected stock return is required.
questions.followup: Describe the stock and financing cash flows that replicate call-minus-put at both dates. Why is borrowing only 95 insufficient to match all intervening cash flows? Would identical terminal payoff reasoning alone justify the same equality for American exercise rights?
questions.followSolution: Hold one underlying unit. Borrow 95 through maturity, repaying one hundred there. Also borrow an amount with current value three and repayment equal to the known dividend at its payment date. The stock dividend cancels that second repayment; terminal net payment is S_T−100. Initial cost is ten. Borrowing only the strike present value leaves an unmatched dividend receipt and therefore costs thirteen rather than ten. With American rights, an early exercise action can change payment timing; a terminal-only equality does not match every available exercise policy. Exact European matching needs the stated contract/financing assumptions.

questions.title: A midpoint discrepancy is not an executable parity trade
questions.prompt: One-period, no-dividend European call and put share strike one hundred. Interest is zero; stock, call and put can each be bought/shorted in unit quantities, with no costs beyond these executable bid/ask pairs: stock [97,101], call [5,8], put [5,8]. Buying uses the ask and selling the bid. Midpoints give \(C-P\)=0 while spot-minus-strike is −1. Can EITHER of the two standard matched parity round trips lock positive initial cash with zero terminal cash flow? Enumerate both directions and all four initial cash flows. Do not infer overall absence of every possible arbitrage merely from checking these two trades.
hints: Compare a sold synthetic forward with a bought stock-minus-strike position.
For the opposite direction buy the synthetic forward and sell the stock-minus-strike position.
Borrowing one hundred receives cash now; depositing one hundred spends cash now.
questions.solution: Direction A: short the call at five, buy the put at eight, buy stock at 101, and borrow one hundred. Initial cash is 5−8−101+100=−4. Its terminal payment is −call+put+S−100=0 in every state. Direction B: buy the call at eight, short the put at five, short stock at 97 and deposit one hundred. Initial cash is −8+5+97−100=−6; terminal payment call−put−S+100 is again zero. Both require a positive initial payment and give no terminal receipt, so neither yields the proposed locked gain. The midpoint discrepancy cannot pay the bid/ask crossings. These calculations concern the two named matched trades and the declared execution/financing terms.
questions.followup: Change the put bid/ask to [12,13], keeping all other terms and shorting availability. Which direction now locks cash, how much, and why are the terminal payments still matched? Identify one realistic omitted constraint that would have to be checked before interpreting actual market quotes this way.
questions.followSolution: Direction B now receives −8+12+97−100=one initially and still has zero terminal net cash for every underlying price. The put CONTRACT did not change, only its executable quote. Direction A has initial cash 5−13−101+100=−9. Actual execution would also need matching quantity availability, financing, short borrow/collateral, fees and consistent contract/dividend terms; the specified exercise assumes those trades feasible. A real discrepancy in midpoints alone does not establish this executable four-leg outcome.
rubric: Write both opposite four-leg trades using the correct bid/ask and funding signs.
Obtain initial cash minus four/minus six and prove terminal cancellation.
Derive the changed-quote receipt one and separate the declared feasible toy trade from additional execution conditions.

questions.title: Three terminal states need not determine one option price
questions.prompt: At time zero a no-dividend stock costs one hundred, and cash has zero interest. The ONLY terminal stock states are 0,100,200, each with strictly positive PHYSICAL probability. One-period stock/cash holdings can be any real signed quantities, with frictionless shorting and borrowing. Add a European strike-one-hundred call with unknown price C. There are no intervening dates or other securities. Show whether stock/cash can exactly replicate the call. Derive the FULL arbitrage-free interval of C, including whether endpoints are included, and prove sufficiency. You may construct positive pricing weights q₀,q₁,q₂ for states 0,100,200 respectively, summing to one and pricing stock at its current value; these are not assumed physical probabilities. Arbitrage means a zero-cost financed terminal payoff nonnegative in every possible state and positive in at least one.
hints: A stock/cash payoff is affine in the terminal stock price; the call payments are 0,0,100.
The stock-pricing constraint gives q₀=q₂ and q₁=1−2q₂.
Use strictly positive pricing weights for sufficiency and explicit endpoint payoff trades for necessity.
questions.solution:
If aS+b matches the call, state zero forces b=0 and state one hundred then forces a=0, contradicting the required payment one hundred at state two hundred. The claim is not redundant with stock and cash.

The positive pricing constraints are

\[\begin{aligned}q_0+q_1+q_2&=1,\\q_1+2q_2&=1.\end{aligned}\]

Thus \(q_0=q_2=z\), \(q_1=1-2z\) and \(0<z<1/2\). The call price is \(C=100z\), giving the OPEN interval \(0<C<50\). For any such C these positive weights correctly price cash, stock and call. Every zero-cost terminal payoff formed from those assets has zero weighted mean; if it is everywhere nonnegative and somewhere positive, the strictly positive weights make that mean positive, a contradiction. This proves sufficiency without choosing physical probabilities.

At C=0, a free long call pays a strictly positive amount in the high state. At C=50, half a stock minus one call costs zero and pays (0,50,0). Both are arbitrages because the relevant physical states have positive probability. For C<0 or C>50, the same respective portfolios have a positive initial receipt; put it in cash to obtain a zero-cost financed arbitrage. Mere nonnegative pricing weights at the boundaries would miss these trades. No-arbitrage leaves a range here rather than an automatic unique expected payoff price.
questions.followup: Add a cash digital paying one ONLY when terminal stock equals one hundred, with price d. Determine the feasible interval for d, the forced call price and an exact stock/digital replication. Does knowing the physical state probabilities by itself impose that same unique price?
questions.followSolution: The digital prices q₁=d, so q₀=q₂=(1−d)/2. Strict positivity requires 0<d<1, and call price is C=50(1−d). The exact payoff identity is call=half a stock minus fifty middle-state digitals: its payments are (0,0,100). At d=0 the digital itself is a free positive payoff; at d=1 cash minus the digital is free and positive in the outer states. Adding the traded digital supplies the missing state-price information and makes this replication possible. Physical probabilities alone describe real-world expectations, not the pricing weights; no equality between those measures was stipulated.
rubric: Prove nonreplicability from all three state payments.
Derive and prove the strict interval 0<C<50, including positive-weight sufficiency.
Construct arbitrages at both endpoints and outside the interval.
Derive digital interval 0<d<1 and the stock/digital identity forcing C=50(1−d).

questions.title: Rebalancing cash belongs in the gamma calculation
questions.prompt: Use a CONSTRUCTED smooth mark function V(S,t)=aS²−bt, with a,b>0 and nonnegative observed stock prices at dates t₀<...<t_n, n≥1. Interest, dividends and fees are initially zero. Hold one long marked contract and short Δ_i=2aS_i stock units over interval [t_i,t_{i+1}); rebalance at interior dates and liquidate at the final date. Fund the initial purchase/short through a cash account so initial TOTAL net wealth is zero; all later trades must be self-financing. Derive the terminal cash wealth, including the cash-account changes at rehedges. Compare paths (100,110,100) and (100,100,100) at dates (0,\(\frac{1}{2}\),1), with a=0.02,b=3. Compare with a frozen initial-delta hedge. The mark function is a mathematical illustration, not a claimed arbitrage-free market price or a general option repricing law.
hints: Over one interval, exact contract change minus the HELD initial delta times stock change simplifies to a squared-move term and time decay.
Changing the short from Δ_{i−1} to Δ_i receives (Δ_i−Δ_{i−1})S_i into cash.
Sum actual interval gains; do not replace the sum of squared moves by the square of the total move.
questions.solution:
Write \(V_0=V(S_0,t_0)\). Start with \(B_0=\Delta_0S_0-V_0\), so \(V_0-\Delta_0S_0+B_0=0\). At each interior rebalance,

\[B_i=B_{i-1}+(\Delta_i-\Delta_{i-1})S_i.\]

The stock trade changes cash and stock holdings by opposite amounts; it does not create an external gain. Write \(V_i=V(S_i,t_i)\), \(x_i=S_{i+1}-S_i\) and \(u_i=t_{i+1}-t_i\). Exact marked interval gain is

\[G_i=V_{i+1}-V_i-\Delta_i x_i,\]

which simplifies to \(G_i=ax_i^2-bu_i\). Therefore final liquidated wealth is

\[\begin{aligned}W_n&=a\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}x_i^2\\&\quad-b(t_n-t_0).\end{aligned}\]

For the first path the two squared moves total two hundred, so W=4−3=one. Direct ledger: V₀=200, Δ₀=4, B₀=200; at 110 delta becomes 4.4 and cash receives 44, giving B₁=244. At maturity V=197 and the stock close costs 440; terminal cash is 244+197−440=one. The flat path has zero price contribution and wealth minus three. A frozen initial-delta hedge in either same-endpoint path gives V_n−V₀−Δ₀(S_n−S₀)=−3. This quadratic function has constant gamma 2a and theta −b, so its interval expression is EXACT; a general smooth instrument would have approximation error and varying sensitivities.
questions.followup: Charge proportional stock trading cost c=0.001 on the absolute trade quantity times execution price, INCLUDING the initial short and final stock close; contract fees stay zero. Keep initial EXTERNAL outlay zero; fund the initial fee through the cash account instead of adding outside money. Derive the cost-adjusted terminal wealth for both paths. Can inserting more hedge dates only increase the sum of squared moves?
questions.followSolution:
Let the held short quantities be Δ₀ through Δ_{\(n-1\)}. Deduct

\[\begin{aligned}c\big(&|\Delta_0|S_0\\&+\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}|\Delta_i-\Delta_{i-1}|S_i\\&+|\Delta_{n-1}|S_n\big).\end{aligned}\]

Initial financing includes the first cost, so initial post-trade marked wealth is minus that fee; it is not reset by an outside cash injection. Interior cash updates subtract their execution cost; the final close subtracts the last cost. First-path cost base is 400+44+440=884, so cost is 0.884 and net wealth 0.116. Flat-path cost base is 400+0+400=800; net wealth is −3.8. Positive gamma alone did not secure positive net wealth.

Refinement is not monotone: splitting an interval with increments x,y replaces (x+y)² by x²+y², a difference −2xy. A reversal can increase the sum; a same-direction split decreases it. Flat endpoints 100→100 give zero before adding an intermediate 110, but two hundred after. Conversely 100→120 gives four hundred before splitting at 110, but two hundred after. More dates also change turnover and omitted real-world risks; the constructed identity does not certify a general strategy.
rubric: Set initial cash to make wealth zero and include every self-financing rebalance.
Derive the exact sum of interval squared moves minus time decay.
Verify dynamic wealth one/minus three and distinguish the frozen hedge.
Include initial/interior/final costs to obtain 0.116 and minus 3.8.
Show both refinement directions and separate the constructed quadratic identity from a general local approximation.

questions.title: One success does not reward the best probability
questions.prompt: Under your fixed pre-outcome information, a binary outcome Y has success probability \(\frac{3}{4}\). You report p before Y occurs, and receive Brier LOSS \((p-Y)^2\), with lower loss better. Your report cannot affect the outcome. What is the EXCESS EXPECTED loss of reporting \(p=1\) rather than p=\(\frac{3}{4}\)? Average over both outcomes; this asks a difference, not either individual loss.
hints: Compute each report’s loss on success and failure, then weight them by \(\frac{3}{4}\) and \(\frac{1}{4}\).
For true probability q, expected loss is (p−q)²+q(1−q).
questions.solution:
Honest reporting has expected loss (\(\frac{3}{4}\))(\(\frac{1}{4}\))²+(\(\frac{1}{4}\))(\(\frac{3}{4}\))²=\(\frac{3}{16}\). Reporting one has zero loss on success but loss one on failure, so its expectation is \(\frac{1}{4}\). The excess is \(\frac{1}{16}\). More generally, for fixed true probability q,

\[E[(p-Y)^2]=(p-q)^2+q(1-q).\]

The irreducible term is the same for both reports; certainty adds avoidable expected error. This argument uses a probability under the specified information, not a success rate estimated after seeing this outcome.
questions.followup: A success occurs and the report one receives loss zero. Does that contradict the comparison? Calculate the realised differences on success and failure and recover the expected excess.
questions.followSolution: On success, loss(one)−loss(honest)=−\(\frac{1}{16}\). On failure it is 1−\(\frac{9}{16}\)=\(\frac{7}{16}\). Their weighted mean is (\(\frac{3}{4}\))(−\(\frac{1}{16}\))+(\(\frac{1}{4}\))(\(\frac{7}{16}\))=\(\frac{1}{16}\). A worse probability can be luckier on a single realisation. Neither a success nor a failure alone certifies long-run calibration.
rubric: Obtain the expected losses \(\frac{3}{16}\) and \(\frac{1}{4}\) and their difference \(\frac{1}{16}\).
Keep the forecast information fixed and average over both binary outcomes.
Explain the realised reversal and recover the expectation without treating one event as calibration evidence.

questions.title: The error units determine the best point estimate
questions.prompt: A positive target Y equals four or sixteen, each with probability one half under your current information. Choose a single estimate x>0 before observing Y. Your objective is to minimise EXPECTED SQUARED log-ratio loss [log(x/Y)]², using natural logs. What is the unique minimising x? Explain why this differs from minimising squared error in the original quantity.
hints: Write z=log(x); the objective becomes squared error for the random variable log(Y).
The mean of the two log values is the log of their geometric mean.
questions.solution:
Let z=log(x). Completing the square gives

\[E[(z-\log Y)^2]=(z-E[\log Y])^2+\operatorname{Var}(\log Y).\]

Here E[log Y]=3 log 2, so x=8 is unique because log is one-to-one on the positive domain. Both possible log errors have magnitude log 2, giving minimum squared loss (log 2)². Ordinary squared error instead selects \(\mathbb E[Y]\)=10. Its minimum is thirty-six, whereas choosing eight gives original-unit squared error forty. The scoring rule, not a universal idea of an accurate estimate, determines which answer is optimal.
questions.followup: Replace SQUARED log-ratio loss by ABSOLUTE log-ratio loss. Is eight still the unique optimum? Also describe what happens when both the target and estimate are converted to units one hundred times larger, or when the target can be zero.
questions.followSolution: Absolute error in log space is minimised by any median. For these two equally likely log values, every z between log 4 and log 16 is a median; thus EVERY x in [4,16] minimises the absolute log loss, with value log 2. Eight remains optimal but is no longer unique. Multiplying both x and Y by one hundred leaves x/Y and both log losses unchanged. A zero target makes this log-ratio objective undefined; adding an arbitrary offset changes the task rather than extending the same loss.
rubric: Transform to log space and derive the unique squared-loss estimate eight.
Compare with the original-unit squared-loss optimum ten and its losses.
Derive the whole absolute-log-loss optimum interval and respect the positive domain and unit conversion.

questions.title: A perfect-looking bin can hide opposite forecasts
questions.prompt: Two pre-outcome forecasts are p₁=0.1 and p₂=0.9. Dataset A pairs them with outcomes (0,1); dataset B pairs them with outcomes (1,0). A diagnostic puts both records in ONE coarse bin. Compare the bin count, mean forecast, observed rate and direct mean Brier loss for the two datasets. Can the three bin summaries reconstruct the loss? Derive the missing relationship using empirical variances and covariance with divisor TWO.
hints: The summaries forget which outcome was paired with which forecast.
Expand the mean of (p−y)² around the two empirical means.
The covariance term changes sign although both marginal lists stay the same.
questions.solution:
Both bins have count two, mean forecast one half and observed rate one half. Their average forecast-minus-outcome gap is zero. But A has loss 0.01 on each record, while B has loss 0.81 on each record. Let empirical means be \(\bar p,\bar y\), and use divisor n in empirical variances and covariance. Expanding centred records yields

\[\begin{aligned}\overline{(p-y)^2}&=(\bar p-\bar y)^2\\&\quad+\operatorname{Var}_{emp}(p)\\&\quad+\operatorname{Var}_{emp}(y)\\&\quad-2\operatorname{Cov}_{emp}(p,y).\end{aligned}\]

Here the forecast variance is 0.16 and outcome variance 0.25. Covariance is +0.2 in A and −0.2 in B, giving 0.01 and 0.81 respectively. Coarse bin averages erase this pairing term. A zero bin gap therefore neither determines Brier loss nor proves population calibration.
questions.followup: Suppose the two outcomes are independent Bernoulli variables with TRUE success probabilities 0.1 and 0.9. What are the probabilities of the two observed datasets? Would the bad score in B prove the model probabilities wrong? Would splitting into one-record bins establish long-run calibration?
questions.followSolution: A has probability (1−0.1)·0.9=0.81, while B has probability 0.1·(1−0.9)=0.01. Other outcome pairs account for the remaining 0.18. B is unusual but possible under the correct probabilities. Singleton bins expose their individual observed discrepancies, yet a binary outcome is not its underlying probability. Preserve matched forecasts, outcome timestamps and an evaluation protocol; use adequate counts and uncertainty rather than proclaiming calibration from this tiny sample. The probability calculation needs the explicitly added independence assumption; the empirical covariance identity does not.
rubric: Calculate equal bin summaries but Brier losses 0.01 and 0.81.
Derive the centred identity with divisor n and the correct covariance signs.
Distinguish lost pairing, a realised score and population calibration; obtain event probabilities under the added independent model.

questions.title: Winning reweights the value behind your signal
questions.prompt: After observing your own signal, common asset value V is one hundred with probability \(\frac{1}{4}\) and zero otherwise. You have ALREADY fixed a first-price bid of ten. Conditional on V AND your current information, two rival bids are independent. Each rival bids below ten with probability 0.8 if V=0 and 0.4 if V=100. You win precisely when both rival bids are below ten, pay ten on winning and pay nothing otherwise. What is E[V | your information, winning]? This is inference at the fixed bid, not an equilibrium bid calculation.
hints: Square each conditional crossing probability before applying Bayes.
The prior weights already include your signal; do not use that signal a second time.
questions.solution: The winning likelihoods are \(\frac{16}{25}\) and \(\frac{4}{25}\). Multiplying by the signal-conditioned prior gives low-value-and-win mass \(\frac{12}{25}\) and high-value-and-win mass \(\frac{1}{25}\). Total winning probability is \(\frac{13}{25}\), so the conditional high-value probability is \(\frac{1}{13}\) and conditional value is \(\frac{100}{13}\). Conditional expected net gain is \(\frac{100}{13}\)−10=−\(\frac{30}{13}\). Ex-ante gain under your present information is (\(\frac{13}{25}\))(−\(\frac{30}{13}\))=−\(\frac{6}{5}\). The signal-only mean twenty-five is insufficient: subtracting ten from it ignores the value-dependent event on which you pay.
questions.followup: Use one rival instead, then m conditionally independent rivals with the same crossing probabilities. Derive the winning posterior. Could you optimise your bid by using this posterior unchanged at every bid?
questions.followSolution:
With one rival, joint winning masses are \(\frac{3}{5}\) and \(\frac{1}{10}\); win probability is \(\frac{7}{10}\), conditional high-value probability \(\frac{1}{7}\), conditional value \(\frac{100}{7}\) and ex-ante gain three. For m rivals,

\[P(V=100\mid\mathrm{Win})=\frac{1}{1+3\cdot2^m}.\]

Its mean is one hundred times that probability. These crossing probabilities are stipulated AT BID TEN. Changing the bid changes the rival crossing events, requiring their laws at the new threshold. No calculation here establishes a best response or equilibrium. Without conditional independence, multiplying crossing probabilities is unjustified.
rubric: Use both rival likelihoods and the signal-conditioned prior exactly once.
Obtain conditional value \(\frac{100}{13}\), win probability \(\frac{13}{25}\) and expected net gain −\(\frac{6}{5}\).
Derive the one-rival and m-rival changes, identifying the independence and fixed-bid boundaries.

questions.title: Optimise the bid and the selection event together
questions.prompt: A risk-neutral bidder’s current information assigns common value V=100 or V=200 equal probability. There are two rivals, whose bids are conditionally independent given V. If V=100, each bid is uniform on [0,100]; if V=200, each is uniform on [100,200]. These rival laws are fixed and exogenous: no equilibrium is asserted. Choose a real first-price bid b in [0,200], win if it exceeds BOTH rival bids, pay b only on winning and receive V then. Otherwise gain is zero. Ties have probability zero, and there are no other costs. Derive expected gain over the WHOLE allowed interval and prove its global maximising bid. Compare that bid with the conditional value on winning.
hints: For b below one hundred, a win is possible only in the low-value state.
For b above one hundred, low-value wins are certain but incur a negative margin.
Compare the maxima of both pieces and all boundaries, not just a stationary point.
questions.solution:
For 0≤b≤100, two independent uniform crossings give

\[G(b)=\tfrac12(100-b)(b/100)^2.\]

Its derivative is \(b(200-3b)/20000\), positive up to \(\frac{200}{3}\) and negative thereafter; boundaries give zero. The interior maximum is therefore at b=\(\frac{200}{3}\) with gain \(\frac{200}{27}\). For 100≤b≤200 write x=(b−100)/100, so x∈[0,1]. The low state always wins and the high state wins with probability x². Hence

\[G(b)=50[-x+(1-x)x^2].\]

For x>0, (1−x)x²<x, so this entire piece is negative; at x=0 it is zero. The low-piece optimum is the global unique maximum. At that bid, winning reveals V=100, with total win probability \(\frac{2}{9}\). Conditional margin is \(\frac{100}{3}\), whose product with \(\frac{2}{9}\) gives \(\frac{200}{27}\). Conditional value ONE HUNDRED is not the optimal bid: raising the bid trades margin against win probability. Bidding the unconditional mean 150 wins with probability \(\frac{5}{8}\), gives winning mean value 120 and expected gain −\(\frac{75}{4}\).
questions.followup: Replace the two rivals by m≥1 conditionally independent rivals with the same state-dependent uniform laws. Find the global optimum and maximum gain. Explain which parts would need reconsideration for a second-price auction or endogenous rival strategies.
questions.followSolution:
The low piece is G(b)=50(1−z)z^m with z=b/100. Its derivative changes sign at z=m/(m+1), yielding

\[b^*=\frac{100m}{m+1},\qquad G(b^*)=\frac{50m^m}{(m+1)^{m+1}}.\]

The upper piece is 50[−x+(1−x)x^m], negative for x>0 because x^m≤x and 1−x<1. Boundaries do not improve the positive interior gain. Within the upper piece the winning high-state probability is x^m/(1+x^m), so the winning value itself changes with the action. Second-price payments depend on the highest rival bid, not your b, altering the margin objective. If rival strategies respond to you, the fixed crossing laws need a strategic model; the present optimum is a best response to specified exogenous laws.
rubric: Derive both expected-gain pieces using conditional joint crossings and first-price payments.
Prove global optimality at \(\frac{200}{3}\) including boundaries and the negative upper piece.
Calculate gain \(\frac{200}{27}\) and distinguish the optimum from conditional value and the raw mean.
Derive the m-rival formula and state precisely what changes with payment rules or strategic responses.

checks.prompt: What is the globally optimal first-price bid?
checks.explanation: The lower segment maximizes (100−b)b²/20000; the upper segment is nonpositive.

checks.prompt: What is its expected gain per opportunity?

questions.title: Can new information improve an already calibrated forecast?
questions.prompt: Let Y be binary, P∈[0,1] a probability report, and G another feature. Both P and G are available BEFORE Y occurs. Under a fixed population joint law define \(R=E[Y\mid P]\) and \(T=E[Y\mid P,G]\); use the exact conditional expectations, not fitted estimates. Prove that R and T are each calibrated and derive the changes in expected Brier loss from P to R and from R to T. Does calibration of P alone rule out a strict improvement from G? State when each improvement is strict.
hints: For any information set, subtract its conditional mean and make the cross term vanish.
R is a function of P, whereas T uses the larger information set.
Apply the tower property to show calibration even when multiple information states produce the same report.
questions.solution:
Because \(E[Y-R\mid P]=0\), expanding squared loss around R gives

\[E[(P-Y)^2]-E[(R-Y)^2]=E[(P-R)^2].\]

Likewise R and T are measurable under the enlarged information (P,G), and \(E[Y-T\mid P,G]=0\), so

\[E[(R-Y)^2]-E[(T-Y)^2]=E[(T-R)^2].\]

The right sides are nonnegative and strictly positive precisely when the corresponding forecasts differ with positive probability. Tower conditioning gives E[Y|R]=E[E[Y|P]|R]=R and E[Y|T]=E[E[Y|P,G]|T]=T. If P is calibrated then R=P almost surely, but T can still vary within a fixed P. For example, two equally likely regimes have conditional success probabilities \(\frac{1}{4}\) and \(\frac{3}{4}\) while P=\(\frac{1}{2}\) in both. P is calibrated globally and has expected loss \(\frac{1}{4}\); the regime-informed T has expected loss \(\frac{3}{16}\), improving by \(\frac{1}{16}\). No independence across successive evaluation records is needed for these population identities; pre-outcome availability and the declared joint law are essential.
questions.followup: A developer estimates T from the same finite dataset used to evaluate it and obtains smaller empirical loss. Does your proof certify future improvement? What if G actually contains the eventual outcome? Specify a valid comparison protocol.
questions.followSolution: The proof concerns exact population conditional means. A fitted estimate can have approximation and estimation error; minimising in-sample residuals can reward overfitting. A feature containing the eventual outcome would make T=Y and give zero retrospective error, but is unavailable for a forecast. Define the feature timestamp and baseline in advance, fit transformations/recalibration only on training data, then evaluate paired pre-outcome forecasts on untouched data with a split appropriate to dependence and deployment time. Report both losses and uncertainty. Finite bin frequencies can help diagnose reliability but neither equal the population means by definition nor guarantee out-of-sample improvement.
rubric: Derive both squared-loss differences through conditional cross-term cancellation.

lessons.title: Count the right sample space
lessons.intro: Before calculating a probability, describe the experiment, what counts as one outcome, and why the outcomes have the probabilities you assign to them.

sections.title: Start with the experiment, outcomes and event
sections.text:
An experiment is the random procedure you carry out: for example, rolling one die or drawing two balls from a bag. An outcome records one possible result of that procedure. You must decide exactly what information the record contains.

The sample space, written \(\Omega\) and read “omega”, is the set of all possible outcomes. An event, written \(A\), is a collection of outcomes that satisfy a condition you care about.

For one fair six-sided die, \(\Omega=\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}\). If the event is “roll an even number”, then \(A=\{2,4,6\}\). The notation \(|\Omega|\) means the number of outcomes in the sample space; \(|A|\) means the number of outcomes in the event. Here these counts are 6 and 3. The vertical bars mean “number of elements”, not absolute value, when their contents are a set.

sections.title: When counting gives a probability
sections.text:
If a finite sample space has equally likely outcomes, every outcome has probability \(1/|\Omega|\). Therefore,

\[P(A)=\frac{|A|}{|\Omega|}.\]

Read this as “the probability of the event equals the number of favourable outcomes divided by the total number of equally likely outcomes”. For the even-number event above, \(P(A)=3/6=1/2\).

“Uniformly chosen” means that each outcome in the specified set has the same probability. It is an assumption about the sampling procedure, not a consequence of merely listing outcomes. A biased coin still has two possible outcomes, heads and tails, but counting one favourable outcome out of two does not establish a probability of one half. When outcomes are not equally likely, add their actual probabilities instead.

sections.title: Two dice: why the outcomes are ordered
sections.text:
Roll two independent fair six-sided dice, one red and one blue. Record an outcome as (red die value, blue die value). The outcome (2,5) differs from (5,2), because the values are assigned to different dice.

There are 6 choices for the red die and, for each choice, 6 choices for the blue die. Thus there are \(6\times6=36\) ordered outcomes. Fairness and independence make each ordered outcome have probability \((1/6)(1/6)=1/36\).

If you instead record only the sum, the possible sums are 2 through 12, but those eleven outcomes are not equally likely. Sum 2 comes only from (1,1), while sum 7 comes from six ordered outcomes. So \(P(\text{sum}=2)=1/36\) and \(P(\text{sum}=7)=6/36\), not one eleventh each. Your choice of sample space must preserve the probabilities.

sections.title: Drawing two balls: define n before counting
sections.text:
Suppose a bag contains \(n\) individually distinguishable balls, where \(n\geq2\). Draw one ball uniformly, keep it out of the bag, then draw a second ball uniformly from the remaining balls. This is sampling without replacement: the same physical ball cannot appear twice.

Now ignore the order in which the two balls were drawn. An unordered pair records which two balls you obtained; drawing A then B and drawing B then A produce the same pair, AB.

There are \(n\) choices for the first ball and \(n-1\) choices for the second, giving \(n(n-1)\) ordered selections. Every unordered pair is counted exactly twice in that total, once in each order. Divide by two:

\[\binom{n}{2}=\frac{n(n-1)}{2}.\]

The notation \(\binom{n}{2}\), read “n choose two”, counts the ways to select two different objects from n objects while ignoring order. For four balls labelled A, B, C and D, the six unordered pairs are AB, AC, AD, BC, BD and CD. The formula gives \(\binom{4}{2}=4\times3/2=6\).

Under the sampling procedure stated above, every unordered pair has the same probability: its two ordered selections each have probability \(1/[n(n-1)]\). Balls of the same colour are still different physical balls. Recording only the colours would group together different numbers of these equally likely pairs.

sections.title: Replacement changes the experiment
sections.text:
With replacement, you return the first ball before the second draw. Without replacement, you leave it out. These are different experiments and can give different probabilities for the same verbal event.

Suppose the bag contains 6 red balls and 4 blue balls, and the event is “the two colours differ”. Without replacement, a red-first draw leaves 4 blue balls among 9 remaining balls. A blue-first draw leaves 6 red balls among 9 remaining balls. The two possible colour orders cannot both occur, so add their probabilities:

\[P(\text{different colours})=\frac6{10}\frac49+\frac4{10}\frac69=\frac8{15}.\]

With replacement, the second draw again uses the original bag of 10 balls:

\[P(\text{different colours})=\frac6{10}\frac4{10}+\frac4{10}\frac6{10}=\frac{12}{25}.\]

The second denominator is 9 in the first experiment and 10 in the second. State the replacement rule before choosing a counting formula.

sections.title: Complements and overlapping events
sections.text:
The complement of an event A, written \(A^c\), contains all outcomes in which A does not happen. Since exactly one of A and its complement happens, \(P(A)=1-P(A^c)\).

For two independent fair coin flips, the equally likely ordered outcomes are HH, HT, TH and TT, where H means heads and T means tails. “At least one head” includes HH, HT and TH. Its complement is “no heads”, which contains only TT. The probability is therefore \(1-1/4=3/4\). Listing the favourable outcomes gives the same result, \(3/4\).

For two events A and B, \(A\cup B\) means “A or B, including both”, and \(A\cap B\) means “both A and B”. The addition rule is

\[P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B).\]

Adding the first two probabilities counts the overlap twice; subtracting it once corrects this. With the two dice above, let A mean “the red die is six” and B mean “the blue die is six”. Each event has probability \(1/6\); both happen with probability \(1/36\). Thus the chance of at least one six is \(1/6+1/6-1/36=11/36\).

sections.title: Independence and disjointness are different
sections.text:
Events are independent when learning that one happened does not change the probability of the other. Their joint probability then satisfies \(P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)\). Fairness describes one die's probabilities; independence describes how the dice relate to one another. Neither assumption replaces the other.

Events are disjoint when they cannot happen together, so \(P(A\cap B)=0\). For disjoint events, the addition rule reduces to \(P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)\).

For one die, “roll 1” and “roll 2” are disjoint. They are not independent: learning that the die rolled 1 makes the probability of rolling 2 zero. For two independent dice, “red die is six” and “blue die is six” are independent, but they are not disjoint because (6,6) satisfies both.

Before solving an interview problem, write down the experiment, the outcome you record, whether order matters, whether replacement is allowed, and the justification for equal likelihood or independence. Then identify the event and count or add probabilities.

lessons.example:
Work through the 6-red, 4-blue example using unordered pairs. There are 10 individually distinguishable balls in total, so \(n=10\). Draw two uniformly without replacement and ignore their order.

The total number of equally likely pairs is \(\binom{10}{2}=10\times9/2=45\). To obtain different colours, choose one of the 6 red balls and one of the 4 blue balls. This produces \(6\times4=24\) favourable unordered pairs; each red-blue pair is counted once. Therefore,

\[P(\text{different colours})=\frac{24}{45}=\frac8{15}.\]

This agrees with the red-then-blue plus blue-then-red calculation above. Both methods describe the same experiment. Counting only “red-red, red-blue, blue-blue” and assigning each probability one third would be wrong: those three colour categories contain different numbers of physical pairs.
lessons.check: For two independent fair coins, what is \(P(\text{at least one H})\)?
lessons.explanation: The four equally likely ordered outcomes are HH, HT, TH and TT. Only TT has no heads. The probability of at least one head is 1 minus \(\frac{1}{4}\), which is \(\frac{3}{4}\).
objectives: Define an experiment, sample space and event before calculating.
Distinguish ordered and unordered sampling with and without replacement.
Justify equal likelihood and separate independence from disjointness.

lessons.title: Condition, then normalise
lessons.intro: Conditioning changes the information you are allowed to use. Rebuild the relevant population before calculating, then use Bayes to compare explanations of what you observed.

sections.title: What does “given” mean?
sections.text:
Let A and B be events in an experiment. The statement “given B” means that you know B happened, so outcomes outside B are no longer possible. You are computing a probability in that restricted population, not in the original one.

Provided \(P(B)>0\), define
\[P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}.\]
The numerator is the probability mass that satisfies both conditions. Dividing by the mass of B rescales the restricted population so its total probability becomes one. If the original outcomes are equally likely, you may count favourable outcomes inside B. Otherwise, retain their probability weights.

The direction matters: “has a positive test given disease” and “has disease given a positive test” condition on different populations. They can have very different answers.

sections.title: A concrete conditional sample space
sections.text:
Roll two independent fair six-sided dice, with the first die distinguishable from the second. Before observing anything there are 36 equally likely ordered pairs. Now learn that the sum is 8. The surviving pairs are (2,6), (3,5), (4,4), (5,3) and (6,2).

Each surviving pair originally had probability \(\frac{1}{36}\). Their total mass is \(\frac{5}{36}\), so each now has conditional probability one fifth. The event “the dice agree” contains only (4,4), giving \(P(\text{double}\mid\text{sum}=8)=1/5\).

Do not keep a denominator of 36: that would compute the chance of a double AND a sum of 8, before receiving the observation. The new question asks about an experiment whose outcome is already known to satisfy the sum constraint.

sections.title: Multiplication and total probability
sections.text:
Rearranging the definition gives \(P(A\cap B)=P(A\mid B)P(B)\). This identity does not require independence. Independence is the additional statement that conditioning on B does not change the probability of A.

Suppose hypotheses \(H_1,\ldots,H_m\) are mutually exclusive and cover every possibility. For an observation D, split its probability into branches:
\[P(D)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}P(D\mid H_i)P(H_i).\]
You multiply along each branch and add across alternatives that cannot occur together. Check that the hypothesis list really covers the population. Omitting an alternative produces the wrong normalising denominator even if every multiplication is correct.

sections.title: Bayes: update weights, then normalise
sections.text:
The prior \(P(H_i)\) is a hypothesis's probability before D. The likelihood \(P(D\mid H_i)\) is the probability of the observation under that hypothesis. The posterior is its updated probability after D:
\[P(H_i\mid D)=\frac{P(D\mid H_i)P(H_i)}{\sum_jP(D\mid H_j)P(H_j)}.\]
A reliable interview method is to write one unnormalised weight for each hypothesis, then divide each weight by their sum. A large likelihood alone does not establish a large posterior: a very rare hypothesis can still have little total weight.

For a fair coin and an always-heads coin selected with equal probability, observing one head gives weights (one half times one half) and (one half times one). Their sum is three quarters, so the always-heads posterior is two thirds.

sections.title: More observations require a sampling model
sections.text:
Keep the SAME selected coin for k flips. Conditional on the fair-coin hypothesis, assume flips are independent. Its likelihood for k consecutive heads is \(2^{-k}\); the always-heads likelihood is one. Equal priors therefore give
\[P(\text{always-heads}\mid k\text{ heads})=\frac{1}{1+2^{-k}}.\]
For k=2 the posterior is four fifths. This formula would not describe a procedure that selects a fresh coin before every flip. An observed tail assigns zero posterior weight to the always-heads hypothesis under this idealised model. If the “always-heads” coin actually has a small tail probability, zero is no longer justified.

Before multiplying likelihoods, ask what remains fixed and which observations are conditionally independent.

sections.title: Exact continuous observations need a different definition
sections.text:
The event formula divides by P(B), so it does not directly define conditioning on an exact value of a continuous variable when that event has probability zero. A continuous signal requires a conditional-density model or another appropriate conditional-probability construction.

For discrete hypotheses and a continuous signal s, posterior weights can use the signal DENSITY under each hypothesis: prior weight times density at s, then normalise. A density is not the probability of that exact signal; it describes probability per unit signal near s. Its value can exceed one without violating probability bounds.

This distinction prevents an otherwise sensible Bayes argument from dividing by zero or treating a density as an event probability. Match likelihoods to whether the observation is a discrete event, an interval or a continuous measurement.

sections.title: Conditioning can create dependence
sections.text:
The two dice were independent before you learned their sum. Given sum 8, if you learn that the first die is 2, the second must be 6. The observation couples variables that previously varied freely.

Conversely, observations can be independent conditional on a hidden hypothesis while being dependent before that hypothesis is known. Repeated heads suggest that the same hidden coin is favourable, changing the prediction of the next flip. Be explicit about whether an independence claim is unconditional or conditional on a specified variable.

Rehearse the argument aloud: state the observation, identify surviving possibilities or hypothesis weights, normalise, and check that the result lies between zero and one. Finally say which sampling assumption would change the answer.

lessons.example: Compare the two dice and coin examples. For dice, the observation removes ordered pairs; for coins, both hypotheses survive but with different weights. In the coin experiment, the joint mass of “always-heads and a head” is one half; the total head probability is three quarters. Dividing yields two thirds. Predict the next flip without picking the most likely coin as if it were certain: \(P(\text{next H}\mid\text{first H})=(2/3)\times1+(1/3)\times(1/2)=5/6\). The posterior still retains uncertainty about the coin.
lessons.check: After seeing H from this mixture, what is \(P(\text{always-heads})\)?
lessons.explanation: The always-heads branch contributes probability \(\frac{1}{2}\); the fair branch contributes \(\frac{1}{4}\). Normalise the first weight by their sum \(\frac{3}{4}\) to obtain \(\frac{2}{3}\).
objectives: Build a conditional sample space and normalise its probabilities.
Distinguish likelihood, prior and posterior.
Explain why conditioning can create dependence.

lessons.title: Expectation without independence
lessons.intro: Expectation is a probability-weighted average. Its linearity lets you break complicated counts into simple indicators, even when their events overlap.

sections.title: A random variable and its mean
sections.text:
A random variable assigns a number to each outcome. For a discrete variable X with possible values x, its expectation is \(E[X]=\sum_x xP(X=x)\), whenever the expectation is well defined. A fair die has expectation (1+2+3+4+5+6)/6=3.5. The mean need not itself be a possible realised value.

For ordinary signed variables, absolute integrability, \(E[|X|]<\infty\), is a convenient condition that makes sums and rearrangements safe. Nonnegative variables can have an infinite expectation; the formula then describes an extended value rather than a finite average. State the assumption before manipulating an infinite series.

sections.title: Why linearity works
sections.text:
For integrable variables X and Y and constants a and b,
\[E[aX+bY]=aE[X]+bE[Y].\]
This follows by averaging the linear expression outcome by outcome. It does not require X and Y to be independent. If Y always equals X, the variables are maximally dependent, yet the mean of their sum is still twice the mean of X.

Independence is needed for other shortcuts. In general \(E[XY]\) does not equal \(E[X]E[Y]\). For a fair die X, the expectation of its square is \(\frac{91}{6}\), whereas the square of its expectation is 12.25. Always distinguish a sum, a product and a nonlinear transformation before selecting a rule.

sections.title: Indicators convert events into arithmetic
sections.text:
For an event A, its indicator \(I_A\) is one when A happens and zero otherwise. Hence \(E[I_A]=P(A)\). If a count C records how many of m events occur, write \(C=\sum_{i=1}^{m}I_i\). Linearity then gives
\[E[C]=\sum_{i=1}^{m}P(I_i=1).\]
You only need each event's individual probability to compute this mean. The indicators may overlap or share a common cause. A useful first step in a counting problem is to ask what one indicator should count: a position, an object, a pair or a distinct category. Choosing the wrong unit can double-count or omit events.

sections.title: Overlapping heads, carefully counted
sections.text:
Flip a fair coin independently 20 times. Let \(I_i\) indicate that flips i and i+1 are both heads, for i from 1 through 19. There are 19 possible adjacent positions, not 20. Each position is HH with probability one quarter, so the expected number of adjacent HH pairs is \(\frac{19}{4}=4.75\).

The sequence HHH contributes two pairs, at its first and second positions. Adjacent indicators are dependent because they share a flip, but their expectations still add. If the head probability is p with independent flips, the corresponding expectation is \((n-1)p^2\) for n flips. If flips are dependent, linearity still works but the individual pair probability may cease to be p squared.

sections.title: Tail sums: count how many thresholds are crossed
sections.text:
For a nonnegative integer-valued variable N, a realised value of three can be written as three ones: it exceeds or equals thresholds 1, 2 and 3. Thus \(N=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}I_{\{N\geq k\}}\), giving
\[E[N]=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}P(N\geq k).\]
Nonnegativity justifies this interchange even if the result is infinite. For a nonnegative continuous variable X, the analogous identity is
\[E[X]=\int_0^{\infty}P(X>t)\,dt.\]
The area under the survival curve represents the mean. Do not apply these nonnegative formulas unchanged to a variable that can take negative values. Separate its positive and negative parts and check finiteness.

sections.title: The maximum of two dice
sections.text:
Let M be the larger of two independent fair dice. For integer k from 1 through 6, both dice are at most k with probability \(P(M\leq k)=k^2/36\). Subtract successive cumulative probabilities to obtain
\[P(M=k)=\frac{k^2-(k-1)^2}{36}=\frac{2k-1}{36}.\]
Multiplying each k by this probability and summing yields \(\frac{161}{36}\), approximately 4.4722. A maximum preferentially selects larger outcomes, so the maximum of the means, 3.5, is not the expected maximum.

As a check, the minimum plus maximum equals the sum of the two dice in every outcome. Their expectations must therefore sum to seven, giving an expected minimum of \(\frac{91}{36}\). This uses a pointwise identity, not an independence assumption about minimum and maximum.

sections.title: What linearity does not tell you
sections.text:
A mean does not describe fluctuation around that mean. For a sum, variance contains covariance terms. With n independent fair flips, the HH-count variance is \((5n-7)/16\) for n at least two: each indicator contributes variance \(\frac{3}{16}\) and each adjacent pair contributes covariance \(\frac{1}{16}\) twice in the sum formula.

You will derive that variance machinery in the dependence lesson. For now, identify exactly where dependence mattered: not in adding means, but in relating indicators jointly. Practise explaining both the short solution and why the longer independence argument is unnecessary.

lessons.example: For two dice, compute the maximum's weighted sum explicitly: the numerator is \(1\times1+2\times3+3\times5+4\times7+5\times9+6\times11=161\), and the denominator is 36. A second route uses \(P(M\geq k)=1-(k-1)^2/36\) for k=1 through 6. Summing gives \(6-(0+1+4+9+16+25)/36=161/36\). Matching two methods is a useful interview check; neither treats the maximum as a fair die.
lessons.check: Do overlapping indicators prevent adding their expectations?
options: Only if they have equal means
lessons.explanation: Linearity of expectation does not require independence.
objectives: Define expectation and turn a count into indicators.
Use linearity without inventing independence.
Derive discrete and continuous tail-sum identities.
optionLabels: Only if they have equal means

lessons.title: Distributions as usable models
lessons.intro: A distribution is a model for how an experiment produces outcomes. Learn its assumptions, support and probabilities before memorising its mean.

sections.title: Describe the distribution before using a formula
sections.text:
For a random variable X, the cumulative distribution function is \(F_X(x)=P(X\leq x)\). Its survival probability is \(P(X>x)=1-F_X(x)\). A discrete probability mass function assigns probabilities to individual values. A continuous density assigns probability through integration over intervals; a density value itself is not a point probability.

Specify the support: the set of allowed values. A \(\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\) variable takes values between zero and one, with constant density one there. Its CDF is zero below zero, x on the unit interval and one above one. An exponential waiting time is nonnegative and unbounded. Mixing these supports is a common source of incorrect integrals.

sections.title: Independent uniform draws and the maximum
sections.text:
Draw n independent \(\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\) variables \(U_1,\ldots,U_n\), with n a positive integer. Let M be their maximum. For x between zero and one, M is at most x precisely when every draw is at most x. Independence gives
\[P(M\leq x)=\prod_{i=1}^{n}P(U_i\leq x)=x^n.\]
Its density is \(nx^{n-1}\) on this interval, obtained by differentiating the CDF. The tail-integral identity also gives
\[E[M]=\int_0^1(1-x^n)\,dx=\frac{n}{n+1}.\]
For one draw the mean is one half; increasing n moves the expected maximum toward one. Both checks are consistent with the experiment.

sections.title: The minimum uses survival probabilities
sections.text:
Let m be the minimum of the same independent draws. The event m>x requires every draw to exceed x, so \(P(m>x)=(1-x)^n\) for x in the unit interval. Therefore,
\[E[m]=\int_0^1(1-x)^n\,dx=\frac{1}{n+1}.\]
For three draws, the minimum's mean is one quarter and the maximum's is three quarters. Those symmetric means result from the \(\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\) model. They are not a general minimum/maximum rule for arbitrary distributions.

If all n draws are actually copies of one shared uniform variable, the independence multiplication fails. The minimum and maximum then both equal that variable and both have mean one half, regardless of n.

sections.title: Exponential waiting times and units
sections.text:
A waiting time T has exponential rate \(\lambda>0\) when its survival probability is \(P(T>t)=e^{-\lambda t}\) for t at least zero. Its density is \(\lambda e^{-\lambda t}\), and integrating the survival curve gives \(E[T]=1/\lambda\).

Rate and mean are different parameters. A rate of two arrivals per minute produces a mean wait of half a minute. A rate of one half per minute produces a mean wait of two minutes. The exponent must be dimensionless: rate times time has no units.

A constant exponential rate models a wait whose instantaneous chance of ending does not depend on its age. Real waits need not satisfy this assumption.

sections.title: Memorylessness: remaining time is not total time
sections.text:
For nonnegative s and t,
\[P(T>s+t\mid T>s)=\frac{e^{-\lambda(s+t)}}{e^{-\lambda s}}=e^{-\lambda t}.\]
Conditional on already waiting s, the remaining wait has the same exponential distribution as a fresh wait. Consequently its expected remaining time is \(\frac1{\text{rate}}\), while expected total time is s plus \(\frac1{\text{rate}}\).

With rate one half per minute and three minutes already elapsed, remaining expectation is two and total expectation is five. This distinction is the whole point of that interview question. For a wait uniformly distributed between zero and ten minutes, surviving past minute nine instead leaves a mean of half a minute; memorylessness fails.

sections.title: Competing independent clocks
sections.text:
Let X and Y be independent exponential waits with rates a and b, respectively. Their minimum exceeds t when both exceed t, so its survival is \(e^{-at}e^{-bt}=e^{-(a+b)t}\). The first ring therefore has exponential rate a+b.

The chance that X wins is
\[P(X<Y)=\int_0^\infty ae^{-at}e^{-bt}\,dt=\frac{a}{a+b}.\]
The integrand combines “X rings around t” with “Y has not rung yet”. Ties have probability zero for these continuous waits. This ratio assumes independent clocks and constant exponential rates; it is not a universal race formula for any waiting-time distributions.

sections.title: Geometric probability depends on the experiment
sections.text:
For the stick-cutting problem, choose two independent uniform positions on a unit stick, then order them as \(U<V\). The three lengths are U, V-U and 1-V. A nondegenerate triangle requires every piece to be less than one half.

The ordered cut locations occupy a triangle of area one half. The valid region satisfies \(U<\frac12\), \(V>\frac12\) and V-\(U<\frac12\), with area one eighth. Their ratio is one quarter. Boundary equalities have probability zero.

Choosing an existing piece first and then cutting that piece defines another experiment and another distribution. Always derive the density on the region you are measuring instead of assuming that every visually plausible region is uniform.

lessons.example: Take two independent exponential clocks with rates three and two per minute. Their first ring has rate five per minute and expected time one fifth of a minute. The rate-three clock wins with probability three fifths. These are different objects: a time and a probability. Their joint density for “clock one wins at time t” is \(3e^{-5t}\), which factors into \((3/5)(5e^{-5t})\). Under this specific model the winner and first-ring time are independent.
lessons.check: Given an Exponential(rate 2) wait has exceeded 5, what is the expected remaining wait?
lessons.explanation: Memorylessness gives a fresh expected wait of \(\frac{1}{2}\).
objectives: Distinguish probability mass, density, CDF and survival.
Derive the extremes of independent uniform draws.
Explain exponential memorylessness and competing clocks.

lessons.title: A state is a sufficient memory
lessons.intro: Overlapping patterns and stopping problems become manageable when you retain exactly the history that affects the future. Turn that history into states and write first-step equations.

sections.title: What are you counting, and when do you stop?
sections.text:
A stopping time is a random time whose decision to stop can be made from observations available so far. Counting flips until the first HH pattern is a stopping-time problem. Deciding at time five whether to stop because flip six will be heads uses future information and is not a stopping time with respect to the observed flips.

State the convention: our wait includes every flip, including the final flips completing the pattern. Distinguish an expected stopping time from a probability of eventually stopping. A process can stop with probability one yet have infinite expected duration. Do not assume a finite answer merely because a recurrence can be written.

sections.title: Choose a sufficient state
sections.text:
Flip a fair coin independently until HH occurs. Before finishing, there are two useful states: state 0 means no trailing head, and state H means the latest flip was a head. State HH is terminal. Earlier history does not change future transition probabilities because the coin flips are independent and only the suffix matters for matching HH.

Let E0 and EH be expected additional flips from the two nonterminal states. The terminal state's expected additional wait is zero. Be precise about “additional”: EH is not the total number of flips already spent reaching H. This choice prevents adding elapsed time twice.

sections.title: First-step equations and their solution
sections.text:
From state 0, pay one flip. A tail leaves you in 0 and a head moves you to H, each with probability one half. From H, a head finishes while a tail returns to 0. Hence
\[E_0=1+\frac{E_0+E_H}{2},\qquad E_H=1+\frac{E_0}{2}.\]
The first equation gives \(E_0=2+E_H\). Substitute the second: \(E_0=3+E_0/2\), so E0=6 and EH=4.

The tempting answer four is the reciprocal of the probability of HH in a fixed two-flip window. Consecutive windows overlap and are not fresh independent attempts. A tail can destroy partial progress; the state recurrence records that information.

sections.title: Why HT has a different waiting time
sections.text:
For HT, retain state H again. From H, a tail finishes and another head leaves the useful suffix H. Thus \(E_H=1+E_H/2\), giving EH=2. The state-0 equation is unchanged, so E0=4.

For HHH, use states with zero, one and two trailing heads. Every tail returns to zero. With terminal wait zero, the equations are
\[E_0=1+(E_0+E_1)/2,\quad E_1=1+(E_0+E_2)/2,\quad E_2=1+E_0/2.\]
Solving yields E0=14. The probability of a particular HHH window is one eighth, but the expected wait is not eight. The distinction between a fixed-window event and a sequential search must remain visible in your explanation.

sections.title: Prove that the wait has a finite mean
sections.text:
For HH, split flips into nonoverlapping blocks of two. Each block is HH with probability one quarter, independently across blocks. Waiting for the first successful block has geometric mean four blocks, or eight flips. The actual HH search stops no later than that block procedure, so its expectation is at most eight and is finite.

This bound is not the exact answer six. Its job is to justify treating the expected-state equations as finite quantities. Similar block arguments work for any fixed finite pattern with positive probability under independent flips. For processes with unbounded states, finiteness may require a different argument.

sections.title: Collecting symbols by stages
sections.text:
Suppose each independent draw returns one of m equally likely symbols, with m a positive integer. After seeing k distinct symbols, a new symbol arrives with probability (m-k)/m. The stage wait is geometric, counting the successful draw, and has mean m/(m-k).

Add expected stage durations using linearity:
\[E[T]=m\sum_{j=1}^{m}\frac1j.\]
For four symbols the terms are 1, \(\frac{4}{3}\), 2 and 4, summing to \(\frac{25}{3}\). Unequal symbol probabilities change the success rate according to WHICH symbols you have seen, not only their count. The state “k distinct symbols” then ceases to be sufficient.

sections.title: A bounded random walk
sections.text:
A fair integer random walk moves one step left or right with equal probability and stops at 0 or N, where N is a positive integer. Let ti be the expected additional steps from position i. The boundary conditions are t0=tN=0 and
\[t_i=1+\frac{t_{i-1}+t_{i+1}}2.\]
The quadratic \(t_i=i(N-i)\) satisfies both the recurrence and boundaries. For N=12 and i=5 it gives 35. A finite interval and positive chance of reaching a boundary in a bounded number of steps imply a finite expected exit time.

For the probability of hitting N first, omit the one-step cost and use boundary probabilities zero and one. The solution is i/N. Means and hitting probabilities solve different equations; identify your target before writing the recurrence.

lessons.example: Solve HH again using a different counting convention. If you have just seen a head, a second head ends the search next flip; a tail consumes one flip and puts you back at the start. Thus EH=1+E0/2. At the start, E0=1+(E0+EH)/2. Solve to obtain EH=4 and E0=6. Explain out loud why EH is still four additional flips even though one head has already been observed: a tail may erase that progress and restart a six-flip expected search.
lessons.check: What is the expected wait for HH in fair coin flips?
lessons.explanation: A tail erases a partial match; solving the two state equations gives 6.
objectives: Define states, terminal conditions and first-step recurrences.
Solve overlapping-pattern waits without treating windows as independent trials.
Check finite expectation and solve a bounded random walk.

lessons.title: Arithmetic with a method
lessons.intro: Mental arithmetic improves when you choose a structure before calculating. Build accuracy with decompositions, reciprocal anchors and checks, then train speed on the same methods.

sections.title: Accuracy first: represent the calculation
sections.text:
Mental math is not only recalling multiplication tables. It is choosing an equivalent expression that uses easier numbers and remembering the intermediate values reliably. Start a drill with a method you can explain; a fast wrong answer is not progress.

For 49 times 21, replace 49 by 50 minus one. Compute 50 times 21 as 1050, then subtract 21 to obtain 1029. The subtraction corrects the deliberate overestimate. If you subtract 49 instead, you are correcting the wrong factor. State what you changed before calculating its correction.

sections.title: Distribute, then compensate
sections.text:
The distributive identity \((a+b)c=ac+bc\) is the basic tool. For 23 times 14, use 23 times (10+4), giving 230+92=322. For 99 times 37, use 100 times 37 minus 37, giving 3663.

When both factors lie near the same anchor, the difference-of-squares identity can be shorter:
\[(a-b)(a+b)=a^2-b^2.\]
Thus 97 times 103 equals 100 squared minus 3 squared, or 9991. The factors must be equally far below and above the anchor. For 97 times 104, that identity does not apply directly; use 100 times 104 minus 3 times 104, giving 10088.

sections.title: Percentages are fractions of the base
sections.text:
