lessons.title: Continuation value and log growth
lessons.intro: Compare the payoff you can keep with the value of the remaining choices. Then see why maximising an expected payoff and maximising expected log wealth produce different decisions.

sections.title: Define the decision and objective
sections.text:
A fair six-sided die is rolled. After observing its value x, you may keep x or reroll once, accepting the second result. Assume no reroll cost, independent rolls, and an objective of maximising expected numerical payoff.

The expected payoff of a fresh roll is 3.5. After observing x, that number is the continuation value of rerolling: it averages the outcomes of your remaining action. Keep x if x exceeds 3.5 and reroll if x is smaller. For integer faces this means keep four, five and six.

The possibility of rolling six does not make rerolling a four optimal. You must compare a certain four with the entire distribution of the alternative, using the specified objective.

sections.title: Average the optimal conditional decisions
sections.text:
Before the first roll, each face occurs with probability one sixth. Optimal conditional values are 3.5 for initial one, two or three, and four, five or six for the other faces. Therefore
\[E[\text{optimal payoff}]=\frac{3(3.5)+4+5+6}{6}=4.25.\]
This is the value of the option to reroll selectively. Rerolling every face would give only 3.5; keeping every face also gives 3.5.

If a reroll costs one payoff unit, continuation becomes 2.5, so keep three through six. The ex-ante optimal value becomes (2×2.5+3+4+5+6)/6=\(\frac{23}{6}\). The action threshold changes because the alternative changed.

sections.title: More stages require backward induction
sections.text:
Let c_k be the value of a fresh roll when you may still reroll up to k times after observing it. With no rerolls, c_0=3.5. A new roll with k≥1 has value
\[c_k=\frac16\sum_{x=1}^6\max(x,c_{k-1}).\]
The previous-stage value is the continuation alternative. Thus c_1=4.25. With two rerolls available, keep five or six and reroll one through four, giving c_2=(4×4.25+5+6)/6=\(\frac{14}{3}\).

This finite-horizon recurrence uses independence and no costs. A different payoff utility, state-dependent cost or dependent roll process needs different states or continuation values. Name the remaining choices before applying a threshold.

sections.title: A good decision can lose this time
sections.text:
Keeping four is optimal in the one-free-reroll game even if a hypothetical reroll would have produced six. That unseen favourable outcome does not change the expected value at the decision point. Conversely, a poor decision can happen to pay off.

Distinguish policy quality, evaluated under the available information and objective, from the realised result. In research, comparing policies requires consistent information and sampling rules; selecting only lucky realised choices distorts the evaluation.

The objective itself matters. A person who strongly dislikes low outcomes may maximise expected utility rather than expected payoff, changing the continuation comparison.

sections.title: Set up the log-wealth model
sections.text:
Consider a repeated even-money bet with known win probability p, where \(0<p<1\). Assume independent rounds, a constant fraction f of current wealth staked each round, no fees, and 0≤f<1. A win multiplies wealth by 1+f; a loss multiplies it by 1-f.

Expected log growth per round is
\[g(f)=p\log(1+f)+(1-p)\log(1-f).\]
Logs convert multiplication of wealth into addition across rounds. This objective differs from expected profit in one round. Betting everything has a possible ruin outcome when \(p<1\) and makes log wealth undefined there, which is why f=1 is excluded.

sections.title: Differentiate and check the constraints
sections.text:
The derivative is \(g'(f)=p/(1+f)-(1-p)/(1-f)\). Setting it to zero gives p(1-f)=(1-p)(1+f), hence f=2p-1. The second derivative is negative throughout the domain, so the function is strictly concave.

With the long-only constraint 0≤f<1, the optimum is max(0,2p-1). At p=0.6 it is 0.2. Substitution gives 0.6 log(1.2)+0.4 log(0.8), about 0.0201 per round in the specified model.

If negative fractions were allowed, the feasible set and interpretation would differ. Derive the stationary point, then check the boundary and permitted actions; a formula without its domain is incomplete.

sections.title: Uncertain probabilities are a different problem
sections.text:
The derivation assumes p is known and the only payoffs are equal-sized wins and losses. An estimate of p from a short sample is uncertain; correlated opportunities, unequal payoffs, fees, liquidity constraints and larger-than-modelled losses also alter the objective.

A sensitivity calculation already shows fragility: changing p from 0.60 to 0.52 changes the toy optimum from 0.20 to 0.04. A model-based fraction cannot be carried directly into real trading without defining those missing features and constraints.

For an interview, present log growth as a mathematical decision model, derive it and explain its limitations. Do not confuse positive expected payoff with a license to increase size indefinitely.

lessons.example: At p=0.6, an even-money fraction \(f=0.2\) gives expected log growth about 0.0201. At f=0.5 it becomes 0.6 log(1.5)+0.4 log(0.5), about -0.03398, even though expected one-round wealth gain is f(2p-1)>0 in both cases. The larger fraction wins on average in the arithmetic one-round objective yet loses in expected log growth. The difference comes from the objective's treatment of downside compounding, not from different win probabilities.
lessons.check: For one free reroll, should you keep an initial 4?
options: Only if the last roll was high
lessons.explanation: Choose by expected continuation payoff rather than the maximum possible outcome.
objectives: Derive the continuation value of a finite reroll game.
Distinguish realised outcomes from the quality of a decision.
Derive a toy log-growth optimum and state its assumptions.
optionLabels: Only if the last roll was high

lessons.title: Risk lives in joint exposures
lessons.intro: Positions interact through their joint payoffs. Measure the combined exposure, then separate an estimated variance from the constraints and tail behaviour it leaves out.

sections.title: Specify weights, units and returns
sections.text:
Let R_1 and R_2 be returns measured over the same horizon, and let w_1 and w_2 be portfolio weights fixed before those returns occur. In a simple linear portfolio, return is R_p=w_1R_1+w_2R_2. State whether weights are capital fractions, notionals or position quantities; the units of the resulting payoff differ.

For weights summing to one, this describes a fully allocated simple-return portfolio under the stated linear model. Shorts and leverage can make weights negative or make total gross exposure exceed one.

Do not combine daily variance with hourly covariance, or return weights with cash-profit variances, without conversion. A precise horizon and unit convention comes before the formula.

sections.title: Expand the square to see covariance
sections.text:
For finite second moments, centre both returns around their means and square the weighted sum. Taking expectations gives
\[\operatorname{Var}(R_p)=w_1^2\sigma_1^2+w_2^2\sigma_2^2+2w_1w_2\operatorname{Cov}(R_1,R_2).\]
Here sigma_i is the standard deviation of asset i. Covariance equals rho times sigma_1 times sigma_2, where rho is their correlation and both standard deviations are positive.

The cross term is why two individually risky assets can offset each other, or reinforce the same risk. With more assets the formula becomes \(w^\top\Sigma w\), where Sigma is the joint covariance matrix, not a list of isolated variances.

sections.title: Work through an equal-weight pair
sections.text:
Suppose both assets have variance four, so each standard deviation is two, and their correlation is 0.5. Their covariance is 0.5×2×2=2. At weights one half each, portfolio variance is
\[\tfrac14(4)+\tfrac14(4)+2(\tfrac12)(\tfrac12)(2)=3.\]
The standard deviation is sqrt(3), not three. At correlation zero variance becomes two; at correlation minus one half it becomes one; at correlation one it becomes four.

These comparisons hold variances and weights fixed. Correlation changing together with volatility can produce a larger risk increase than this isolated calculation suggests.

sections.title: Diversification depends on shared causes
sections.text:
Two instruments with different names may load on the same interest-rate, volatility or market factor. A schematic model R_i=beta_i F+epsilon_i separates a common factor F from residual components. Under uncorrelated factor and residuals, the portfolio's factor contribution is (sum of w_i beta_i)F.

Adding more positions does not necessarily reduce that shared loading. If all beta_i have the same sign, the common exposure can persist while independent residual noise averages away.

Explain what economic or statistical event could make the positions move together. Historical pairwise correlation is a summary of past joint variation, not a promise that dependencies stay fixed during stress.

sections.title: Stress the inputs and constraints
sections.text:
A covariance estimate has sampling error and may change with the regime. Recalculate portfolio behaviour under larger volatilities, stronger positive correlations and concentrated common shocks. Check whether the assumed covariance matrix is mathematically valid: every weighted variance must be nonnegative.

A capital limit, exposure cap or liquidity requirement is a constraint on permitted actions, not just a term inside expected profit. A trade with positive expected edge may breach a limit or be impossible to exit at the assumed size.

Stress scenarios are explicit alternatives, not forecasts with automatically known probabilities. Report which inputs moved, what stayed fixed and which constraint becomes binding.

sections.title: Variance does not specify the tail
sections.text:
Two payoff distributions can have the same mean and variance but different probabilities of severe loss. A normal approximation may miss jumps or a mixture with rare large negative outcomes. State the distributional assumption before turning a standard deviation into a tail-loss probability.

Even a numerical quantile does not describe how bad losses beyond it can be. Liquidity can also disappear in precisely the state when reducing exposure is most valuable.

Ask about downside magnitude, timing, financing and feasible exits separately. No single variance estimate answers every risk question, and a narrow confidence interval for a mean does not guarantee a harmless payoff distribution.

sections.title: Hedges leave model and nonlinear risk
sections.text:
Offsetting a linear factor loading can reduce first-order exposure, but estimated hedge coefficients can be wrong and change over time. Nonlinear instruments also have curvature and sensitivity to other state variables.

A delta-neutral option position, for example, removes a local first derivative with respect to the underlying at the current state. It can retain gamma, volatility and time exposure. A hedge that is neutral now may not remain so after a price move.

A strong interview answer computes the specified combined risk, identifies what the model omits and tests the conclusion under changed assumptions. It does not call a portfolio safe merely because it contains many positions or has a positive mean.

lessons.example: For the equal-weight, variance-four pair, covariance two gives variance three. If correlation rises from 0.5 to one while individual standard deviations also rise from two to three, the new covariance is nine and the portfolio variance is (\(\frac{1}{4}\))9+(\(\frac{1}{4}\))9+(\(\frac{1}{2}\))9=9. Standard deviation rises from sqrt(3) to three. Merely changing correlation at the old volatility would have predicted variance four and understated this joint stress. This is a scenario calculation, not an estimated probability that the scenario will occur.
lessons.check: Does positive expected value imply a trade should always be taken?
options: No; constraints, risk and costs matter
lessons.explanation: Expected value does not describe feasibility or the full distribution.
objectives: Calculate portfolio variance including covariance.
Stress correlations and identify shared exposures.
Distinguish a risk estimate from feasibility and tail-loss control.
optionLabels: No; constraints, risk and costs matter

lessons.title: The small mathematical-finance core
lessons.intro: Use payoff identities and local derivatives to understand the mathematical-finance essentials. Keep exercise style, financing and the meaning of each sensitivity explicit.

sections.title: Write the terminal payoff first
sections.text:
A European call with strike K and maturity T pays max(S_T-K,0), where S_T is the underlying price at maturity. A European put with the same strike and maturity pays max(K-S_T,0). European exercise means the payoff is determined at maturity; early exercise is not an available action.

Subtracting put payoff from call payoff gives S_T-K in both cases: if S_T≥K, the call contributes S_T-K and the put zero; if S_T<K, the call is zero and subtracting the put gives -(K-S_T).

This identity is exact at maturity. It is not an approximation and does not require knowing a volatility or a probability distribution.

sections.title: Replicate the difference today
sections.text:
Assume a non-dividend-paying underlying, a constant continuously compounded risk-free rate r, and frictionless trading with borrowing, lending and shorting available. Holding one unit of underlying and borrowing \(Ke^{-rT}\) today produces terminal value S_T-K, because the debt grows to K.

The call-minus-put portfolio has the same terminal payoff, so no-arbitrage implies
\[C-P=S_0-Ke^{-rT}.\]
Here C and P are current option prices and S_0 is the current underlying price. If equal payoffs had different prices under these assumptions, buying the cheaper portfolio and selling the more expensive one would create a price discrepancy with offsetting terminal payoffs.

Costs and trading constraints can prevent the idealised arbitrage trade. State them before interpreting a small observed discrepancy.

sections.title: Check the assumptions and direction
sections.text:
At S_0=100, \(K=100\) and \(r=0\), parity gives C-P=0. It states that call and put prices are equal for this setup, not that both options cost zero. Each can have positive value because its payoff is nonnegative and uncertain.

A known dividend changes the underlying replication's cash flows. American exercise introduces an early-exercise right, so the same European equality cannot simply be reused. Different strikes or maturities also destroy the matched payoff identity.

For an interview, derive the two terminal cases first. Then identify the portfolio replicating their difference and discount the deterministic debt. This is more robust than recalling a formula with an uncertain sign.

sections.title: Define local sensitivities
sections.text:
Let V(S,t) be the current value of a smooth instrument as a function of underlying price S and calendar time t, holding other model inputs fixed. Define delta as \(\Delta=\partial V/\partial S\), gamma as \(\Gamma=\partial^2V/\partial S^2\), and theta as \(\Theta=\partial V/\partial t\).

Delta describes the local linear response to price. Gamma describes the change in that slope as price changes. Theta describes the response to passing calendar time with the other inputs held fixed.

If a model instead uses time remaining tau=T-t, its derivative with respect to tau has the opposite sign to calendar-time theta. Specify which clock you differentiate before assigning a sign.

sections.title: Use a Taylor expansion carefully
sections.text:
For small changes, a common approximation keeps second order in price and first order in time:
\[\delta V\approx\Delta\,\delta S+\tfrac12\Gamma(\delta S)^2+\Theta\,\delta t.\]
This deliberately drops higher price terms, time curvature and cross terms. It is not an exact full second-order expansion in every variable. Volatility and rate changes require additional sensitivities when they occur.

At delta zero, gamma 0.08 and a price move of five, with no time or other input change, the retained gamma term is (\(\frac{1}{2}\))×0.08×25=1. Reversing the sign of the price move leaves that term unchanged because it is squared.

sections.title: Neutrality is local and variable-specific
sections.text:
Delta-neutral means the combined first derivative with respect to S is zero at the current state. It does not make gamma zero, remove time exposure or fix the response to volatility. After S changes, delta itself generally changes approximately by gamma times the price move.

A finite move can also make the Taylor approximation inaccurate, especially near a discontinuity or when omitted derivatives are large. Compare with full model repricing when available, and identify the step size over which the approximation is reasonable.

Greeks depend on the pricing model and its state inputs. A derivative calculated correctly inside a misspecified model can still misdescribe realised exposure.

sections.title: Check units, net positions and payoff logic
sections.text:
For an option value measured in currency and an underlying price in currency per unit, delta has units of underlying quantity, and gamma has units that make gamma times squared price change a currency amount. Theta must match the time unit: a per-year theta cannot be multiplied directly by a number of days.

Sum sensitivities across positions with their signed quantities before calling the portfolio neutral. Buying and selling identical contracts offset exposures; different strikes or maturities can offset one derivative while retaining others.

The small core is payoff replication plus explicit local approximations. These tools help you reason about a changed contract or assumption without memorising product trivia.

lessons.example: Suppose a portfolio has delta 0.4, gamma 0.08 and theta -0.2 per day. For an underlying increase of five over one day, holding other inputs fixed, the retained approximation is 0.4×5+(\(\frac{1}{2}\))×0.08×25-0.2×1=2.8. For a decrease of five it is -2+1-0.2=-1.2. The gamma contribution is one in both directions; the delta contribution changes sign. These are approximate value changes using sensitivities at the initial state, not guaranteed realised profits.
lessons.check: Which term captures curvature in the underlying price?
lessons.explanation: Gamma is the second derivative with respect to the underlying.
objectives: Derive European put-call parity from terminal payoffs.
Interpret delta, gamma and theta with correct variables and units.
Explain why local neutrality does not remove all risk.

lessons.title: Strategic inference and calibration
lessons.intro: Condition on the other side’s decision, and evaluate forecasts with a loss that matches the task. Winning, confidence and numerical precision can each hide a selection problem.

sections.title: Common value and private value differ
sections.text:
In a common-value auction, the eventual object value V is shared across bidders but initially uncertain. Each bidder receives a noisy private signal about it. The highest estimate can win partly because it contains an unusually favourable error.

In a private-value model, bidders instead have their own values for the object. Other bidders' low valuations do not necessarily mean your own consumption value is low. Strategic bidding still matters, but the information problem differs.

Specify which model applies, what signals reveal, how bids relate to signals, and the auction format. There is no single correct bid formula for every auction or every noisy estimate.

sections.title: Winning is an additional observation
sections.text:
Suppose m≥2 bidders observe signals s_i=V+epsilon_i, where the noises are independent of V and of each other, have a continuous cumulative distribution F, and higher signals lead to higher bids. Ignore reserves and ties. Conditional on your signal s and value v, you win when all other noises are below s-v.

Consequently,
\[P(\text{win}\mid V=v,s_i=s)=F(s-v)^{m-1}.\]
For a fixed s, this likelihood decreases as v increases. A high true value would make the other bidders' signals high too, making it less likely that your observed s beats all of them.

Conditioning on your signal alone omits this information from the winning event.

sections.title: Write the posterior correction
sections.text:
When the prior and noise have densities, the posterior after observing signal s and winning is proportional to
\[f_V(v)f_\varepsilon(s-v)F(s-v)^{m-1}.\]
The first two factors describe inference from your signal alone. The extra winning factor gives relatively more weight to smaller common values under this model. Normalise the product before taking its expected value.

This explains the winner's-curse correction: evaluate value conditional on both your signal and winning, rather than bidding from the signal-only estimate. It does not by itself solve strategic equilibrium bidding. Payment rules, competitors' strategies and your objective are additional parts of that problem.

sections.title: Forecast probabilities rather than certainty
sections.text:
A probability forecast p describes an uncertain binary outcome Y∈{0,1}. A forecast of 0.7 does not mean each event will succeed or that an observed failure proves the forecast wrong. Over many comparable events with that forecast, a calibrated forecaster should see a success rate near 0.7, allowing for sampling variability.

Calibration compares predicted probabilities with observed frequencies. It is different from sharpness: how much forecasts vary away from the base rate. A constant base-rate forecast may be calibrated while failing to distinguish easier from harder cases.

Assess groups of forecasts with sufficient data, a defined population and honest evaluation timestamps. Repeated outcomes about the same event do not create independent calibration observations.

sections.title: Derive the Brier score
sections.text:
For one binary outcome, the Brier loss is (p-Y)². For n forecasts, the score is their average loss; lower is better. If the true conditional success probability is q, expected loss is
\[q(1-p)^2+(1-q)p^2=(p-q)^2+q(1-q).\]
The second term is irreducible uncertainty at that information set. The first is minimised by reporting p=q. Thus this loss rewards an honest probability under the model rather than an artificially confident zero or one.

This expectation result does not say the honest forecast beats every other forecast on every realised event. A single realised outcome can make an overconfident lucky prediction look better.

sections.title: Evaluate out of sample with the right context
sections.text:
Suppose ten comparable forecasts are all 0.7 and seven outcomes succeed. Each success contributes 0.09 and each failure 0.49, so the average Brier score is (7×0.09+3×0.49)/10=0.21.

That group matches the advertised frequency exactly, but ten events are too few to establish precise long-run calibration. Compare with a meaningful base-rate forecast and evaluate on data not used to adjust probabilities. If the sample base rate is estimated from those same ten outcomes, recognise that this baseline used evaluation information.

A score aggregates performance. Inspect reliability by probability range and whether the forecasts distinguish subgroups without selecting favourable bins after looking at the outcomes.

sections.title: Use an error scale that matches the quantity
sections.text:
For a positive quantity y and positive estimate x, absolute log-ratio error |log(x/y)| treats multiplication by two and division by two symmetrically: both have error log(2). Ordinary absolute error gives very different penalties depending on the unit and magnitude.

This can suit order-of-magnitude estimates, but it is undefined at zero and penalises near-zero values strongly. Choose the loss because of the task, not because it makes a chosen estimate look good. A range with stated assumptions is often more informative than a highly precise unsupported number.

Across auctions and forecasts, the recurring discipline is the same: identify the information used, model how observations were selected and score the conclusion with an explicit objective.

lessons.example: For a binary common value V∈{0,100} with equal prior weights, imagine your signal has equal likelihood under both values. Before considering the win, your posterior is still one half each. Suppose the probability of winning conditional on that signal is 0.8 when V=0 and 0.2 when V=100. After winning, the unnormalised weights are 0.4 and 0.1, so the high-value posterior is \(\frac{0.1}{0.5}\)=0.2 and conditional expected value is 20. This deliberately specified likelihood example shows why a signal-only value of 50 can be too high. Computing an actual bid also requires the auction's payment and strategic rules.
